Bill No. 207, for the relief of William Ewan Laurie.-Mr. Baker.
Bill No. 208, for the relief of Margaret Van Dusen.-Mr. Schaffner.
On the Orders of the Day being called:
Has a survey party been sent by the Government to locate a line of railway between St. Peter's and Sydney, as stated in the newspapers?
There are some survey parties at work along the line of the Intercolonial, but I cannot say at the moment if there is a party in the locality mentioned.
This survey is not along the line of the Intercolonial; it is for the purpose of locating a new line between St. Peter's and Sydney.
I will make inquiry.

Bill No. 291, to amend the St. John and Quebec Railway Act-Hon. J. D. Reid (acting Minister of Railways and Canals)
read the third time and passed.
Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works) moved .second reading of Bill No. 205, to amend the Dry-docks Subsidies Act, 1910.

Should this Bill become law, will it apply to dry-docks in regard to which contracts have been entered into, but in respect to which work has not yet been undertaken? Some considerable time ago a contract was entered into for a dry-dock at Vancouver, but no work has been undertaken with the exception of acquiring the site, which was done when I was minister.

This amendment to the Act will not apply to any contract that has been let. In the case of Vancouver no contract has been let, and those who had prospected doing the work some years ago, apparently have failed in their endeavour. I do not know whether they will apply under the present amended Act. At all events the amendment would not apply to dry-docks where contracts have already been let.

Motion agreed to, and Bi1! :ead the second time.
The House then went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:
May I ask the Minister of Public Works how much money has been paid out since 1910 in connection with the Act of that year?
I do not appear to have the figures as to the amounts paid out since 1910, but I can get them for my hon. friend if he desires to see them.

If my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works intends that this Bill shall not apply to ports where contracts have been entered into for the construction of dry-docks, I consider that this section, if passed, will not carry out his view, because it provides that paragraph (a) of section 8 of the Dry-docks Subsidies Act of 1910 is repealed. Therefore, when this Bill passes, there will be no law except it in existence under which subsidies can be paid, because the previous Act which authorizes the Governor in Council to make payment of a subsidy of 3J per cent is repealed, and this will be the law providing for a. subsidy at the rate of 4 per cent. I do not complain in regard to the matter; I am inclined to think it better that it should be so, because even Governments to-day are obliged to pay 4 per cent for money; and in the case of docks which have not yet been actually undertaken

4 per cent is a reasonable rate of interest, when we bear in mind that the principal is not guaranteed and that the subsidy is only for a limited time.
I think my hon. friend is rather in error in regard to this matter. Paragraph (a) refers to subsidies on dry-docks of the first class.
I am spea,king now of dry-docks of the first class.
It does not apply to any of the others, and I do not think it will have the effect stated by my hon. friend, and it is not intended that it should have that effect.

Would not that necessarily be the effect as to dry-docks of the first class? The moment you repeal a statute under which the Governor in Council has authority to pay money and substitute for that another statute, then all payments must be made under the substituted statute or not made at all.

Might I suggest that the minister or the Prime Minister give the House a short statement as to the meaning of this Bill and as to how much money it is proposed to expend under it? I do not think the members understand what is proposed to be done.

This Bill is introduced in order that the Government may be able to secure the construction of a first-class dry-dock at Vancouver. Under the old law, it was impossible to find any company willing to undertake the construction and financing of a dry-dock on a basis of a subsidy of 3i per cent, and this Bill is to increase the subsidy to 4 per cent. In view of the increased cost of money at the present time, my hon. friend will understand that it is very difficult, in fact, impossible to finance on a basis of 34 per cent. The Bill was intended to correct this condition of affairs so that we might be able to secure the construction of a dry-dock at Vancouver.

Why confine it to
Vancouver? There are points that I know of that might have consideration just as well as Vancouver. '
Once this Bill is passed, it will not be confined to Vancouver, but will apply to any other first-class dTy-docks that may be built in future in any part of Canada.

Has my hon/ friend
given consideration to the very urgent request made on behalf of the people of St. John for a change in the plan for the construction of a dry-dock at that port? The present contract, as my hon. friend is aware, provides for a dock only 900 feet in length. Since that contract has been entered into, there has been a very great advance in the construction of steamships, the tendency being to build larger ships. As the Government is aware, that view has been presented very strongly by the people of Quebec, and I believe the Government is now engaged in the construction of .a dry-dock, at the port of Quebec of a length of 1,100 or 1,150 feet. The people of St. John are strongly of the opinion that a dry-dock of the same length should be constructed at their port so as to be able to accommodate the largest steamships likely to cross, the Atlantic. If their request is acceded to and a new contract entered into for an enlarged dock, will this Bill, when it becomes law, apply to that enlarged dock as well as to docks which may be constructed at Vancouver and otheT places?

This matter was discussed when the resolution was introduced, and, as my hon. friend is aware, the people of St. John were anxious for the extension of the dry-dock at that port to a length of 1,100 feet. Application was made informally by the contractors who had in charge the work at that port, and we informed them that we were quite prepared to amend the contract to provide for a dry-dock 1,100 feet in length on the basis of the contract made for the 900 feet first-class dock. If the contractors are willing to come to an arrangement, we shall be very pleased to enter into a contract with them. I have word from Mr. Griffiths, who has that contract, that he will be on his way in a day or two to Canada, and this matter will be taken up with him when he arrives here. The Government will give it every consideration; and, if an arrangement can be come to with Mr. Griffiths the Government are prepared to be very reasonable in dealing with him with a view of supplying St. John as liberally as possible with a dry-dock of a larger dimension. I do not wish it, however, to be understood in the meantime that we would agree to the subsidy being fixed at four per cent, as the matter has not as yet been considered by the Government.

This Bill gives the
Governor in Council the authority to make the subsidy four per cent, if it is considered desirable to do so?
Yes, if the Government considers it desirable to do so.

I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works that, this being a general law, it should take in dry-docks of tire second and third classes as well as those of the first class. It is just as difficult for people to raise money or to float bonds for the purposes of one of these works as for the other. The effect of increasing the bonus to one class and not to the other will be to give a preference to the larger ports to the disadvantage of the smaller ports which in the future may try to secure dry-docks but which cannot maintain docks of the first class. I would suggest that the minister amend subsections a, b, and c of section 8 of the Act of 1910, in order to make this change applicable to all dry-docks.
There is another clause in the Act of 1910 which I would bring to the attention of the minister. It may be a matter concerning which I am not very well informed, but I know something of the company that proposed to build a dry-dock in the city of Sydney harbour. Section 3 of the Act reads:
The Governor in Council may, as an aid to the construction of any dry-dock, authorize the payment out of any unappropriated money.
When the promoters of a dry-dock go into the market for money, those who are asked to advance the money will turn up the Act, and there they see this word ' unappropriated They ask:	What would
happen if at any time there were no 'unappropriated ' money forming part of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada? I understand this question has been actually raised by financiers who have been approached on the raising of money for dry-docks. They do not understand why the word ' unappropriated ' is there. The Act should be so worded that there could be no doubt about the Governor in Council giving this money at the rate of three and one-half per cent or four per cent, whatever it may be, when the dry-dock has been completed to the satisfaction of the minister and his engineers.

That is a point I have
never before heard raised, and so far as the department is aware the word in the statute to which the hon. gentleman calls attention has never caused any difficulty. It seems to me clear that the money must be paid out of the consolidated revenue, and, of course, out of money unappropriated.
fMr, Pugsiev.l

But the minister can
see the possibility of there being no ' unappropriated ' money in the consolidated revenue fund.

I was Minister of Public Works when the statute was framed, and it seemed to me then that we could not make it broader than it is. The Be-ceiver General is authorized to make these payments out of any funds that may be available, and I do not know any language which could more completely assure its being paid. Of course, Parliament could not declare that it should be paid out of any part of the revenues, for if money . were appropriated for other purposes it would have to be paid for those purposes. But when it is provided that the money shall be paid out of the unappropriated portion of the revenue, I think that is the widest power that could be given.
I agree entirely with my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) that it is desirable that if the rate of interest is to be changed it should be changed in respect of any dry-dock the building of which the Governor in Council may think it desirable to encourage. Quite a number of years ago, when the Government undertook to aid the construction of dry-docks, the rate of interest was put at 3 per cent. That was afterwards found to be too low, and it was increased to 34 per cent. Then, that rate was found to be too low, except for two or three places, like Port Arthur and Toronto. It has been found difficult to finance these undertakings under present legislation. The Minister of Public Works knows that the Government guarantee on railway bonds a few years ago was 3 per cent, and bonds so guaranteed could he sold nearly at par. But with the increased demand for money and extended opportunities for investment, the rate of interest has gone up, and to-day bonds guaranteed by the Government and bearing 4 per cent will mot bring very much more than 3 per cent guaranteed bonds would bring a few years ago. If the Minister of Public Works sincerely desires to encourage dry-docks, ought not he to take the bull by the horns and make the general guarantee 4 per cent? He knows that in the case of Halifax and Quebec, dry-docks could not be constructed unless the guarantee were 4 per cent, and in order to get over the difficulty the Government has determined to build the dry-dock at Halifax, I believe, to the length

of 1,100 feet, also the dry-dock at Quebec and the diy-dock at Victoria. So far as St. John, Vancouver, Sydney and many other places in Canada are concerned, where it would be of advantage to have dry-docks, it is left to private enterprise to finance the undertakings. If it is to be left to private enterprise, the terms ought to be made liberal enough to make the work of the promoters possible:	.

There is some force in
what is said with reference to the extension of the subsidy of 4 per cent to second and third-class docks. But we have no application or request far these in the department iat Jthe present time. Should such an application be made and should it be found impossible to secure the docks on a basis >at 3i per cent, I should be glad to come down to the House again and ask for further extension.

I rather agree with
the remarks of the hon. membeir for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) that the guarantee of 4 per cent should not only apply to dry-docks of the first-class but to those of the second and the third-class as well. A dry-dock which answers the purposes designed and costs only $1,500,000 ought to receive a guarantee at the same rate of interest as a more expensive dock. Take, for example, the dry-dock on the inland lakes; it is not fair to compel us to build a dry-dock there which is more than sufficient for the requirements of the traffic simply to enable us to get the four per cent rate. Two years ago when the town of Owen Sound granted a bonus of $100,900 for the purpose of constructing a dry-dock in that town, the plans for which were approved and entirely satisfactory to the Department of Public Works, owing to financial difficulties, one of which was the low rate of interest, the proposition fell through. We have stuck to the project and we are submitting another by-law on June 6 under which the town of Owen Sound will give a straight cash subsidy of $10,000 a year for twenty years. I think that if we are willing to go down into our pockets for that amount in order to build a dry-dock which will cost in the neighbourhood of one and one-half million dollars, we are entitled to as much as the other dry-docks, a subsidy of four per cent. I do not see any just reason why the cheaper*class of dry-docks, provided they answer all the purposes for which they are intended, should not be
entitled to the same rate of interest as the larger dry-docks, which are more easily financed and which, in my humble opinion, would be financed even more readily at three and a-half per cent than at four per cent. A first-class dry-dock receives a four per cent rate, a third-class dry-dock receives only a three per cent rate, while the intermediate class receives a three and a-half per cent rate. I think that that is more than an injustice to the poorer class of dry-dock which does not receive the same rate as the others. If the dry-dock were not answering the purposes for which it was intended, that would be an argument against the granting of the four per cent rate, but when it is fulfilling all its purposes I think that it is entitled to the same rate of interest as is granted to the first-class dry-dock. I have not had time to speak to the minister personally on the subject; I received only this morning a letter from Owen Sound asking me to urge this matter on the Government.

To meet the suggestions
made, I beg to move:
That a new section be added as section 3, as follows:
The second section of this Act shall not apply to any agreement heretofore entered into between His Majesty and any incorporated company under the Dry-dock Subsidies Act, 1910, and paragraph (a) of section 8 of the said Act shall remain in full force and effect for the purpose of every such agreement and with respect to every matter and thing connected therewith.

I think my hon. friend will agree that this matter ought to stand. The amendment proposes to change altogether the recommendation which His Royal Highness made to Parliament, which was that paragraph (a) of the section be repealed altogether and that a new law be passed providing for the rate of subsidy at four per cent. My hon. friend proposes entirely to change the resolution and still to keep the old Act in force as to contracts which have already been entered into. Apart from the merits of the ease, I think that if this new section were to be introduced the committee would have to rise and a new resolution be submitted to the House. I do think that my hon. friend ought to be reasonable with regard to aid to dry-docks. We know that when Mr. Monk was Minister of Public Works he wanted to assist dry-docks. When the hon. member for Ar-genteuil (Mr. Perley), was acting for him, I urged upon him that this change in the rate of interest should be made in order to make it possible for the people of Owen

Sound-a very enterprising town, where it has been felt- for a long time that a dry-dock ought to be constructed-the people, of Sydney, the people of Quebec, of Halifax, of Vancouver and of other places, have dry-docks. Instead of accepting my suggestion, he left the rate of interest as it was and provided that there might be paid this subsidy upon a largely increased cost. I pointed out to him that that would not do any good; that the only way in which the increased bonus could be got would be by having the dock nominally cost a great deal more than it actually does cost and that, therefore, it was utterly absurd to make such a change. The hen. member for Argenteuil will remember my having brought his attention to that point. Notwithstanding that, the Government insisted on pushing the Bill through. It had no good result whatever; nothing was accomplished by it. Speaking of docks of the second-class, the dry-dock at Port Arthur is of the second-class, and no dry-dock ever built in Canada has done better work for the country than the one at Port Arthur. Not long ago there was turned out from the shipyard there in connection with the dry-dock one of the most magnificent freight carriers that is to be found in any country, the Grant Morden, a vessel of large capacity, splendidly built, the pride of the people of Canada. In order to secure the construction of a dry-dock there-it was my great pleasure to turn the first sod when I was Minister of Public Works-it became necessary for the people of Port Arthur to make a very large contribution toward the work; I think they furnished a site as well. Works of this kind are of a national character, and the people of the community should not be called upon to impose any burdens upon themselves in order to secure their construction. In the case of Owen Sound, I am quite familiar with all that the hon. member for North Grey has said. Application was made to me when I was minister; I am inclined to think that the contract was actually entered into; at any rate, the town of Owen Sound was prepared to do everything possible to assist in the work. But if a dry-dock at Owen Sound, in connection with the shipping upon the Great Lakes, which is of enormous importance and of enormous magnitude, is as important in respect of Canadian trade as a dry-dock at an ocean port, why should the rate of interest in respect of a dock upon the Great Lakes be 3 per cent, and the rate of interest upon a dock at Vancouver be 4 per cent? What reason can be suggested [ Mr. Pugsley,]
for it, unless it be that the hon. member for Vancouver has more influence with the Government and has been more wideawake in this matter than the hon. member for North Grey? No other reason can possibly be suggested.
I am opposed to this amendment also upon the ground that it is an injustice to the people of St. John. The hon. Minister of Public Works knows very well that there is a contract for a dry-dock at that port in connection with other harbour work of great magnitude and of exceedingly great difficulty. No substantial progress has yet been made in the construction of a dry-dock. When the contract was entered into the people of St. John were asked to put their hands in their pockets and assist the work, and they were willing to do so. They were then put upon the same footing as Quebec, as Halifax and as Victoria. But since that time the Government have chosen to take hold of the dry-docks at these three ports as Government works, and propose to construct them out of the public moneys of Canada. The Government, therefore, will be able to manage those dry-docks and to make the rate for the repairs of vessels just as low as they may think desirable in order to encourage shipbuilding and ship repairing at those ports. But in the case of St. John, the shipping which occupies the dry-dock-and it will be the same at Vancouver and at the ports on the Great Lakes-will be called upon to bear the burden of the necessary interest in order to keep good the securities which will have to be issued upon these docks. These ports are being placed in an unfair position, particularly the port of St. John. The people of St. John find that today the Government are not only taking hold of these docks at other ports as Government works, but are proposing to make them 1,100 or 1,150 feet in length. At St. John the contract is for 900 feet. The people there want it to be 1,150 feet. A contract has been entered into with a company for the construction of a dock of the smaller size, and my hon. friend is now asking the committee to adopt an amendment which will tie his hands in respect to the dry-dock at St. John and compel him to say to the people of St. John: Parliament has tied my hands; I cannot increase the subsidy beyond three and one-half per cent, what it is today; even although I can do so in regard to Vancouver or Sydney, I cannot give you further assistance.* There has been very great delay in connection with the construction of the dry-dock at St. John and with

other work with which the Government has to do in connection with railway terminals at Courtenay bay. I am not going to speak about that, but there has been great and inexcusable delay. Now, my hon. friend, knowing that the people of St. John will come to him and ask the same measure of justice as is being meted out to other cities, and that interest up to four per cent should be given for an enlarged dock, asks the committee to tie his hands so that even if the Government may think it desirable to give four per cent he will be able to say that his hands are tied and he cannot give more than three and one-half per cent. Let me appeal to the sense of reason and fair play of my hon. friend. Let him not treat St. John with a less measure of justice than he treats other places. It is true that St. John is not represented by a supporter of the Government, so far as the city is concerned; but my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) occupies the position of representative of the city of St. John and the county of St. John as well. So far as the people of the city are concerned, he is my colleague; he represents a somewhat different constituency to what I do because he takes in the parishes of the county as well. I want him to speak on this question. I want my hon. friend to intercede with the Minister of Public Works and ask that this matter shall stand over for a little so that a consultation may be had and so that the hands of the Government may be left free to give the same assistance to the dry-dock at St. John as it is proposed to give at Vancouver, in order that that work may be completed without delay. The people of St. John are getting very discouraged at the delay in undertaking this dry-dock. They are beginning to blame the Minister of Marine. They ought not to blame him, because I do not believe that the delay is his fault. The delay is due to his colleagues who override him and with whom he does not seem to have that influence which one of the ability and the long political experience and the high standing of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ought to have. I do appeal to my hon. friend now, when this matter is before the committee, to appeal to the Minister of Public Works and endeavour to have this Bill so framed that my hon. friend will be able to go to him and ask him to enlarge this dock to 1,150 feet, making it the same length as the dry-docks at Halifax and Quebec are to be. made, and as I presume the dry-dock at Vancouver is to be made, because the people of that city will not be content with anything less. Let my hon. friend have this legislation so framed that the Minister of Public Works will be free to accede to the demands of the people of St. John and to his demand, and that the work of constructing this dry-dock upon the enlarged scale to which a port of the great importance of St. John is entitled may be speedily undertaken.

speechtext:
As far as my hon.
friend's point of order is concerned, it does not seem to me that there is anything in it, for two very plain reasons. In the first place, this amendment does not increase the burden upon the public treasury; according to my hon. friend's argument, it diminishes that burden. In the next place, it does not change the appropriation of the money. Therefore, I can see absolutely nothing in the point of order which my hon. friend has raised. So far as docks of the second and third class are concerned, there is a great deal in what my hon. friend from North Grey has suggested. But, as pointed out by the Minister of Public Works, there is not at the present time before the department any application in respect of either the one or the other class.
What sort of dry-dock is to be constructed at the .harbour of Sydney by the Canadian Shipbuilding Company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am pointing out the
observation made by the Minister of Public Works; I am not familiar with the details of these several applications. If any application of that kind should be made to the Government, it would be a very appropriate thing for the Minister of Public Works to take into consideration a further amendment of the statute. He has already stated that such a proposal would receive his favourable consideration, but he does not think it desirable, at this stage of the session, to bring down a further resolution in view of the fact that applications of that character are not pending.
So far as the city of St. John is concerned, I think that the contract was entered into upon tenders called for by the hon. member from the city of St. John; in those tenders, as I understand, the dimensions of the dock were fixed. His present observations are therefore a reflection on his own conduct as Minister of Public Works, because, according to his own statement, he did not take sufficiently into con-

sideration the legitimate demands of the port of St. John. I would therefore be inclined to regard the observations of my hon. friend as either critical of his own conduct or as apologetic for it. The present Admih-istration has made a contract, if I remember correctly, upon the very tenders which the hon. gentleman called for. Up to the present time I am not aware of any application to vary the terms of that contract. It is possible that there may have been some application of which I am not aware, but none has come to my personal attention. If my hon. friend will bear these considerations in mind, I think he will come to the conclusion that if there is any blame in the matter it is blame attributable solely to his own conduct.

I regret very much that my right hon. friend has the habit, of always, or nearly always, trying to justify some shortcomings of himself and his colleagues by reference to what the previous Government did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was saying it was a
shortcoming of my hon. friend.

As an excuse for the
shortcomings of the hon. gentlemen opposite. That is no excuse. Suppose that, three or four years ago, I thought a dry-dock of 900 feet would be ample for the purposes of any of the ports of Canada, and suppose that since that time public opinion upon this subject had materially changed, would it not be reasonable that a change should be made if the attention of the Government was called to the changed condition? Matters move very rapidly in Canada. When I was present at the ceremonial of turning the first sod for the dry-dock at Port Arthur, if anybody had told me that at such an early date as this they would be engaged in shipbuilding and turning out magnificent steamships from that shipyard, I would scarcely have believed it possible. It has been possible, they buili the dry-dock in a marvellously short space of time, and I believe that they want additional accommodation. Take Col-lingwood, it was thought a few years ago that one dry-dock would be sufficient; but even before I left the position of Minister of Public Works I was called upon to enter into a contract for a second dry-dock there in order to accommodate the vessels which come to that port. My right hon. friend suggests that when I called for ten-

ders for a dry-dock at St. John, we had under consideration the building of dry-docks at Quebec and at Vancouver, and that 900 feet was considered the limit of length that would be required in a dry-dock. Nine hundred feet was considered the ultimate length to which these docks would ha-ve to be built. When this Government undertook to deal wfith dry docks they properly decided that, as far as Quebec and Halifax were concerned, docks should be 1,150 feet in length. Why should they have not so decided for St. John as well? Why should St. John be discriminated against? Why should it be said that there should be dry docks of greater length in these other ports and that yet, as far as St. John is concerned, the length of the dry-dock there should be that which three or four years ago was considered quite sufficient? My right hon. friend says that he has not heard of any request from St. John to change the length of the dry-dock. That is making a very strong indictment against my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that the people of St. John have requested that the length should be extended to 1,150 feet. It has been called to his attention, it has been reported in the public press, the board of trade has urged it, all the newspapers have urged it, and yet the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has not apparently thought it of sufficient importance to speak to the Prime Minister on the subject. I cannot conceive it possible that my hon. friend wmuld view the matter so lightly as that, and I think that the Prime Minister must have forgotten what has been said to him with regard to it. The matter is one which is felt by the people of St. John to be of the very greatest importance.
The point I take now is this. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that there is a contract for the harbour work at Courtenay bay, and that included in that contract is provision for a dry dock 900 feet in length. He knows perfectly well, and no one knows better than he, that the people of St. John feel very strongly, no matter how they may have felt four years ago, that, in view of the changed conditions, the dock should be extended to 1,150 feet. They are asking that the contract be changed. If, in the case of Vancouver, where there is a great deal of shipping, and where there will be a great deal of ship-repairing work to do, it is found necessary, in order to secure the construe-

tion of the work, to increase the rate of interest to 4 per cent, it surely will be equally desirable and necessary, in the case of the dry-dock at St. John, particularly in view of this change in the conditions, so that you may then have a dry-dock 1,150 feet in length. I ask in all sincerity: Why does the Minister of Public Works want to have his hands tied so that he cannot increase the rate of interest for a dry-dock at St. John the same as he is proposing to do at Vancouver and other ports where no contract has been entered into? No work on this dry-dock has actually been done, and it has not been determined as yet to extend it to 1,150 feet. I do not ask the Minister of Public Works to increase the rate to 4 per cent, but I ask him not to press this amendment. I appeal to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to urge him to leave the matter open, so that when an application of a more formal character comes before him, if he thinks it reasonable to increase the rate of interest the same as he can do in regard to Vancouver and other places, he will be able to do so, and he will not be able to say: Parliament, at my instance, and at the instance of the Government, it is true, has tied my hands, and I cannot give you additional assistance in the way of this increased rate to the extent of i per cent.
I ask that his hands be left free, that the hands of the Government be left free, so that they may take up this question of enlarging the dry-dock, and then, if it is found necessary, make the rate of interest 4 per cent. The Bill does not say that it shall be 4 per cent, but it only says that it shall not exceed 4 per cent; the present Act says that it shall not exceed 34 per cent. Surely it is only reasonable that it should be left discretionary with the Governor in Council to say what the rate of interest shall be.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friend fTom St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has succeeded in demonstrating anything in regard to the length of the dry-dock at St. John, it is that my hon. friend when Minister of Public Works did not possess a sufficiently comprehensive or wide vision to look ahead for a period of three or four years. My hon. friend from St. John now condemns his own action of three or four years ago in asking for the construction of a dry-dock at St. John which was to be 900 feet in length. His remarks prove that and nothing more. Now, I distinctly remember the speeches of the hon. gentleman and I
remember that he was pointing out in St. John that he had made provision for the construction of one of the finest dry-docks to be found anywhere in the civilized world-
So it was at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
-a dry dock, to use the
hon. gentleman's language on the public platform, which would serve the 12 noon, needs of St. John for twenty-five or thirty years. Therefore, the hon. gentleman's statement simply proves if it proves anything, that the hon. gentlemen had not a sufficiently wide	vision	to look	ahead a fewyears and to realize	what	changes
might come. The hon. gentleman knows better than any man in this House, because he was all through the negotiations, that the question of whether the interest to be paid on the expenditure in connection with the dry-dock at St. John was 3i or 4 per cent did not influence that transaction in the slightest degree. The dock is ostensibly and nominally being built under the provisions of the Dry-Dock Act, but neither at St. John nor anywhere else has a company been got to build a dry-dock under the Act without something else being connected therewith. Therefore, in asking for tenders for the construction of improvements at Courtenay bay my hon. friend gave it to be understood that, in addition to the work specified in the call for tenders, whoever got the contract for the work in Courtenay bay, would, in addition to the dredging, building of the breakwater and docks, also have to build a dry-dock under the provisions of the Dry Dock Act. But for the dry-dock having been connected with the harbour works, the dry-dock would not have been built under the provisions of the Dry-Dock Act. In making out their tenders for this work, and knowing that they had to construct a dry-dock as well as the other works that were called for, the tenderers only submitted figures for the work proposed up to date and these contractors now say that if they are called upon to extend the dry-dock by 200 feet they are not willing to do that under the provisions of the Dry-Dock Act. _,They say that whether the interest be 4 per, cent or not they should have the right to revise their whole figures because it was on the whole of the works that they tendered, that they did not offer to build the dry-dock as a separate work and that in making up their figures for the other work they were able to make provision for what it would cost to build the dry-dock

over and above the aid provided by the Dry-Docks Act. These matters have been considered by the contractor, Mr. Norton Griffiths, my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works and myself. We have had a number of interviews concerning the matter and the Minister of Public Works has expressly said, not only publicly but privately, that he is willing to enter into an agreement with Mr. Griffiths for the extension of the dry-dock to 1,150 feet instead of 900 feet on the same basis as he is now undertaking the other contracts. That is a matter for negotiation, which is being carried on. The last communication I had with Mr. Griffiths was that he would be here within a very short time, and would be prepared to take the matter up for consideration.
There is no doubt that a dock 900 feet long, as provided for by my hon. friend, is long enough for present purposes, and as stated by the hon. gentleman on the public platform it is one of the largest docks in the world. But having regard to the larger'ships that are now being built it would seem that though this dock may be sufficient-not for twenty-five or thirty years as stated by the hon. gentleman, but for a considerable period-it might be (better now to extend it to 1,100 feet rather than be called on in ten years or so to do it when it would cost relatively more than if done while the work is under construction. It is very desirable, if it can be done on proper terms, that the Minister of Public Works should undertake it. It should not be forgotten that the Minister of Public Works is hampered by the fact that the contract has been entered into and signed, that work has begun under that contract, that the breakwater is very largely constructed at Courtenay bay, and that considerable has been done on the dry-dock. The hon. gentleman says that very little progress has been made. I think he is mistaken in that. There has been considerable excavation of rock at the site of the dry-dock, and while that can still be easily extended without any great interference with the work, yet new arrangements have to be entered into, and I am in hopes that the Minister of Public Works will be able to (bring these agreements about. I have been working with that end in view. I do not believe that the question whether the interest under the Dry-dock Act is to be three and a half per cent or four per cent will influence this contract to any extent, because it has been made under other circumstances entirely apart from what would have been the case had the dock been built

under the provisions of the Dry-dock Act alone, and without any other contract being entered into at the same time.
I can afford to pass by in silence and contempt the statement made by my hon.
' friend that I have no influence with my colleagues in the Government. So far as my influence with my colleagues in the Government is concerned, I am quite prepared to put it side by side, looking at the results to our province, with the influence which the hon. member had with his colleagues in the Liberal Government. I shall say nothing further about that. I do not think the expression was worthy of my hon. friend, and I think he must regret having made it. At all events, it gives the impression to this House and to the country that in uttering such words the hon. gentleman is more desirous of making political capital against me than he is of assisting the constituency of the city of St. John.

I am sorry I offended
my hon. friend. My misfortune is that whenever I state facts with regard to my hon. friend's position and apparent ' influence in the Government, I am liable to offend him. I am sorry for that. The reason I made the statement was because we have had such abundant evidence that my hon. friend does not seem to have the influence with his colleagues which he ought to have and which I think he is entitled to have, not only by reason of his great ability and strong personality, but by reason of has representing a constituency of the importance of St. John. My hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) contrasts his influence with his colleagues with my own, but of course, the public must judge as to that.
It would not do for me to say as to whether or not I had much influence with my colleagues, but we have this evidence to-day from the mouth of my hon. friend, that in the case of the improvements at Courtenay bay, even although the contract was not let until he came into office, he simply followed out to the letter what I, as Minister of Public Works, had planned and arranged for when the late Government was in power. That shows, at all events, that I must have had some little influence so far as my constituency is concerned. If my hon. friend will take other matters, such as the drill hall at St. John, the new post office, the wharves on the west side of the harbour, he will find that	all these works	are simply
being carried out as planned and laid down

by the late Government, when I was Minister of Public Works, and that appropriations had actually been made by Parliament for them then. If it were not that my hon. friend had the trail blazed for him, he would not have done much for the constituency he represents. He has nothing at all to which he can point with any degree of pride except work he has been carrying out in the way of completing what had been organized by the late Government.
My hon. friend says that I had called for tenders for a dock of 900 feet in length, and that therefore this Government is in no way responsible if it is too small to meet the requirements of the future. That is no excuse, because although I had called for tenders the present Government entered into the contract after they came into office. They were not obliged to do it, and they could have called for new tenders. My hon. friend knows very well that if he had not been able to say to his colleagues: you must do what the Liberal Government has planned out with regard to the port St. John, he could not have accomplished what had been planned for him and the carrying out of which had been made so easy for him. Does my hon. friend approve of extending the dry-docks to 1,150 feet or does he not? The people of St. John want to know this as they want to know about the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement. Since my hon. friend says I insult him when I say he has no influence with the Government, let me ask him if he was an approving party to that Gutelius-Bosworth agreement. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that at the last session of Parliament the Postmaster General asked this Parliament for an appropriation of $1,000,000 for the purpose of providing for an Atlantic steamship service, and he said that amount would be divided between six fast steamers, I think: the Calgarian, the Alsatian, the two Empresses, and the two ships of the Royal Line. The Postmaster General said then that there would be an open door, that iSt. John and Halifax would be placed upon an equality, that there would be no preference given either port and that the Government would see to it that each port should be given absolutely fair play. The people of St, John relied with confidence upon that assurance and believed that they would get fair play. That went on until the time came for the steamship lines to chose the ports for their winter service, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, through their officials, had a list of sailings published which showed that the Empresses
were to come to the port of St. John last winter. Tenders were called for from the grocers of St. John to supply these steamers, and the longshoremen were expecting the work to come to them as in previous years. But all at once came an announcement that the programme had been changed-that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had not previously been able to make a satisfactory arrangement for the bringing of freight and passengers over the Intercolonial railway between Halifax and St. John, but that they had now made an arrangement and were going to have the steamers stop at the port of Halifax. The result of that arrangement was that, during the present year, of the mail steamers, the Empresses and faster steamers of the Allan liners stopped at the port of Halifax. There was great indignation on the part of the people of St. John when they learned of that larrangement some weeks before it was -to go into effect; and they called upon my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as their representative, to prevent that contract from going into effect. They were told that it had not yet been signed by the Minister of Railways, and that therefore it had not at that time received the sanction of the Government. They pressed in the strongest way possible my hon. friend to secure justice and fair-play for the port of St. John. Did my hon. friend do so? He did not. Had he influence with his colleagues which would have enabled him to do justice? He in effect says that he had. He in effect tells this committee that they may well believe that he is a gentleman of large influence with his colleagues, and that therefore he can get whatever in reason he may ask of them. Did he ask them not to allow that contract to go into force, which my hon. friend must have believed to be a discrimination of the very worst character against the port of St. John? Did he ask his colleagues to prevent that outrage from being perpetrated against the port of St. John? I belive that he must have done so. If he had that great influence, which he wants us bo believe he had then and has now with his colleagues-and I would really like to see him have all the influence possible, because he would then be able to do good for the port of fit. John-to induce them to do what he thought reasonable and fair, then the only inference is that he did not seek to bring any influence to bear upon the Government, and that this contract was entered into and carried into effect with the full approval of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

I have not been able to be present very much during this session of Parliament; but I have watched the newspapers with interest in the hope that I might ascertain the views of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with regard to that contract, if he had any views upon the subject at all. He was challenged by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Gar-vell), to state his views with regard to it. I have not observed that he has done so. I venture to say that my hon. friend believed that that contract was discriminatory against the port of St. John, and that it was an outrage upon the people of that enterprising city. We in St. John want no discrimination against our sister port; of Halifax, whose enterprise and energy we admire; but we want and we demand fair play, and when we have a representative in the Government, we expect him to demand fair play and justice for the constituency which he represents. Yet my hon. friend wil not venture to tell this committee that that was a just and equitable contract so far as the port of St. John was concerned. He knows it was not; he knows it was discriminatory; he knows that, after the Postmaster General said that the doors should be opened and that mo favouritism should be shown to either port, the Government, of which he is a member, through the Department of Railways and Canals, acting through the general manager of the Government railways, made a bargain with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company which induced them to stop their steamers at the port of Halifax and to change the arrangement which they had consummated for bringing those steamers to the port of St. John. He knows that, under that arrangement, passengers and freight were carried between the city of Halifax and the city of St. John at one-fifth, or perhaps even less than that, of the usual charges against the ordinary shipper of freight over that railway and against the ordinary passenger using that railway. I challenge my hon. friend to state to-day that that was a reasonable and fair contract; that it did not discriminate against the port of St. John. My hon. friend surely cannot say, what he said to the people of St. John as long ago as October last, namely, that he had not looked into the matter and that he could not say whether or not it was discriminatory, because it was his duty as a representative 
of the city of St. John to look into the matter carefully and ascertain whether or not it was discriminatory. If my hon. friend thought it was discriminatory-and he knew of the matter weeks before the arrangement came into force-then he must accept either one or the other of these two positions. He must say either that, knowing of this contract which was unfair and discriminatory and unjust to his constituents, he did not intercede with his colleagues in order to prevent it from going into effect, or that he did intercede bub that he had not influence enough with his colleagues to prevent this injustice from being consummated. If my hon. friend has the great influence with his colleagues which he in effect says he has, which I would like to see him have, it cannot be that he interceded unsuccessfully. Therefore we are driven to the other alternative, that my hon. friend, knowing of this contract weeks before it went into effect, and knowing its injustice and discriminatory character against the port of St. John, did not think it worth while to go to the trouble of interceding with his colleagues. I do not know which to believe. I hate to say that my hon. friend has not the influence, in view of what he has told the committee; and I hate to think for a moment that my hon. friend, knowing that this blow was about to fall upon the constituency which he represents, would not go to the trouble of interviewing his colleagues and pointing out clearly to them the discriminatory nature of the contract and the injustice! which was being inflicted on the people of the city of St. .John by it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I ought perhaps to apologize to the committee for taking up their time in replying to the remarks of my hon. friend, considering that the committee are engaged in considering a Bill of very great importance, because it is possible that they are not very much interested in the political screed which has just been delivered by my hon. friend for simply one purpose, namely, to attempt to make party capital in the constituency from which we both come. I should have thought, did I not know the hon. gentleman so well, that a parliamentarian of his experience and standing would not have thought it necessary to put into my mouth words and statements which I never used. Knowing him so well, however, I know that there is no more unfair opponent in debate anywhere ; and I am not surprised at his quoting

me as saying things which I did not say, and which a reference to ' Hansard,' in which my remarks will appear side by side with his, will make it abundantly clear that I have never said.
Now, the hon. gentleman has referred to what he has done for the constituency of St. John. In the city of St. John the hon. gentleman is known as ' the great promiser.' The hon. gentleman was very strong in promise, but very shy in fulfilment. He was especially strong in promise on the eve of a general election. Although he was for years in the Government, he can hardly point to a public work in St. John, with the exception of the armoury, on which work was commenced during the time he was in office. In 1908, before the elections, he came down to St. John with plans for building a great harbour in Courtenay bay. He stated that if he wa<s elected in 1908, within twelve months thereafter ships of ten thousand tons and over would be sailing into Courtenay bay. But when we came to the elections of 1911 not a single blow had been struck. If he possessed the influence he would have us believe he had, how was it he did not get the contract signed for Courtenay bay before the election? Everything shows us that it was owing to the fact that he could not persuade his colleagues to sign that contract. Everybody knows how anxious he was to start that work. Tenders had been received. Why was it, with his position and influence with his colleagues, that he was unable to get that contract entered into before the general elections of 1911? It had to wait until the present Government came into power; and judging by my hon. friend's record in promise and fulfilment, I have no doubt it would have waited many, many months and years if there had not been a change of government and if I had not come back as representative of the city and county of St. John. Let me tell him, when he talks of public opinion in St. John, that that is what public opinion in St. John believes.
What else did he do? He talks about the mail contracts and about protecting the interests of St. John. I should think he would be ashamed to refer, either in this Parliament or anywhere else, to the mail contract and his connection with it. During all the years when the hon. gentleman was in Parliament as minister of the Crown he never insisted upon having the port of St. John placed upon the same level as the port of Halifax as to the receiving and sending of mail. It was 259
not until after the present Administration came into power that a fair opportunity was given to St. John to handle mails, because under the contract entered into by my hon. friend's Government from year to year, the mails had to be taken on and had to be discharged at Halifax, St. John being made a sort of way-port, the vessels coming from Halifax to St. John, going back from St. John to Halifax, taking on the mails there and sailing with them across the water. Since the present Administration came into power, for the first time in the history of Canada and of St. John, the port of St, John has been placed in an equal position with Halifax so far as carrying the mails is concerned. Last winter we had regular sailings into and out of the port of St. John, carrying the mails inward and taking the mails from Canada across the Atlantic. Had the hon. gentleman remained in power, the old state of affairs would no doubt have continued, no choice being given to the contractors, they not being allowed the slightest discretion, but compelled by the Government and the contract made under the Government to take these mails at Halifax and to discharge the mails at Halifax. Therefore it is, that I say that I am astonished that my hon. friend, having regard to his own record in this matter, should have the temerity to bring this subject before the House to-day with a view to making capital out of it. He knows that last winter was the first opportunity the port of St. John has had to show whether it could compete with other great mail ports on the Atlantic or not. The hon. gentleman has referred to the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement. Again I am surprised at his temerity. What was the action of the Board of Trade of St. John in regard to that. They asked that the agreement should be referred to the Railway Commission of Canada to determine whether it was or was not a fair agreement from a railway standpoint or not, and whether it was discriminatory to the port of St. John or not. The Government acceded to that request at once. The Railway Commission of Canada has been willing at any time to take up that matter for consideration. The Board of Trade of St. John retained counsel, one of whom was my hon. and learned friend, to present their case before the Railway Commission. And-will you believe it, Mr. Chairman-though retained by the Board of Trade of St. John, from that day down to the present hour my hon. friend, whether acting under their directions or

not, I do not know, has never taken the matter before the railway commissioners with a view to having the determination of the commission upon it? Whether that agreement, from a railway standpoint, was a proper agreement or not, is not for me to say. That is to be determined by men who are experts in railway matters. I could very easily come to a conclusion with regard to the matter, but would my conclusion be of value? It is a question for railway experts, for men like the railway commissioners, whose business it is to deal with matters of this kind. Mr. Gutelius, the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, entered into an arrangement, not to give running rights to the Canadian Pacific railway over the Intercolonial railway, but to haul the Canadian Pacific railway cars over the tracks of the Intercolonial railway between St. John and Halifax at certain rates. Had these been two railway companies, one company or the other would have gone to the Railway Commission and asked that the terms should be imposed upon what rights of this sort might be given. That not being the position, an agreement was entered into between Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Bosworth as to rates. As I say, the Government is perfectly willing that this should be submitted to the Railway Commission, and yet there has been no authoritative finding on it up to the present time. But whether these rates were justifiable from a railway standpoint or not, whether they are high enough to give a proper profit to the Intercolonial railway or not, this fact remains, that they are far, far higher than the rates agreed upon by the Government of which my hon. friend was a member with the Canadian Northern railway for the hauling of traffic from the city of Quebec to the city of Halifax. The figures on that point have been given to this House time and time again, and it is not necessary for me to take up the time of the House in referring to them now.
I do not think it will be necessary for me to trespass further on the time of the House. I do not propose to enter into a controversy with my hon. friend as to whether he possessed more influence with the Government of which he was a member than I possess with the Government of which I am a member. I can only say that my relations with my colleagues have been of the most friendly character, and have always found my colleagues willing to pay attention to any suggestions I have

ever made. As to the result of any influence which he possessed and which I possess, apart from the larger question affecting the general policy of the country, that is a matter, I repeat, which I am willing to leave to our constituents and to fight out before them when the proper time comes. But I might refer to the fact that a few years ago he was interviewed by the merchants of the city of St. John, the city council and the board of trade to have conveyors constructed from the elevator of the Canadian Pacific railway to the wharfs of the harbour, so that there might be better facilities for handling grain in the port, and he was unable to accomplish what the people so anxiously wished in that direction. The matter was taken up with me again last year, and the result is that these conveyers have been constructed by the Government of Canada and very great facilities have thereby been added to the means by which grain can be handled in the port and harbour of St. John. As to my hon. friend's position, my reference to it was based not un my own authority but on the authority of a gentleman occupying a very high official position in the city of St. John, a gentleman recently elected again by the public to the high position which he occupies, and who made the statement in public before a large delegation when this matter was being considered.
Who is the gentleman?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The mayor of St. John, Mr. Frink. In view of those facts I think that my hon. friend should not try to enter into a discussion before this committee which can be neither edifying nor instructive to hon. members of the House, concerning matters which are largely of local import to our constituents. I. certainly would not have entered upon the discussion if my hon. friend had not done so. He himself brought it on by asserting that I had no influence with my colleagues in the Government. Having made the assertion himself, my hon. friend must not feel offended-and he spoke with a feeling and a passion that seldom characterizes his language in this House-must not be offended, I say, if I simply reply in kind. I repeat that he himself is responsible for bringing up this matter, which is one of merely local import and which we will both have an opportunity of discussing in the future before those to whom we are responsible for our seats in Parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the discussion is going far from the item under consideration.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that I have a right to reply briefly to what my hon. friend has said. My hon. friend is wrong in saying that this is purely a local matter; a matter of local interest. I think the question whether or not a department of the Government should discriminate against any one city or any one community or any one province in the operation or management of the Intercolonial railway, which is owned by the people of Canada, is a national matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that I did not refer to that as a local matter; what I referred to as a local matter was his charge that I did not possess as much influence with the Government of the country as the hon. gentleman did with his colleagues. My hon. friend is starting out by misrepresenting what I said.
I never stated that the hon. gentleman did not possess as much influence with his colleagues as I did with mine; it was the hon. gentleman himself who made the comparison.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is misrepresenting the facts again. I made no comparison; the hon. gentleman himself brought that subject before the committee.

My hon. friend has an
air of sincerity and truthfulness that is likely to impress those who observe him when he makes these assertions. But I wish to ask my hon. friend if, after I said that he 'does not seem to possess that influence with his colleagues which he ought to, he was not the first one to suggest that he would be willing to compare his influence with his colleagues with the influence which I had with my colleagues? It was the hon. gentleman himself who first sought to make the comparison. I am altogether too modest a man to suggest for a single moment that I had anything like the influence *with my colleagues that the hon. gentleman ought to be able to exercise, by reason of his commanding ability and his high standing in the Conservative party. My hon. friend says that I spoke with heat. I did, Mr. Chairman; I spoke with heat because of the indignation among the people of my constituency at the way in which they have been treated. Personally, I suppose it does not make any difference to me, except that I am a citizen of Canada, whether an in-259i
justice is meted out to any portion of the people of Canada or not; but I have to speak for my constituency, as representing the port of St. John, and I cannot help it if my hon. friend feels that something is getting him on the raw. It is my duty to speak for my constituency, and my hon. friend afforded me the first opportunity which I had of speaking about the Bosworth-Gutelius agreement. We are in this position that, after many months, my hon. friend rises in his place as a member of the Government and a representative of the constituency of St. John, and says that he really does not know whether or not that agreement was discriminatory against the port of St. John; that Mr. Gutelius says it was not, and what Mr. Gutelius says goes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that I said nothing of the sort.
That is the effect of what the hon. gentleman said.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not at all.

Does not my hon. friend know that when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, through its officials, advertised a list of sailings for the port of St. John, they did it under the then existing tariff arrangements with the Government railways? Does he not know that they said in effect that they would not go to Halifax but that they would go direct to St. John unless, so far as they were concerned, a more favourable arrangement was made? Does he not know that the Government, through Mr. Gutelius, made an arrangement more favourable than before, altering the tariff altogether so far as they were concerned, and that under the new and favourable arrangement which the Government made with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company they decided to abandon the port of St. John so far as their fast mail steamers were concerned and go to the port of Halifax? Is that not discrimination? I do not care whether the Intercolonial made five cents or five dollars a day out of this. The fact is that they changed the tariff upon the Intercolonial railway in order to induce the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to turn down the port of St. John. That was the object of it; that was the effect of it. They gave this tariff agreement to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in respect of freight and passengers upon the mail steamers which made their terminus at Halifax. Under that

agreement, if, after landing the mail, the steamers were to go on to the port of St. John and discharge their freight, this agreement would not apply to them. It was only in case they discriminated in that way against the port of St. John that they would have the benefit of this remarkable agreement which the Government through Mr. Gutelius entered into with them. I regret that my hon. friend has misled the committee in a very important particular; that is, with regard to the determination of this matter by the Board of Railway Commissioners. My hon. friend says that the Board of Trade made a request to the Government to submit that agreement to the Board of Railway 'Commissioners and he says that the Government readily acceded to the request. Does not my hon. friend know that before the Board of Railway Commissioners could take that up at all the matter would have to be submitted to	them	by	the Minister ofRailways?	Does	not	my hon.	friendknow that he promised the people of St. John	that	the	agreement	wouldbe submitted to	the	Minister of	Railways, and is it not true that from that day to this the Minister of Railways has not submitted the agreement to the Board of Railway Commissioners? Does he not know also that I was appointed counsel on behalf of the city of St. John, together with the .recorder, to plead the case of the city of St. John before the Board of Railway Commissioners? Does he not know-and if he does not know I will tell him-that I communicated with the law clerk of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and asked him - if the agreement had been submitted; that he replied that it had not and that I asked him to advise me when it was submitted in order that I might take the matter up with the Board of Railway Commissioners? Never from that day to this did I, though I was the senior counsel on behalf of the city, receive any communication from the Board or from the Government or any information that the agreement had been submitted to the Railway Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The chairman of the
board, Mr. Drayton, told me that he was willing to appoint a time to take that up, whenever an application was made to him, and no such application was made.
And he was notified accordingly.

But does not my hon.
friend know that the initiative would have to be taken to the Minister of Railways?
No.
And does he not know that he telegraphed to the people of St. John, to the Board of Trade, that the Minister of Railways would submit the agreement to the Board of Railway Commissioners?
I think the Minister of Railways notified the Chairman of the Railway Commission that he was prepared-, at any time the member for St. John wished, to take it up.

I never was so informed; I made application in due form as senior cousel of the board, but never was informed that it had been submitted. I was informed of the promise to submit it, but never that it had been submitted. But what took place further at the Board of Trade when we had the pleasure of meeting the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Marine? I rose there and asked that the agreement should be submitted to the board. That was some fifteen days or so before the agreement went into effect. I asked also that its operation might be stayed until the Board of Railway Commissioners could decide the question. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in answer to my inquiries, made the statement that no matter what the Board of Railway Commissioners would decide, that agreement would become effective on the 15th of November and remain in force until the 15th of May. Is that true or is it not true?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That statement is substantially true.
The hon. member is certainly aware that the Railway Department were prepared, at any time he wished, to have that agreement taken into consideration by the Railway Commission.

Certainly the Minister
of Railways took a strange way of letting me know, by keeping absolutely silent on the subject and never communicating with me.
Did the hon. gentleman ever ask for an appointment, for a hearing by the Railway Commission?
Yes, in this way-
At a certain time?

I communicated with the law clerk of the board asking if the minister had submitted the agreement and asking to be advised immediately of its being sub-

mitted; and from that day to this I have never heard from the Minister of Railways upon the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: All the hon. gentleman had to do was to apply and ask them to fix a day for hearing discussion on that agreement, and they would have fixed it at once.

Under the statute, the Board of Railway Commissioners has no power over this agreement, and the only way it could have been brought to the Board of Railway Commissioners was by a voluntary ^commitment with that board by the Government.
That was done too.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Board of Railway Commissioners, it was understood, could not jlegally be called upon to do it. The Minister of Railways communicated with Mr. Drayton and asked him if the board would take it up and give a decision on it. Mr. Drayton expressed his willingness to do so; the Board of Trade of St. John were informed of his willingness to do it, and all that they had to do was to apply to him to name a day and a day would have been fixed, i

Surely the Minister of Railways ought to have submitted the agreement to the board and asked the board to decide the matter, and then, in the ordinary course, the Board of Railway Commissioners would have notified the counsel.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Who was asking that this
should be submitted? It was not the Minister of Railways who was asking for the submission, it was the Board of Trade of St. John. The Minister of Railways got Mr. Drayton to consent that he would take) it up if an application was made for the purpose; and surely it was the business cf the Board of Trade to make the application.

The Board of Trade was not a party to the agreement; the city of St. John was not a party to the agreement. The city of St. John was complaining of the agreement as being unjust to it and asked the Government to have the minister submit it to the Board of Railway Commissioners. They were assuming that the minister would submit it to the board. The minister, as far as I have been informed, did not lay it before the board or submit it to them. That is the only way this agreement could have got there. More than that, at the meeting of the Board of Trade in St. John, some two or three weeks before
the agreement was to come into effect, the Minister of Marine, in answer to my inquiry, made the astonishing -statement to the Board of Trade that no matter what the Board of Railway Commissioners might-decide as to its discriminatory character or otherwise, the agreement would go initio effect on the 15th of November and remain in force until its date of expiry, the 15th of May. That statement was made by the Minister of Marine as the minister now admits. We were making a reasonable appeal to the minister. We claimed that this agreement was unjust and discriminatory in its character; and the whole of the people of Canada were interested in it because it was proposing to use one of the great departments of the Government by way of discrimination against an -important sec-, tion of the people of Canada, and it was proposed to do this at the expense of the people of Canada. We asked that the operation of that agreement be suspended until after the Board of Railway Commissioners had decided; we were willing to argue it! before the board at any moment; but in the meantime we asked to have its operation suspended.. To our astonishment and utter amazement, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries said: No, the agreement goes into effect on the 15th of November, no matter what decision may be come to by the board, and it will remain in effect during the term of its operation.

Did the hon. member
ever make any complaint in writing of the lack of submission, or did he ask for an appointment in writing i.n- order that this matter should be heard?

What took place is
exactly as I have stated. I -have stated fully what took place, and I think it is unnecessary to state -anything further. With regard to the influence of my hon. friend, far be it from me to detract for a moment from the position which my hon. friend has taken, that he has strong influence with his colleagues. I am prepared to believe he has.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I never said so. I said I left that to our constituents to determine.

But my hon. friend said he had stronger influence with his colleagues than I had with -mine, because he was willing to compare the two. That must be because the result of the comparison would be that he had a greater influence

than I ever had with my colleagues. I hold the Minister of Railways responsible for what Mr. Gutelius did. No head of a department can shelter himself behind his deputy or his chief official and say the deputy did so and so, or my chief official did so and so; under our system the minister must take the responsibility. If I had been a member of the Government, and the Department of Railways were proposing to enter into an agreement which I believed to he unjust to any portion of Canada, particularly to my own constituency, I would have made a pretty good kick before I would have allowed it to go into effect; 'and if my kick had not been effectual I would have said to my colleagues: I cannot become a party to or responsible for the wrong which you propose perpetrating upon a portion of the people of Canada; I will hand back my seat to the people who sent me here, and see what they will say about it; I will not remain for a single moment in a Government which proposes to do injustice of that character. That is what I would have done. My hon. friend, however, does not seem to have felt it necessary to take that course.
My hon. friend says: Look at St. John and see how the late Minister of Public Works made promises which he never performed. If you go to St. John, you will see that with the exception of a little wharf upon the west side of the harbour to be used as a depot for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, every other work which has been going on there since my hon. friend became minister is work which was planned out and authorized by Parliament before the present Government came into office. That speaks louder than any words of either my hon. friend or myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not so.

I did make the way
easy for my hon. friend. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works came down to St. John and said that we had undertaken the Courtenay bay work too soon. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who now takes credit to himself for the Courtenay bay work, knows that Dr. Daniel, the late member. for St. John, said that Pugsley had planned out work which would take fifty years to accomplish. Judging by the slowness with which the present Government is going on with the railway terminals about Courtenay bay I think that they are trying to make

true the prediction of Dr. Daniel and that it will certainly take fifty years to accomplish the work planned out. They got Parliament to vote last year the money for the spur line to Courtenay bay but they have not turned a sod, they have not spent a dollar and all about the head of Courtenay bay, where the Grand Trunk Pacific four years ago, bought land for the purpose of going ahead with their terminals, is as silent as a graveyard, not a thing being done and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, with his self-complacency, allows this state of affairs to continue. Notwithstanding the approach to completion of the line in the West, we find that not a thing is being done in regard to the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific in St. John and, I believe, the same is the case in the other eastern provinces of Canada.
Like Quebec.

Like Quebec; it is on a par with their policy of degrading the Grand Trunk Pacific east of Cochrane. They seem to be wanting to bring some sort of lethargy, if not disaster, to the Grand Trunk Pacific in order to carry out some idea that they may have in their brains but what it is the people of Canada do not know. I will warn my hon. friend that the people of St. John are arriving at a stage when they will not stand very much more of the treatment which they are receiving from my hon. friend without protest.
At one o'clock the Committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at three o'clock.
I am sorry the Minister of Marine is not present now, as I have a few observations to make in reply to his last statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman think I have been generous enough in allowing the debate to travel so wide of the question before the House?
You have been so generous that I know you will not prevent me adding a few more remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman try to make them brief?
