I will be very short.
The Minister of Marine said he thought I ought to be ashamed to refer to the Atlantic mail contract, because he said that the first time the port of St. John had been given

an opportunity to show its capability as a winter port was during last winter. While the Government, through the Department oi the Postmaster General, said that the dooT would be wide open, through the Department of Railways and Canals it took every possible opportunity of closing the door in the face of the people of St. John. By pretending to give an open door it in reality closed it up by reason of this iniquitous arrangement which was made by the Government through Mir. Gutelius, with the Canadian Pacific railway. Further, my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) said that no doubt had the Liberal party remained in power the old arrangement would have continued. That old arrangement, was inaugurated in 1896, after the Government led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power, and all the mail steamers were obliged to make their winter terminus at St. John. Before that time they had been allowed to nun to Portland, Maine. Notwithstanding the protests made over and over again by the people of St. John, the Conservative Government allowed Portland, Miaine, to be the terminus of the Atlantic, steamers-. When the Liberal party came into power there was a change and the mail steamers were compelled to make their termini at Canadian ports.
That existed before.

No. Before that they had stopped at Halifax and gone on to' Portland, and the Minister of Marine will have the unhappy recollection of remembering that in 1896, after years of agitation, the people of St. John made up their minds they would not allow this injustice to continue any longer, and my hon. friend went down to defeat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that was not the reason.
It was.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
What was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The remedial school legislation had caused the hon. gentleman to run as an independent candidate, in order to split the Conservative vote; my hon. friend then belonged to the Conservative party.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well that the chief thing which then agitated the people of St. John was the injustice they laboured under, and they were getting tired of it. il remember that
at one time, when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce represented King's County, several gentlemen spoke against this injustice which was being perpetrated upon the people of Canada, of allowing these subsidized mail steamers to go to a foreign port, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that it was a small thing for people to make a row about insinuating that it was rather beneath the dignity of the people of New Brunswick. That was what caused my hon. friend to go down to defeat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Oh yes, there is no question about that. The people of St. John have the same feeling to-day as they had then; it will take a miracle to prevent my hon. friend going down to defeat again.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will see when the time comes. I am quite sure I will get more votes than my hon. friend did in 1896.
That is true, but in 1896 I was running with Mr. Hathaway, a good Conservative-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not Mr. Hathaway.

He was the president of the association under whose guidance we were running, but we were fighting for a cause in which we believed, and we were fighting between the two parties. We had a good many Liberals to support us and a good many Conservatives, more Conservatives than Liberals I should think, but these same 1,400 men are watching my hon. friend to-day and they remember how badly he acted towards St. John in 1896.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a very cheap remark.
Which one?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows.

I am not aware of having made a cheap remark; it depends upon the viewpoint. My hon. friend thinks that any remark made in criticism of him or his Government is a cheap remark. During all these years the Liberals were in power the business of the port of St. John kept growing and as my hon. friend says, in all probability if the Liberal party had remained in power the same arrangement as to the steamers would have continued, and the result would be that both St. John and Halifax would have these great steamers coming into their ports. But with the change of Government, during the last winter port season, the exports of the

port of St. John fell away seven million dollars. That is the change of which my hon. friend seems to be so proud.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that what caused the fall in the exports from Boston?
It is a fact that the exports fell away at St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is that which caused the fall in exports from Portland and Boston.

I do not know anything about the exports falling away in the port of Boston. I know that the exports from Fort William and Port Arthur were greater than ever before in the history of_ Canada, and I do believe that that Canadian traflie should have found its way naturally to the seaport of St. John and the seaports of the Maritime provinces, and it is an extraordinary thing, in view of this immense increase in exports from the head of the lakes, that for the first time in the history of St. John as a winter port, the exports decreased to an enormous amount. If my hon. friend takes any pride in that he is welcome to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know that the large increase of $17,000,000 from the port of Montreal was due to the improved manner in which the railways last year handled the grain traffic from the West, as compared with the year before? The result was that millions of bushels of grain were brought out by the St. Lawrence route during the open season of navigation, that could not be brought out during the previous year because of the failure of the railways to handle the crop expeditiously. Therefore there was not as much grain left to be handled during the winter season as there was the season before.

Does not my hon. friend know that the export of grain does not account for the decrease, and that there must have been a vast decrease in the package freight? At all events', the fact is that during the years the Liberal party was in power the business was increasing year after year from the Canadian ports, and the moment my hon. friend had an opportunity of dealing with the subject and made a change in the steamship service* the very first winter in which this change was effective the exports from the port of St. John fell away to the extent of $7,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend think that the exports of St. John fell away because the Empresses went to Halifax and

the Canadian Northern steamers came to St. John?

To my mind that would account to a very considerable extent as the Empresses carry large cargoes and the Royals are essentially passenger boats and carry very little cargo. More than that, the Empresses previously were working in harmony with the great Canadian Pacific Railway system at St. John, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company brought in all the freight they possibly could to St. John for the purpose of its being shipped in the Empresses. It is a lamentable fact that, for the first time in the history of St. John as one of the winter ports of Canada, many longshoremen during a large portion of last winter were without employment. Among them are many of our best, our most industrious and deserving citizens; and for the first time since 1896, when the port of St. John was successfully started as a winter port by the Liberal Government-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By the Liberal Government?
Yes, in 1897.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, I am astonished.

My hon. friend has in mind a small subsidy of $25,000 which was given to the Beaver line previous to 1896, under circumstances which, I may say, did not reflect very much credit upon the Government which my hon. friend at that time was supporting. That was a very small and insignificant commencement; the real commencement was in 1897, after the Liberal Government came into power, when they cancelled the mail contracts for the service to Portland, Me., and when the mail steamers were obliged to come into the port of St. John. From that time on the progress of the port was great; its exports increased year after year, until, as I said, during the winter before last they were very large; but when this change took place, they fell off to the enormous extent of $7,000,000.
My hon. friend did not seem to like the criticism which I was directing towards him. I do not think it shows good judgment on the part of a member of the Government to complain of criticism. Hon. members are here for the purpose of criticising what they do not approve. It is riiy duty, as a representative of one of the constituencies of this country, to criticise where I find good reason for so doing, and in this particular case I have the best pos-

sible reason for criticising the conduct of the Government and that of my hon. friend as a member of the Government.
My hon. friend says that he almost felt inclined to pass over my remarks with silent contempt. Have I misquoted my hon. friend in that? Let me say that, for one who seriously thought my remarks deserving of silent contempt, my hon. friend has taken up a good deal of the time of the committee in endeavouring to make answer to them, particularly at a time when the Government are anxious for us to turn our faces away from them and to go to our homes so that they may avoid all criticism in Parliament, for some months at all events. No hon. member of the Government would venture to pass by the remarks of a member of this House with silent contempt. My hon. friend may have a great liking for treating protests with silent contempt. The people of St. John and their protests have been treated with silent con-tept by my hon. friend and by the members of this Government; but no member of this House and no member of the Government, unless he has a swelled head, would attempt to treat, with silent contempt and as unreasonable, criticism directed against the Administration of which he is a supporter. I would be sorry to think that my hon. friend, who was formerly reasonable, modest, gentlemanly and courteous, has such a swelled head as to render him unreasonable and discourteous. I will never fail in my duty as a member of this House in directing criticism against the department of my hon. friend, or against the Government, when I feel it is my duty to do so. My hon. friend, through his Government, has treated-I affirm it in the most positive manner-the people of St. John in a most unjust, unfair and indefensible manner. Since my hon. friend has been the representative of that constituency in this Government, he has taken away from St. John the opportunity afforded to it of becoming a great shipbuilding port. That is the first blow he struck at the port.. He has followed that up by the course which he allowed to be pursued with respect to the mail steamers. In respect to the suburban railway service into the city of St. John, the people have also been treated with silent contempt by my hon. friend and by his colleagues; but while I am a member of this House, I do not think that my hon. friend will venture to treat the remarks which I make with silent contempt, no matter how desirous he may be of so doing. He will find it necessary to answer the facts which I present.
He will endeavour to present ingenious and fallacious arguments in order to draw the attention of the House and the people of the country, and especially the people of his own constituency, away from the facts, but I do not think he can do so; and if I can prevent him, he will not be able to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I feel I must again apologise for trespassing upon the time of the committee. The fault is not mine; it is the fault of the hon. member for St. John, and it must be attributed to the most extraordinary address which he has just delivered to the committee. I presume I ought to be very thankful to my hon. friend for this lecture which, from his exalted) wisdom, he has thought necessary to address to me in this Chamber, but I would like to inform my hon. friend that I have faced him too often and for too many years, not only in this Parliament but in another legislature, to be impressed by such remarks as he has just made, or to be influenced at all by the hon. gentleman's braggadocios and boasting as to what he has done for the constituency from which he comes.
My hon. friend has said that I stated that his remarks had better be treated with silent contempt. The hon. gentleman did not tell the whole truth. The remarks that I referred to when I stated that they had better be treated with silent contempt were not any arguments that my hon. friend advanced in regard to the city of St. John or the business of the country, but his personal references to myself, because I presumed that they were of no interest to the House. The hon. gentleman knows that; but, with the unfairness which the hon. gentleman always displays in debate, he twists that and says that I said his arguments regarding St. John had better be treated with silent contempt. The hon. gentleman knows that I said nothing of the sort. He knows that he has misrepresented me; that he has given to my remarks a meaning that they do not convey, and that he is twisting them into something that is not justified by what I said or by anything that has taken place in this House this afternoon. 1 must again express my surprise that a gentleman of his parliamentary experience should think it in good taste or good parliamentary manners or policy to endeavour to twist unfairly the remarks of a man who is discussing a serious question with him.
The hon. gentleman says I have treated with silent contempt the wishes of the peo-

pie of St. John. My hon. friend knows that that is not true. He knows that, in every matter in which St. John is interested, I have done my duty as its representative. He knows that no man in this House has been more zealous in the interest of his constituency than I have been in that of the constituency I represent now, or of the constituency I represented in another chamber. I can afford to throw back that statement in my hon. friend's face, and I say that it does not contain a single word of truth in regard to my conduct while I have been a member of Parliament or of The provinicial legislature.
My hon. friend always harks back to the election of 1896, although he does not refer to the part he played in that election. He at that time betrayed the party with which he had been associated for a good many years; for he had left the Liberal party to come to the Conservative, as he afterwards left the Conservative party to go back to the Liberals. In 1896 he was neither Liberal or Conservative; he was neither fish, flesh, fowl nor a good red herring. The hon. gentleman himself, talking to me here in Ottawa before the elections, told me that he saw no proper course for me to take but to support the Conservative party and its policy on the Remedial Bill. Yet the hon. gentleman in the city of St. John accepted the nomination from a branch of the Conservative party hostile to myself and to Mr. Chesley, because of our vote on the Remedial Bill, and ran as a candidate in opposition to that measure, not condemning the Conservative party, stating .on the hustings that he had no confidence in either party, and that he had no confidence in my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), under whom he afterwards served as a minister. [DOT]
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman denies it. I can produce-I think I can produce it -the report in a newspaper supporting him in that election, of a speech he made at the court house on nomination day, when he made that statement. I am making no statement now that I am not prepared to stand by. That was the statement of my hon. friend then. Now he harks back to 1896 and says I was defeated because the city of St. John was not satisfied with matters that had occurred in regard to the port. That was not the reason for my defeat. The hon. gentleman knows that the reason was the vote I gave in connection with the Remedial Bill. The hon. gentle-
man's own candidature was a protest against that action of mine, and he carried away from me, undoubtedly, a considerable wing of the Conservative party who, exercising the judgment they had a perfect right to exercise, did not approve my conduct in that matter and so voted against me.
The hon. gentleman refers to the fact that Mr. Frank Hathaway was the chairman of the committee under whose banner he was then running. That is true. But to-day I have no better supporter than Mr. Frank Hathaway; and I venture to say that there is not a gentleman in the city of St. John who knows Mr. Hathaway who will deny that that gentleman is deeply interested in matters affecting the port of St. John. To-day, as I have said, he is one of my warmest supporters and believes that I have done everything possible to advance the interests of the port. So, I do not think it does the hon. gentleman much good to bring forward Mr. Hathaway's name.
The hon. gentleman claims credit for developing the winter port business in St. John. The credit for that is due to the Conservative party, and while I do not wish to claim undue credit for myself, yet the fact is that the beginning of that movement was in the subsidy for a line of steamers from St. John to Liverpool, which my colleague and I were largely instrumental in obtaining. Certainly that was brought about when I represented the constituency, and very largely through my representation. From that beginning has followed the great business that has been built up in the years since thpn. When the Liberals came into power in 1896, the mail boats continued to run to Portland. The hon. gentleman has misunderstood my remarks, I think intentionally. What I said was that this is the first time St. John has had the opportunity to demonstrate that it is as good a port for the mail between Canada and Great Britain as any other Canadian port. For this is the first winter,
I think, in the history of St. John when the post office has delivered mails to steamers in St. John to be carried to Liverpool and other British centres, and has accepted mail from Liverpool, Bristol and other ports to be carried directly to St. John instead of having the business, as was the case under his Government, filtered through Halifax, when there were no direct sailings from St. John to the old country of steamers with mails. What has occurred this year has demonstrated that St. John

is able to hold its own in competition with other ports.
I have spoken because I cannot allow the hon. gentleman to make the statements, the absolute misrepresentations, he has made-that I have treated with contempt, or said that I could treat with contempt, arguments advanced by him in connection with the interests of St. John. He says, boastingly, that he will see to it that I shall not treat them with contempt. He [DOT]speaks as though I would be alarmed at the great and mighty man that he is. He must know me well enough by this time- we have opposed each other long enough- to know that I am not afraid of any argument that he may advance or any threat that he may make. I have been willing to meet him on fair terms, and am now, in this Parliament or any other; and I will not be deterred from doing what I consider to be my duty to my constituency, to my province, and to the country as a whole, as member and minister, by any remarks or braggadocio of my hon. friend. His statements are for campaign purposes in St.
. John and for nothing else, and for that he has taken up the time of the House. And he accuses me of taking up the time of the House. The hon. gentleman's coolness is something to admire, in view of the fact that he raised this question, and, when I responded to him very briefly, he started again introducing a lot of other matter entirely extraneous to the subject before the House, making it necessary for me to reply. Then he replied at great length. And, after all, he has what might be called the coolness-perhaps a stronger term might be used, but I will not use it-to charge that I have taken up the time of the House unnecessarily. For the time that has been unnecessarily taken up, the hon. gentleman, I think, must himself admit that he is responsible. I am not complaining of his taking up time as a member, for that is his right. But for some reason he thinks that political capital might be made against me by charging me with taking up time unnecessarily. That is not my custom, as I think hon. members will admit. I do not speak when there is no need of it, and, speaking, I generally confine my remarks to matters of my own department or my own province, matters in which I can give information to the House that will assist in the debate. So, I think the hon. gentleman's remarks in regard to myself taking up too much time are very unfortunate and
ill-natured, and especially unfortunate from a gentleman whose absence this session we have regretted but who, during the sessions he has been here, has occupied very often unnecessarily, more of the time of the House than almost any other member on either side.
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid that this whole discussion is out of order.
But, Mr. Chairman, you did not call the minister to order,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I was replying to the hon. gentleman.

But I commenced this
discussion, and under the amenities of debate, should have the final reply. My hon. friend has said that he will not be deterred by any remarks of mine from neglecting to do his duty. My only hope, Heaven knows, is, that he may be stirred up into doing his duty-that is all I ask. I want to put a little ginger into him; to stiffen his back; to put him in a better position to fight his colleagues who have ignored him. If I can strengthen him; give him greater vitality; make his voice stronger and his influence with the Government greater, so that justice will be done to the constituency he represents, nobody will be better pleased than I.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-1910, chapter 17, section 8 amended:

I have brought to the
attention of the Minister of Public Works my opinion that he is treating the matter of subsidies to dry-docks in a very small manner under this legislation. He takes out clause (a) of section 8 of the original Act of 1911 and amends it by giving to persons who put their money into first-class dry-docks the benefit of a 4 per cent rate. First-class dry-docks, mean, of course, dry-docks which aire first-class only because they have a larger capacity than those which are dealt with in clause (b) and (c) of that section, and I do not think that the minister is dealing fairly with the matter when he does not take in the whole of the sub-sections and give the same increase, 4 per cent, to the persons who put their money in dry-docks of the second and third-classes. He has said that there are no applications be-

lore his department for second and third-class dry-docks. If in any of our public harbours to-day a company were desirous of building a second-class dry-dock, which is a very large dry-dock and the most that many of our public harbours would be looking for, they would see that under this legislation they are allowed only 3 per cent. The minister has given us as a reason for introducing this amendment the fact that money is dearer, but money is no dearer to the builder of the first-class dry-dock than it is to the builder of the second-class dry-dock. If when making their applications they do not feel that they are going to get the 4 per cent subsidy, they may be deterred from taking action. The minister says that when applications come before him the law may be changed; I say that now is the proper time to change the law and to make it uniform in respect of the three classes of dry-docks which are anticipated by this law. I understand that application has been received from a company which has in view the building of a dry-dock in Sydney hairbour and obtaining a subsidy under the second clause of this section. There were two applications, one at the time the hon. member for the city of St. John was Minister of Public Works, in connection with the naval proposals of the then Government, and since that time another on a smaller scale, which would come within sub-section (b) of section 8 of the original Act. I say that a public Act should not be amended on the ground that there is pending an application for subsidies, under that Act. The law should be so amended that all persons interested in building dry-docks, whether of the first, second, or third class, should be put on an equal basis. It would be too late to amend the law after the applications were received, because persons who are desirous of putting their money into second and third class dry-docks will be deterred from making application if they are not sure whether or not there is going to be an amendment to the Act to bring them within the law as provided in the first section. The hon. minister may say that it is too late now to do this. If he feels that way about it, I would ask him to bring down an amendment at the first possible opportunity in order to make the law uniform. I am speaking generally for the ports of this country, where second and third class dry-docks would be a possibility, and where first class dry-docks might not 
be a possibility, but I have in mind especially the fact that the city of Sydney has voted 11,000,000 as a subsidy towards the building of dry-docks, and it would be an unfortunate thing if they should not have an opportunity of getting the same subsidy from this Government as any company which builds larger dry-docks in such places as British Columbia or in any of our larger harbours. The minister may have good intentions, and he may be in a position to say that he will arrange the matter if applications are received, but my hon. friend will not always be here, and his department should, when contemplating an amendment to any law, try to make it uniform in all particulars. I say again that if he thinks it would take too much time to send the resolution back this session and have it approved by the Governor in Council, he should at the earliest possible moment, at the next session of Parliament, bring down legislation to amend sub-sections (b) and (c) of section 8 of the original Act and make it conform with the amendment which he has now introduced.

I entirely appreciate the force of my hon. friend's argument. It is quite true that this amendment covers only the case of first-class dry-docks, and it is equally true that in view of the arguments that have been put forward to-day both by my hon. friend the member for North Grey and by the hon. member for South Cape Breton, perhaps it wbuld have been better if we had included the second and third class dry-docks as well. T can only say that it would be impossible for us to do this now under the present resolution, but I shall have the matter looked into so far as Sydney and Owen Sound are concerned, and if there is any possibility of there being applications in respect of dry-docks at those ports during the present summer, I will come down with a further clause to extend this provision to second and third-class dry-docks, because I quite agree that they are just as much entitled to it as are the first-class dry-docks. If no applications are liable to be received, I think we can reasonably depend upon such legislation being brought down at the next sitting of Parliament.
Amendment agreed to, and Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The House again in Committee on Bill No. 193, to amend the Act respecting the

national battlefields at Quebec-Hon. W. T. White; Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 3-approval of Parliament:
Has my hon. friend with him the plans of the work which has been done by the commission ?

I am informed that the plans are in the department and that they have been approved by the Governor in Council. I understand that the right hon. leader of the Opposition wished to know the reason for the change in clause 3. I shall submit to the House the memorandum sent by Sir George Garneau, president of the commission, giving the reasons for these changes. The memorandum reads: Quebec, January 3, 1913.
To the Hon. W. T. White,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. White,-
As explained in a conversation which I had with you a short time ago in Ottawa, the work of the National Battlefields Commission has been seriously hampered by the necessity of having to ask the approval of the Governor in Council at almost every step, even in matters of administration which could be handled more advantageously to the public interest if the commission had more discretionary power.
In the acquiring of lands for the park, after Parliament has specified the properties that may be acquired, it is particularly important that the commission should be enabled to act promptly so as to guard against the speculative increase of values which is the almost inevitable result of prospective acquirement of lands for public purposes. The commission has suffered seriously from this in the past.
It is interesting to note that Mr. Justice Audette, of the Exchequer Court of Canada, before whom a number of expropriation cases for the commission were heard last April, expressed the opinion on the Bench to the effect that he realized, under the Act as it now stood, that the commission was placed under a serious disadvantage in discussing prices with owners of land, owing to the fact that it could not conclude a purchase on terms which would be deemed very satisfactory without submitting the amount arrived at to the Governor in Council before the whole matter could be finally adjusted.	.
The obligation under which the commission is to submit to the Governor in Council the amount of a tender considered fair and just, after having investigated for their information the value of the land, does not give the commissioners that untrammelled power conducive to produce good results, it is not consistent with good business acumen. It involves procrastination, want of finality at the time the offer is made, and necessarily fails to achieve anything satisfactorily. An offer made to-day might not be approved by the Governor in Council for months and months, m the meantime the property goes up in value, the owner changes his mind and asks for a higher price. This of course may be renewed ad infinitum until the matter is forced into court.
Those are the main reasons given by Sir George Garneau, as chairman of the commission, for these changes. Further on he explains the matter from another point of view. He says:
I beg to submit to you, herewith, two drafts of amendments, approved by the commission at a sitting held on the 18tli of November last and which the commission thinks it is desirable to make to its charter (7-8 Edward VII., chapter 57), these amendments being calculated to do away with or, at least, to minimize the inconveniences found to result from the necessity of constantly referring to Ottawa before any of its projects can be carried out.
Under the first draft, the commission would only be required to have inuicated by Parliament the land it might acquire, and, then, it could go on with its operations to the extent of the funds at its disposal.
Considering the fact that these funds come from various sources, it seems reasonable that the commission should have authority to spend them for the attainment of its objects without being subjected to have each detail specially authorized by Parliament or by the Government. I understand that Parliament would not wish the commission to undertake anything which might involve expenditures not provided for, but this objection disappears by restricting the commission, as the first draft proposes, to the expenditure of money actually at its disposal.
The National Battlefields Commission strongly recommends that its charter be amended as per the first of the drafts here submitted; however, should it not be found advisable or possible to obtain an amendment along the lines of this first draft, it then recommends the acceptance of the second draft.
Under the provisions of the latter, the lands to be acquired would still have to be determined by Parliament, and the commission could make expenditures only to the extent of the funds actually at its disposal. The works of improvement, of construction or other upon the lands acquired could be proceeded with only after the approval, by the Government, of the plans and descriptions thereof and, naturally, the Government would be entitled, before giving its approval, to require such information concerning the proposed expenditure as it might deem fit. The commission would be only obliged to submit the plans and get them approved unless the Government expressly asked for further information. As to everything else, within the purview of the commission's charter, it would be invested with full authority to act without any special reference to Parliament or to the Government.
I am passing over a paragraph which refers more particularly to clause 4 of the Bill, which I may read when we come to that clause. The conclusion of the memorandum is as follows:
These additional powers are evidently necessary and I do not foresee that any objections could be made to their being granted.
I earnestly hope that you will feel justified in strongly recommending these amendments to the acceptance of the Government and that the commission will be given the powers necessary

to carry out successfully what it considers a great public trust.
Believe me,
Tours very sincerely,
(Sgd) J. Geo. Garneau,
Chairman N.B.C.
I may inform the right hon. leader of the Opposition' that it is the second draft submitted by Sir George Garneau that we have accepted. We thought that there was more guarantee under it from the public point of view, and the idea of the second draft has been accepted with some rearrangement as to form which the law officers thought right. But we have kept this idea, and it is embodied in the Bill now before the House.

The whole
object of the amendment contained in this clause is to remove the control of Parliament which was put in the statute when it was passed in 1908. Section 10 of the statute reads as follows:
No land or immovable property shall be purchased or acquired by the commission except with the previous authority of Parliament, and no expenditure shall be made by the commission until it has been approved by Parliament.
The amendment seeks to eliminate the last sentence:
No expenditure shall be made by the commission until it has been approved by Parliament.
Subsection 2 is as follows:
The commission shall, before entering upon any work of improvement or construction, or any other work involving the expenditure of money upon the lands taken or acquired under the authority of this Act, cause to be prepared plans of the proposed works showing locations, and submit the said plans for the approval of the Governor in Council, and the commission shall furnish such further descriptions or information to the Governor in Council as are required ; and no such works shall be proceeded with until approved by the Governor in Council ; and in like manner plans of the museum or any building to be erected within the park shall be subject, before the commencement of the work of building, to the approval, of Parliament.
The clause that it is now sought to insert in the Act in substitution of that reads as follows:
No expenditure shall be made and no liabilities shall be incurred by the commission until funds sufficient to cover such expenditure or liabilities shall be at its disposal for the purposes of this Act, and the commission shall, before entering upon any work of improvement or construction, or any other work involving the expenditure of money, upon the lands taken or acquired under the authority of this Act, cause to be prepared plans of the proposed works showing locations, and submit the said plans for the approval of the Governor in

Council, and the Commission shall furnish such further descriptions or information to the Governor in Council as are required; and no such works shall be proceeded with until approved by the Governor in Council.
As stated by my hon. friend, though the language is different, this clause is identical with the clause that is sought to be replaced, and with that I find no fault. The only exception is that the control of Parliament is at an end. The works authorized under this clause of the Act could not toe undertaken until they had received the approval of Parliament. I may say to my hon. friend, who was not in Parliament at the time, that the Bill, when first introduced in 1908, was very carefully considered, and the provision placing the control in the hands of Parliament was inserted deliberately. I thought at the time myself that it would perhaps be an impediment to the commission, that they would find themselves hampered in their proceedings, and that certain results might take place which would to some extent ' paralyse their actions. When we introduced the Bill there was no provision for the control of Parliament, but it was at the suggestion of my hon. friends on the other side of the House, then sitting on this side, that this provision for the control of Parliament was introduced. I refer my hon. friend to 'Hansard,' 1907-8, vol.
III.,	page 4,400. We were in committee upon this clause, which gave the Governor in Council control. Speaking on the second reading, or at all events on the second stage of the Bill, the then leader of the Opposition, now the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), had suggested that there should be control by Parliament. When we came to clause 10, after having read the clause, I contributed these words:
My hon. friend (Mr. Borden) wants to have ' Parliament ' substituted for the Governor in Council ' in this clause. I have no objection to that. My hon friend can express the idea as he wants to.
Mr. Foster:	Suppose property were purchased and Parliament were not in session?
Sir Wilfrid Laurier : Parliament would have to authorize it.
Mr. R. L. Borden:	Is it necessary to put
this Bill through tonight?
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	We want to proceed
as fast as possible with it.
Mr. Foster : The Senate will not be in session until the 10th of March.
Mr. R. L. Borden:	This would require a
little consideration. I would not like to put it into such shape as to make it unworkable, but I would like Parliament to have some voice in it.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I will reserve this sec-

tion and my hon. friend can think it over and make his suggestion.
On the following day the Bill came up again for discussion; the right hon. gentleman was not present, but the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said that he had talked the matter over with the then leader of the Opposition:
Mr. Foster:	I talked the matter over with
the leader of the Opposition this morning. He had carefully gone over the two clauses of this section, and he could see nothing better than to substitute, as was suggested by the right hon. gentleman himself, the Parliament ol Canada for the Governor in Council. .	.
I would suggest that the clause read as follows :	' No land or immovable property shall
be purchased or acquired by the commission except with the previous authority of Parliament, and no expenditure shall be made by the commission, except for the celebration of the tercentenary, until it has1 been approved by Parliament.'
After some discussion, the idea was accepted and embodied in the Bill that the control should rest in Parliament, and that nothing should be done by the commission, land purchased or money expended, except under the authority of Parliament. I think that then everybody must have been aware that it would mean the curtailment of the privileges of the commission, and that it would entail upon them perhaps some embarrassment. I am not surprised that Sir George Garneau states in his letter that the commission has been hampered in this way. The choice was presented to us of having the system of control or not having it. We adopted that policy deliberately, knowing what would happen, and notwithstanding any inconvenience which may have resulted to the commission, I do not see any reason why we should depart from the policy which was then laid down. I apprehended the difficulty which has taken place. The only remedy is to take proceedings for expropriation and secure a vote of Parliament. This law was in the first place very carefully prepared; the commission has worked satisfactorily, and even if, from the point of view of the commissioners, there have been some inconveniences, the interest not only of the commissioners but of the whole country were taken into consideration, and I see no reason why the law which was amended at the suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite should be changed.

I do not think there is any great change in the clause which we propose to substitute. There is a change in the wording, but not in the substance. If my right hon. friend will compare the
law as it stood with the amendment sought to be made in this Bill, he will see that we retain the control of Parliament. The law as it stands now contains the clause which my right hon. friend has just read, and it says that:
No expenditure shall be made by the commission until it has been approved by Parliament.
These words disappear, I admit, but we re-enact in clause 11 something which was not there before, and which again gives to Parliament the control of the money. Clause 11 says that:
No expenditure shall be made and no liabilities shall be incurred by the Commission until funds sufficient to cover such expenditure or liabilities shall be at its disposal for the purposes of this Act.
In order to have funds at the disposal of the commission they must be voted by Parliament. The words which I have just read are not to be found in the law as it stands. Really, we do not take away from Parliament the power to control, but we express it in a different manner, because Sir George Garneau has found, and the officers of the department concur with him, that the Act, as it reads, is unworkable. The first paragraph of section 10 of the old Act reads as follows:
No land or immovable property shall be purchased or acquired by the commission except with the previous authority of Parliament, and no expenditures shall be made by the commission until it has been approved by Parliament.
The commission could not spend one cent until it had the authorization of Parliament. But the change 4 p.m. which is proposed, and which, in fact, has been made the practice, is that we come to Parliament, and ask for an appropriation, and by vote of Parliament we put a certain amount, in the Estimates to be at the disposal of the commission for such purposes. This Parliament votes the money, but after it has been voted the commissioners are still obliged to submit plans and get the authorization of the Governor in Council as to details.

If the moneys at the disposal of the Commission came from this Parliament alone, the answer of the Postmaster General would be sufficient, but he knows that the commission expends other moneys than those voted by this Parliament.
That was true then, but it is not true to the same extent now.

It may happen again that the provinces may choose to vote money for this purpose. At the time, I personally thought we were overcautious and that perhaps we might dispense (with some of the restrictions on the commission, hut Parliament came to the conclusion that it was better to err on the side of excessive caution. Notwithstanding the high authority of my friend, Sir George Garneau, for whom I have the highest respect and who has managed and will continue to manage the commission most satisfactorily, I believe there is no reason to change now what Parliament did deliberately then.

When that statute
was passed, there was a large sum at the disposal of the commission which had been voted, not alone by this Parliament, but which was the result of general subscriptions, and grants by the provincial Parliaments.
It came from all over the empire.

Yes, and the commission had this money at its disposal, available for certain purposes; but now it is different. The commission has nothing at its disposal now but the money voted by this Parliament, except a sum for the purchase of land. On the 30th of April last, the balance available for the purchase of land was $105,193.63, from which is to be deducted judgments in expropriation proceedings paid since that date amounting to $55,437.26, leaving a balance available of $49,756.37. That is all that is left of the different amounts which came from all over the empire, and that is only available for the purchase of property. The commission does not and cannot employ that money for the work it is now carrying on, and Sir George Garneau and his fellow commissioners are now in the position of any other commission appointed by the Government to spend money voted and controlled by this Parliament. 'A hen the commission had moneys not voted by this Parliament, there was very good reason for the proviso to which the right hon. gentleman has referred, but that reason has disappeared to a very great extent, and I think we might well trust the commission that they will not employ that money for any other purpose than that for which it remains in their hands. Sir George Garneau made these representations for himself and on behalf of the whole commission unanimously, as he stated, and the Minister 
of Finance' and myself came to the conclusion that we would not stand in the way.
I might mention to my right hon. friend that I will not insist more than I should to have these amendments adopted; we are simply doing it to meet the wishes of Sir George Garneau and of the commission. Mr. Ross, the very efficient officer of the Finance Department, tells me that in view of the changed situation he thinks the law as it is now is unworkable.
Are there any other properties remaining to be expropriated by the commission?
There is one or two 1 think.
Is it a large property?

It is the property belonging to the Ursuline Sisters. Sir George Garneau did his (best to settle it and I have done everything I could, but the matter still remains under negotiation. Of course nothing cian 'be done except under the statute.

I have nothing more to say upon the subject. I wish to asK the Postmaster General if the commission has acquired from the Militia Department, or if the Militia Department has consented to give them, the magazine which is called the permanent building.

I am glad to say that
is settled, or practically settled.

I have nothing to say
with respect to the merits of this particular Bill, but I take this opportunity of suggesting to the Government and to Parliament that it would be wise to enlarge the scope of this Act, or to have another Act passed, with the object of taking in all of the more or less important battlefields in the whole Dominion.
Hear, hear.

It is true that Quebec is the great battle-ground of Canada, but at tne same time many important battles were fought in various portions of the Dominion, tne result of which made possible the result of the great battle at Quebec. In a measure, it may toe said that these smaller battlefields are of as much moment in our history as are the Plains of Abraham.
I cannot say that I am as well acquainted as I ought to be with all the battlefields in Canada, but I have some knowledge of some of the battlefields in the Maritime

(provinces. At least four of them come to my mind. Louisburg was the scene of a struggle covering a long period of years,; and it occupied a strategic position. The result of the fight in those days had a bearing on the outcome of the fight at Quebec. There is the old Fort Royal at Annapolis, Fort Beausejour in the constituency of my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Em-merson), and Fort Monckton. All these forts had much to do with the early history of this country. With the exception of the fort at Annapolis, which has been taken care of in a piecemeal way by some special effort on the part of a group of individuals at Annapolis in previous years, these forts have been sadly neglected and are in a deplorable condition. The ravages of time have been such that, in a very few years, if they are allowed to continue as they have been in the past, they will ibe almost completely obliterated. It seems to me that now is the time to take charge of these battlefields and preserve them, so that future generations may have some idea of what they looked like in earlier days and of learning a lesson from them. A large expenditure of money is not necessary; a small amount judiciously expended would be of great benefit. The great thing is to have a comprehensive scheme of taking care of these various landmarks, with the view of teaching younger Canadians that we have a history of which we may well be proud, and that we do not have to go south of the 49th parallel or across the ocean to study history. We could go a very great way in encouraging the Canadian spirit by broadening the scope of this Bill so as to take in other battlefields. I commend this suggestion to the Government and to the House, and I hope that before another session of Parliament has passed some comprehensive scheme will !be brought down to carry out the object which I have briefly outlined.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is a good deal of force in the observations of my right hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). The subject has engaged to a certain extent the attention of the Government. The suggestion is made that the scope of the commission which we are now discussing should be enlarged for the purpose mentioned, and it has also been suggested that an independent commission should be constituted for the purpose which my hon. friend advocates. As far as the Quebec battlefields are concerned, I think the locations on 260
which they were fought are very largely private property. In some cases, however, very important historical spots, which were formerly in the ownership of the Crown, have passed into private ownership. I think all the lands in Louisburg are in private ownership.
Beausejour is entirely owned by the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What about Cumberland?
The same, and the same with Annapolis.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The property at Louisburg, to which our attention has been more than once directed, has passed out of the Crown. In other places the property never was vested in the Crown. I cannot say more than this at the moment. In the earlier part of the session we hoped to bring down a measure in one form or another. The minister who had charge of the matter was not able to give the necessary attention to the subject, and therefore it will have to stand over for another session. There is, however, a good deal in what the hon. member has stated which commends itself to the attention of the Government.

I hope that some day
not too far distant the Ross rifle factory will disappear from where it is, because it is a ghastly sight there. The Martello tower is used as a water tank to provide water for the factory.
There are, I must say, no two opinions as regards the statement just made by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), namely, that the battlefields of this country should be landmarks preserved by the Crown for the country. Last summer it was my privilege to be present, with the right hon. Prime Minister, at the centenary of the battle of Chrysler's .farm, and there was a splendid demonstration there. To my surprise, however, the day afterwards I read in the newspapers that the owner of that farm had offered it for sale at auction on the day of the demonstration, thinking that the great concourse of people there might help in the *sale. It was not sold, however, and it seems to me that this farm should not be sold except to the Government. The same remarks apply to the Chateauguay battlefield and to the other battlefields mentioned by my hon. friend. They should be pages of our history, so to speak, which belong to the people of Canada. I was very much
revised edition

shocked when I saw, the day after that great demonstration, that the descendent of Chrysler was offering at auction, before that concourse of about 15,000 people, the farm where the battle had taken place. Fortunately he did not find a high enough bidder; and 1 hope that, if the opportunity should occur again, the Government will avail itself of that opportunity and secure the farm for the people of Canada.

Might I venture to
differ from some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this point in so far as to say that it is unnecessary to buy material monuments in order to remember the great actions, either of individuals or of nations of the 'past; Nearly all the great things that have happened in this world-in fact, what we may call the great triumphs, either of the mind or of strategy-are stored in our remembrance, and serve their purpose in cultivating the nobler nature of mankind, not by the fact that they happened in a certain place, but by the fact that they happened under certain circumstances, at certain crises and were due to certain great moving principles. Simply to buy a farm-what is that? It does not signify anything. It does not signify that something took place there. What took place was an exhibition of Canadian patriotism. Look at the trackless deep. Look

at the mighty conflicts that have taken place on the ocean. Would you put a monument upon the ocean? Not at all.
From the beginning of the world you will find that in ninety-nine per cent of the cases it is impossible to locate the precise spot where these great things have happened. Therefore, I insist, it is far better to do something of a benevolent character -make a gift to the sick children's hospital in memory of the hero of Waterloo, do something for the orphans, something for the protection of women and children in memory of De Salaberry, Wolfe, Montcalm, or anybody else. But simply to buy a farm-there is nothing in that.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-the commission may make by-laws:

I suppose there is no objection to that. This amends section 7 of the Act. Here is what Sir George Gar-neau says:
The commission further recommends that section 7 of its charter he amended in accordance with the project here appended which provides all the powers necessary for the internal government of the commission and for the maintenance, conservation and upkeep of the property of the commission or under its control.
The suggestions made by Sir George Garneau in this respect have been adopted with almost no change, except those which the law officer has thought it best to make in order to give it effect.
That seems all right.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-approval of the Governor in Council:
There is no reason for that.

When this was put in the statute of 1908 there was some further property to be acquired. But by the statutes passed in 1911 under my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), all the other properties which were necessary were given in the statute with all the descriptions. Now the Battlefields Commission is authorized by the statutes of 1911 to purchase these properties. So, if we have the authority of Parliament, it is deemed unnecessary to have the authority of the Governor in Council, and Sir George Garneau says that they may be handicapped

in the purchase of property; it would take longer, and the price might go up.
Yes, but why leave out the control of the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not read the report of Sir George Garneau, but looking over the * statute it is provided that the properties may be purchased, acquired and held subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. It was deemed undesirable that the limitation upon their holding should still continue, Parliament in the meantime having ratified it.

I cannot see
that. This is a very valuable control we are asked to give up. The commission cannot go beyond the statute in the purchase of the properties; and what (about the prices? The Governor in Council should approve the prices paid by the commission.

Nearly all the properties are now acquired and they are negotiating about the one or two properties still needed. As a matter of fact, they might close at any moment without waiting for an Order in Council. And we believe-the Tight hon. gentleman might not be of the same opinion-that we can trust the commission to do what is right. I know what has occurred about the Ursuline Sisters' property. They have been on the point of agreeing several times.
Why not expropriate it?
We would rather agree about the price; expropriation, we fear, being sometimes very uncertain. We might get the property cheaper by agreement than Dy expropriation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Does the former statute
require the approval of the Governor in Council as to price?
Yes; and that is an important safeguard. I do not see why it should be taken away. I know some of the difficulties, of course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think there is a good
deal in what the right hon. gentleman says as to retaining control over prices. If that is removed, I think the Bill should be modified.

Since there is objection, and in view of the objection made by the Prime Minister as to the need of control of the Governor in Council, I think we 2G0i
might provide for contingencies such as Sir George Garneau refers to by authorizing the commission to purchase providing it does not exceed a certain price. Then they, might use their powers at any moment..
Section 5 struck out.	-
Who are the new members of the commission?

That has not yet been
