Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 173 respecting British Nationality Naturalization and Aliens. He said:
It may be desirable that in making this motion I should say something of the causes and conditions that have led to its being submitted to this House, as well as in explanation of some of the important modifications which it makes in the law of British nationality and the law of naturalization as we now have it. The Bill deals with these two subjects. It is divided into three parts, the first of them dealing with British nationality, that is to say with the definition of what constitutes a natural born British subject. The second part deals with the naturalization of aliens, that is to say, with the methods by which persons who are not naturally bom British subjects may acquire the quality of British subjects. The third part of the Bill is general, making dispositions with regard to the carrying into effect of the provisions contained in these two first parts, and furthermore making some, provisions with regard to the manner by which a person possessing the quality of a British subject may throw off that quality, and to the status of aliens.
For many years there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction, both in the mother country and, in the Dominions with regard to the law respecting naturalization. As long ago as 18% a special committee was formed in the old country to study that law, to consider what amendments were advisable to it and to devise plans for its improvement. That committee made a report, but it does not appear that any action was ever taken upon it. The question may be said to have become an absolutely live question subsequent to or at the time of the report that was made

by the interdepartmental committee appointed in 1899 and which, after a very careful study of the questions submitted to it, made its report in 1901. I think it may be said that there were two principal faults found with the law as it stood at the time of their investigation and as, I think, for practical purposes it still stands to-day; firstly, that it gave room for a large number of cases in which persons found themselves having a double nationality. In consequence of this, many people were so situated that there were two different countries of which they were entitled to consider themselves subjects or citizens, and two different countries which might claim from them the fulfilment of the obligations of such subjects or citizens. This with regard to the law fixing the status of a natural-born British subject. Principally, at all events, it was from the [DOT]condition of the law in that regard that this difficulty arose.
The other outstanding difficulty that it was sought to remedy or to obviate resulted from the fact that while unquestionably the Parliament of the United Kingdom possessed the power of enacting a naturalization law, and while, I think I may say equally unquestionably, the parliaments of the different British possessions scattered over the world possessed that same power, at all events in so far as regards a naturalization effective within their own respective limits, it was certainly, to say the very least of it, doubtful whether any one of these parliaments- either the legislatures of the overseas possessions or the home Parliament itself, under the legislation as it existed-provided for a naturalization effective throughout the entirety of the empire. The question is not free from difficulty. Everybody, I think, is perfectly agreed that the powers possessed by the legislatures of the different possessions did not go so far as to enable them to provide for a naturalization that would be effective to make the person availing himself of the provisions of the law to that purpose a British subject outside of the British possession in accordance with whose laws he had been naturalized. The question whether, under the existing legislation of the United Kingdom, a naturalization granted under its law was effective beyond the limits of the United Kingdom itself, and more particularly was effective within the limits of the self-governing possessions, may be said to have been, at the very least, doubtful. For my own part, however, after giving to
the question the best consideration of which I was capable, it seemed to me, and it seems to me still, that, under the legislation of the United Kingdom as it now stands, the naturalization provided for and granted under its provisions does not extend to make the person availing himself of those provisions a British subject in the overseas possessions; at all events, in the self-governing dominions upon whom has been conferred the power of legislating with regard to naturalization. I do not know that it is necessary to go into the discussion of the reasons that lead one to this conclusion. I may say that as long ago as 1874 the law officers of the United Kingdom, in a circular addressed to the governments of the different dominions, clearly accepted this view, and the text of the legislation upon the subject, to my mind, very clearly-perhaps it is too strong to say that, because there has been a good deal of divergence of opinion about it, but as I read it myself at all events- clearly supports that view. The history of that legislation is not very lengthy. There was no general legislation on the subject of naturalization in the United Kingdom before 1844. Before that time an alien became a British subject either by denization or denizenation, which consisted in the conferring upon him of that quality by the sovereign in the exercise of his prerogative, or by a special enactment for the case of the particular individual. It was only in 1844 that any general legislation providing for naturalization was enacted in the United Kingdom. Strangely enough, the possessions had preceded the home country by a very great distance in dealing with this matter. I understand that naturalization laws enacted by the legislatures of the different possessions go as far back as the reign of Charles II.; in 1535, so far as I have been able to ascertain, the first naturalization act was passed in Jamaica. When the Parliament of the United Kingdom enacted its first law upon the subject, the law itself did not in express terms, if my memory serves me rightly, declare what the territorial effect of that	law was	to	be.
but by subsequent legislation, by the Act of 1847, Parliament expressly declared that that Act of 1844 did not extend to the British possessions other than the United Kingdom, and furthermore went on to expressly declare that all past legislation as well as all future legislation that might be enacted by the legislatures of the different

possessions providing for the conferring upon aliens the privileges and rights of British subjects within the limits of those possessions bad been and should be effective. The law was in this condition at the time of the enactment of the British North America Act, which, as all know, conferred upon the Parliament of Canada general power to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada. Among the particular subjects which it expressly declared to come within that description, although the enumeration was not intended to limit the powers, was the subject of aliens and naturalization. I think there can be but little doubt that power to legislate with regard to naturalization, as conferred by that Act, can only be taken to mean a power to legislate with regard to naturalization as the Parliament of the United Kingdom understood naturalization at the time of the enactment. The best evidence of what is meant by a statute is to be found in other statutes of the Parliament which make clear, what in the view of the Parliament legislating is understood by the particular terms in the statute that is sought to be interpreted; and when the power of legislating with regard to aliens and naturalization, as part of the general power to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada, was conferred upon the Parliament of this Dominion, there was standing on the statute-book this special enactment of the statute of 1847 under which Parliament has clearly declared naturalization to be a local thing. After Confederation, by the Naturalization Act of 1870, the same principle was still recognized, and in attaching effect to the naturalization provided for in that Act, Parliament attached those effects in exact and precise terms within the United Kingdom; and the Act repeated substantially the provisions recognizing the validity of legislation passed in future by the legislatures of the different possessions providing for naturalization within their limits.
As I have said, there has been a good deal of difference of opinion as to whether or not the statutes of the United Kingdom, operate within the outside possessions in such a manner as to make a person naturalized under them a British subject within those possessions. For the reasons that I have given, and notwithstanding the very great respect I have for the opinions of people who take a different view, it seems to
me that we can accept the situation as having been and as being as we have stood under the laws .since the legislation of 1844 -because the legislation of 1847 was declaratory as to the effect of that Act-and as we stand to-day, there is no Parliament within the Empire that constitutionally can provide for a naturalization that shall be effective throughout the Empire, .and that to produce	that result
in a constitutional manner you must necessarily have co-operation between the home Parliament and the Parliament of the self-governing dominions, I have said constitutionally, because I do not for a moment want to be understood as suggesting that there is not legal power in the Parliament of the United Kingdom to pass any law and expressly declare it to be applicable within all or any of the British possessions. That legal power undoubtedly exists. The home Parliament enacted the British North America Act and the home Parliament, looking .ait it from a lawyer's point of view, simply could repeal the British North America Act; and where there is power to repeal there is power to modify, and the action of the home Parliament, if it chose to do so, in legislating with regard! to a matter coming within the legislative power of this Parliament, for instance, and making that law applicable within this Dominion, would be an overriding of the provisions of the British North America Act and, in effect, a repeal of that particular provision under which the Parliament had power to legislate in the matter in so far as the particular measure was concerned. But while we can all agree that there is that legal power, I think it is equally clear that the exercise of that legal: power would be absolutely unconstitutional. It is not a solitary instance under the British system of Government where there exists a legal power whose exercises would be unconstitutional and, for my own part, I have not the slightest doubt that if the home Parliament, after the enactment of the British North America Act, which is the constitution of Canada, should undertake to legislate with regard to this particular subject matter, or any other subject matter legislative power over which is conferred upon this Parliament, and declare that legislation effective within this Dominion, while that legislation would be law and the courts would have to Tespect it, nevertheless the action of the home Parliament in so legislating would be

a violation of the constitution that has been conferred upon us and so being a violation of that constitution, that legislation would be unconstitutional. It follows if this view be right, and I may say without undertaking to pronounce any opinion upon the question of whether it was or was not right, that the home Government, when it was suggested to them, readily agreed to act as though it was right and declared expressly that they had no intention of seeking to have enacted iby the Parliament of the United Kingdom a law conferring the benefits of naturalization on persons in Canada without the co-operation of the Parliament of Canada. I may say further, as evidence of the acceptance by the people of this country of the view that certificates issued under existing legislation of the United Kingdom do not confer the benefit and advantage of naturalization within this country, I may point to the fact that in 1907 this Parliament passed an Act which would have been utterly unnecessary and absolutely useless so far as the United Kingdom was concerned, if the certificates issued by the United Kingdom were pro-prio vigore in effect in this country, whereby it was provided that person's holding such certificates should be an titled to be naturalized in this country vi ithout complying with the usual conditions with regard to residence; and that same enactment was made applicable to certificates of naturalization issued under the laws of any of the self-governing dominions. While our certificates were undoubtedly of no effect elsewhere within the empire, in virtue of this legislation of 1907, we did recognize and attribute a certain'effect to the certificates of the United Kingdom and the other self-governing dominions. I do not mention that to criticise but I mention it as evidence that this Parliament shared the view of the law officers of the Crown in 1874 that naturalization under the law of the United Kingdom was not, of its own force, effective within this country. I think people are pretty generally agreed now that it is a desirable thing that we should have a naturalization effective throughout the empire and the question that had to be faced was how that result was to be brought about without sacrifice on the part of the self-gove.ning dominions, of any portion whatever of the powers conferred upon them by their respective constitutions; in our case, without any sacrifice whatever of the powers conferred upon us by the British North America Act. The
£Mr. Doherty,]
matter was dealt with at the Imperial Conference of 1902, the Imperial Conference of 1907, and, finally, at the Imperial Conference of 1911. After the conference of 1902, and, if I mistake not, after the conference of 1907, Bills were prepared intended to be passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom for the purpose of bringing about imperial naturalization. These Bills, or the latter of them at all events, were discussed at the conference of 1911. The result of the discussion was that the Bills were not considered to be satisfactory. That conference agreed that a Bill should be drafted and submitted to the different dominions looking to the creation of an imperial naturalization and they agreed upon five things as being essentia] to such legislation, namely:
(1)	Imperial nationality should be worldwide and uniform, each dominion being left free to grant local nationality on such terms as its legislature thinks fit.
(2)	The mother country finds it necessary to maintain five years as a qualifying period. This is a safeguard to the dominions as well as to us, but five years anywhere in the empire should be as good as five years in the United Kingdom.
This latter sentence is an observation of Mr. Churchill.
(3)	The grant of nationality is in every case discretionary and this should be exercised by those responsible in the area in which the applicant has spent the last twelve months.
(4)	The Imperial Act should be so framed as to enable each self-governing dominion to adopt it.
(5)	Nothing now proposed would affect the validity and effectiveness of local law regulating immigration and the like or differentiating between the classes of British subjects.
In pursuance of the agreement so arrived at, a Bill was drafted and communicated to the different dominions1, I have said that the Bill was drafted in pursuance of the agreement so arrived at, but in some respects and in one very important respect, it did not seem to us to be in accord with all of these conditions. The other dominions, to which the Bill as originally drawn was submitted, accepted it. As so drafted and submitted, as I have said, the Bill did not seem to us to comply with one very essential condition of the conditions so laid down and agreed upon, namely, it did not provide that the effectiveness in Canada of the naturalization under the Bill itself, which was the Bill proposed to be passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, should depend upon its adoption by the Parliament of Canada. It did
5 p.m. provide that the effect of the Canadian certificates outside of

Canada should depend upon the adoption by Canada ot the Bill which had been drafted and which it was proposed the home Parliament should pass. That did not seem to us to be a recognition of our absolute control over naturalization so far as its effects within the Dominion of Canada were concerned.
I did not quite catch the objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The objection that we
had to the first Bill was that while it did provide that Canadian certificates should not be valid in the United Kingdom or in the remainder of the empire unless- we adopted the Bill providing for naturalization, it made no such condition in regard to the effectiveness within Canada of the certificates to be issued under that Act itself by the Home Government. Under the Bill as it was submitted to us, and as I understand it was accepted by the other dominions, Canadian naturalization would be effective outside of Canada only conditionally on our accepting the provisions of this draft Bill and adopting them. Naturalization under that draft Bill by the authorities of the mother country would be effective in Canada whether we adopted that law or not. That seemed to us to be manifestly an invasion of our constitutional right to control naturalization in Canada and it seemed furthermore to us not to be in accord with the provisions agreed to at the conference of 1911 and more especially with the condition which made the proposed legislation and its effects adoptive by the Parliament of the self-governing dominions. It created a situation where we could get no further effect of our naturalization unless we adopted that law but it subjected us absolutely to the obligation of recognizing the certificate of the United Kingdom whether we adopted that law or not.
In the course of the correspondence, the Home Secretary agreed that if the Act produced that effect-and it was recognized it did produce the effect I had pointed out-it did not carry out the intention. After an interchange of suggestions for modification we arrived at the Bill which is now before the House. The purpose of the modification fixing who is to 'be considered a British subject by birth, is, to, as far as possible, obviate double nationality. Under the law as it stands to-day a person is a natural-'bom British subject if he is born within the realm, or if, being bom without the realm, his father is a natura'l-born British subject,
or if his grandfather was a natural-born British subject. The change does away with the provision in favour of the grandchild. A person born without the realm will hereafter be a British subject if his father, at the time of his birth, was a British subject. It was considered that the extension of the privilege gave rise to a large number of eases of double nationality, and that by putting an end to this privilege in favour of the grandchild you reduce very largely the number of such cases although the law does not pretend to obviate entirely that objectionable condition. I do not know that until all the nations of the world will have agreed upon some one definition of what should make a person a citizen of theirs, it ever will be possible to obviate the condition of double nationality. Under the common law, the essential condition of being a British subject by birth was to be born within the realm.
With regard to the subject of naturalization, the changes are in the conditions for acquiring nationality, and as compared with our existing law there are three substantial changes. Our law at present requires a residence within the Dominion of three years. Under the proposed Bill

which in that respect is identical (with the law now before the British House of Commons-the period of residence is fixed at five years. That period, however, is not required to be within the particular portion of the British dominions in which the naturalization is asked for and granted. The last twelve months of residence must be within that particular portion, but the five years may be made up of one year in Canada and four years passed within some other part of the British possessions, provided the period of four years be within the last eight years before the application. While you have a more severe requirement than at present, from the point of view of length of time, you have a less severe requirement in that the person asking for naturalization is not held down to passing the entire period within the particular possession in which he applies. He can fulfil the requirement by residence within different British possessions, provided he has passed twelve months in the particular possession in which he seeks naturalization, and has passed four years, within the last eight years, in the British dominions. It is required that he should have an adequate knowledge, under our Act, of either the English or the French language. The Act passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom provides for an adequate know-

ledge of the English language, but it goes on further to recognize that in any of the possessions in which any other -than the English language is official, the requirement may be an adequate knowledge of either the English language, or the other official language. And so we are providing in our Bill for an adequate knowledge of the English or the French language. The effects attached to the naturalization so granted are, I think, in substance the effects attached to naturalization under our law as it stands. The section sets forth in express terms that a naturalized person, would be entitled not merely to all the powers and privileges that -belong to a British subject by birth, but -that he is to have from the date of his naturalization, to all intents and purposes, the status of a born British subject. One purpose of the legislation is to do away with, as far as possible, distinctions between natural born subjects and naturalized British subjects. One respect in which that distinction is done away with is in connection with the nationality of the child. Under the law as it stood a child born out of the dominions in order to he a British subject, must be a child or a grandchild of a natu-ral-born British subject, while under this clause he must be the immediate child of a British subject, and he fulfils the requirement if his parent was either a natural born or a naturalized British subject.
There are other provisions, several of which are but the reproduction of the old law, and some of which are new, so far as they deal with the status of the child as regards naturalization.
What is the meaning of the words ' eight years before the application ' ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That means that the period of four years may be made up at any time within the preceding eight years. In other words, a man who comes to Canada to-day and who three years ago passed a period of four years in some part of the British Dominions, may pass a year in Canada and then be qualified for naturalization in so far as th,e period of residence is concerned.
Sections 8 and 9 are the sections which do our part towards meeting the requirements of adoption of the law now being enacted in the United Kingdom, in order to make the certificates of the United Kingdom effective within this country and to fulfil the condition upon Much our certificates are to be effective in the United Kingdom.

They also provide for the recognition of the effectiveness of the certificates issued by the Governments of the other selfgoverning Dominions in this country, and fulfil the conditions upon which our certificates are to be effective in those Dominions. By the legislation of the home Parliament, power is conferred upon the Government of any of the British possessions in general to grant naturalization under it. That general power is subjected, so far as the self-governing Dominions, namely, Canada, Newfoundland, South Africa, New Zealand and Australia, are concerned, to the condition of the adoption of that legislation. By sections 8 and 9 we in turn confer the same power upon the Secretary of State of the United Kingdom and the Governors of all the other Dominions who adopt this legislation to issue certificates which shall be effective in Canada, provided always that they are issued pursuant to the Bill now going through the home Parliament; and provided, as regards the other Dominions, that they adopt that legislation. Under this provision the British certificates and the certificates of all the other Dominions that shall adopt this legislation are issued, not only under the authority of their own legislation, but under the authority of our legislation; and because they are issued under the authority of our legislation, they are effective in Canada. Because they are issued under the authority of the legislation of the United Kingdom or of the legislation of the different self-governing possessions, they become effective, as regards those of the United Kingdom, throughout all the rest of the British possessions save any self-governing dominion that does not adopt the law; and because the law is adopted by the selfgoverning dominions, they become equally effective there. In other words, we -act, not only under our own legislation as regards the granting of certificates, but under the legislation of the home Government and that of every other self-governing dominion that shall adopt the same legislation. In the same way, the home authorities, and the authorities of the other self-governing dominions that shall adopt this legislation in issuing their certificates, will be acting, not only in virtue of the legislation of their own parliaments, but in virtue of the legislation of ours. The result is that, though the certificates of all these other dominions are valid certificates in Canada and give a man naturalization, they are so because this Parliament has so enacted and, vice

versa, when our certificates become effective elsewhere than in Canada, they are so effective because the proper Parliament, having jurisdiction in those other dominions, has empowered the issuing of our certificates. We think that we have arrived at a system that while it perfectly protects and leaves unimpaired our absolute control of who shall be naturalized in Canada, at the same time enables us, by co-operation with the home Parliament and with the parliaments of the other self-governing dominions, to create a situation where both their naturalization certificates and ours shall have an Empire-wide effect.
Under the legislation of the United Kingdom, it is provided that the effectiveness of the certificates in any of the selfgoverning Dominions depends upon the adoption by the Parliament of that selfgoverning Dominion of the' legislation under which those certificates shall be issued. It is further provided that this Parliament shall always, whenever it deems proper, be at liberty to rescind or repeal that adoption. Such an act on our part, of course, will put us where we were before this legislation, and will end the possibility of an Empirewide naturalization. I point out the fact of this provision, which I think is an absolutely essential one. If to maintain our right to control naturalization within Canada, the provision had been merely that a certificate would be effective in Canada only if the legislation were adopted by our Parliament, and stopped there, there might have been a grave question whether or not we, by the adoption, having given effect to the legislation, would be in a position to repeal that legislation, to repeal our adoption, and thereby put an end to it. We have, however, provided for that, so that we stand to-day in a position where, not by the subordination of any legislature or Parliament to any other, but by co-operation between the home Parliament and the parliaments of the different dominions, we bring about an Empire-wide naturalization; and each one of the dominions, as well, of course, as the United Kingdom, remains at liberty, if that system or the conditions that are now agreed upon or made common throughout, should prove unsatisfactory to any particular parliament, to repeal what it has done and go back to the position as it exists today.
The third part of the Bill deals with the status of married women and infant children, dependent persons, and makes certain
rules with regard to them which I think will be found not to be materially different from our law or from the law of the United Kingdom as it now stands. The principal difference will be found in this, that where there were provisions in our law and the British law especially dealing with that class of persons who had been British subjects and who had become persons that were called statutory aliens, under which provisions they had special methods of resuming their British nationality, all those provisions have been done away with; and, just as the naturalized British subject stands upon the same footing as the natural-born British subject, so also does the alien, who has become a statutory alien, an alien by reason of expatriation, or, in the case of a married woman, by reason of her marriage, stand in the same position as another alien, and require naturalization by the same process.
As regards our own procedure for the obtaining of naturalization, we have made some changes which, I trust, will be found advantageous and which aTe certainly important.
Under the law as it stands to-day a man proving his qualification for naturalization would simply go before a commissioner, justice of the peace or clerk of the court, and swear to his possession of the qualifications. That affidavit is kept by the commissioner, justice or clerk, and brought into court and handed in, and then it was hung up in the office of the court and notice of some kind given. Then, if, within a certain delay, no one came forward to make objection, the man got his naturalization, ipso facto.
The affidavit was read in the opening of the court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes; but no provision was made requiring proof before the court other than that affidavit. So, the only person who controlled the proof at all was this officer, of whatever kind he might be, who happened to take the affidavit, and the court was not called upon to look into the matter at all unless somebody was interested enough to come forward and make opposition. It might reasonably be expected that there would be, and I have had representation from all parts of the country that there have been, very grave abuses indeed-that these naturalizations were effected wholesale in many instances, people swearing to the affidavits having little if any comprehension of them, and, at all events, there was no effective control

over their statements and we were much exposed, and I think there is reason to believe that there must have been, under that system, many naturalizations which should never have been effected at all. The method, by which we propose to remove that is to leave in the hands of the courts the verification of the qualifications of the men to be naturalized-to require that proof shall be made before the court.
Under oath?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill does not prescribe the specific terms, but under it there is power to make regulations. But it is required that there shall be proof to the satisfaction of the judge of the possession of the required qualifications. On the judge being satisfied, the procedure will not be, as now, for the judge to issue the certificates, but his decision finding that the proof is sufficient and that the facts are established will be transmitted to the Secretary of State, and the certificate will be issued by the Secretary of State upon that decision. It is thought wise to surround with these additional precautions the procedure necessary to the acquisition of naturalization. It is thought desirable because, in the first place, we do not want people to be naturalized unless we are satisfied that they meet the requirements the law prescribes, and in the second place because it is a' good thing to impress upon the person seeking naturalization that what he is seeking is a something that is worth having, that it is not a mere incidental ceremony-as I have been told it has been represented to be in a good many cases-in virtue whereof the party is hustled into an election booth and his vote polled. We wish to bring home to the people seeking our naturalization that, from our point of view at all events, it is a serious and important thing and in consequence that we require proof, real proof, of the possession of the requirements, and we surround the making of that proof and the issuing of the certificate with such procedure as will impress upon the individual that the matter is one of importance and that he is receiving-what he really is receiving-a very valuable gift.
Is there a delay for the issuing of the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have not fixed any specific delay. That might be a matter for consideration.

Do I understand
that the Act will require a personal appearance of the party before the judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to say what the regulations will prescribe absolutely, though I must say that unless there should be shown to be some very serious objection to it, I think that would be a very wise requirement to be inserted in the regulation.

I do not think the Act
provides for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 21 provides:
The applicant shall produce to the court such evidence, that he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this Act, as may be required by the court,-
That means evidence under oath; any judge would hold that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly.
-subject to such regulations as may be made hereunder.
We propose to make regulations which will require evidence under oath, and, as I say, unless there is some objection which I do not foresee, will require the presence of the party, or at least will entitle the judge to require his presence, in the court. That is all the more necessary mow because we have the requirements not only of residence but also of good character and what may be called the educational requirement-a knowledge of the language of the country. These are things which require careful consideration.
There is another provision that is of importance, and that is as to how certificates fraudulently obtained may be dealt with. Under the law as at present we have serious difficulty. In England they have no provision on the subject. In our country we have the provision under which a person who falsely swears the affidavit may be prosecuted for perjury and if convicted may forfeit the benefit of naturalization. That was very well when you could prove absolute intentional perjury. But there was no remedy provided by the statute where there was simply a misstatement of fact that might be the result of error. In at least one case the person has absolutely admitted that he had not the qualifications, but says: When I swore to that document I did not understand it. Still, such a person is in possession of the qualification of a British subject, and there is no method, at all events no clear method, of getting rid of that certificate and dispossessing

him of the qualification. We have provided, and the new English Act provides, power in the Secretary of State to withdraw the certificate where fraud has been established.
I do not know that any good purpose would be served by my going more into detail at this moment. My excuse for going so far into detail as I have done is that the matter is of importance and it seemed to me desirable, before we come to the details of the Bill in committee, that there should be put before the House, so far as I am capable of doing it, a clear general explanation of the purpose of the Bill and of the provisions that we think should be made.

I followed the minister's remarks as carefully as I could, and I desire to ask at this stage a question that occurs to my mind as to the effect this measure will have upon applications for patents in the prairie provinces. The minister knows that a man earns his patent in three years. Will the effect of this Bill be to hold up all patents for two years after they have been earned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I understand the law as it stands now-the hon. member is probably more familiar with it than I am- it is not in so many years that the settler earns his patents, but that after three years in order to have his patent he must be a British subject. The effect of this legislation, as I understand it, will be that he will not be a British subject as early as he otherwise would be.
What about his patent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He will not be able to get his patent in three years now, of course. If it is understood that there is any right that is injuriously affected by that provision that difficulty could be met by legislation for the issue of the patent after the man had resided three years in the country even if he had not already obtained naturalization. I think it would be better to meet that particular question in that way than to modify our whole system of naturalization -if this proposed system be considered, as I certainly do consider it, to be an improved system-merely to meet that transitory condition. A man who hereafter comes and takes land with a knowledge that he will not be entitled to his patent until he has become a British subject will take it with the knowledge of how long be has to wait. I may further point out that many people will not have to wait so
long, because there are people who come into this country after having resided two or three or four years in some other part of the empire. These people will have to wait only one year or two years, as the case may be; so that the law will work both ways.

I am sorry that I was called away during the very interesting address of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and that, therefore, I missed part of what he said. The chief object of this Bill is to deal with the effect of the certificate of naturalization which is given in any one of the dominions of the empire. At present we have the power to grant naturalization letters to an alien, but the effect of them is limited to our own country. This has always been considered to be a very serious objection to the law. A very obvious illustration, one which has been quoted more than once in this House-is that of a man who is a British subject and who, if he goes to London, is no longer a British subject; he may be a German or a Frenchman or an American. The object, therefore, of this legislation is to provide that the naturalization which is given shall henceforth carry its effect all over the British Empire. Of course, we cannot, with the powers that we have, given to our certificate any such effect. If I understand my hon. friend aright, it is provided that in this matter there shall be reciprocity of legislation and reciprocity of powers among the dominions. I understand the purpose of this legislation to be that a British subject naturalized in Canada may present his certificate in London, or in any other part of the British Empire, and that it shall have the same effect as it has in Canada. That is very important legislation, which has been in contemplation for many years, and I am very glad that my hon. friend has at last achieved the making of these provisions. In Canada, the provisions of this legislation will create some confusion in respect to our naturalization laws, especially in the new provinces. I am aware that the British Government has been very chary of giving naturalization, and that the dominions, on the contrary, for very obvious reasons, have been very free with their legislation with regard to naturalization. We have been inviting persons from all over the world to settle amongst us, and this invitation has carried with it the idea that at the earliest opportunity we would give them every

right that we give to our own citizens. The period of probation before the letters of naturalization could be granted has been three years. I am aware that the British Government at one time objected very .strongly to the length of that period, and wanted to have it made longer. It may be presumed that it is in consequence of that that this important modification in our laws has been adopted, and that the period of probation will henceforth be not three but five years. As I say, this will certainly throw some confusion into the administration of the land laws in the western provinces. I suppose that the remedy for this may be found, not under this legislation, but by introducing an amendment to the Lands Act. There is nothing to prevent the period of probation before the patent is issued being limited to three years, which it is at the present time, and I suppose the Lands Act can be amended accordingly.
Mr. MAOlfONALD: That at last all the self-governing dominions of the empire have agreed upon certain common rules which shall entitle a person receiving a naturalization certificate from the authorities of any one British possession to be recognized as a British subject throughout the whole empire and abroad, is a matter of great satisfaction. I am not sure that my hon. friend, however, in drafting this Bill, has not made the situation a little too drastic. If I recall correctly the discussion that we had last year upon this question, it rather went upon the view that each one of these selfgoverning colonies, having statutory powers conferred upon it similar to those given to us in 1867, could stipulate the conditions under which persons could become British subjects within its own territory It w&s suggested that there might be in this coun,-try and in the others dominions a system which would provide for naturalization which would give the rights of citizenship within that particular dominion and that there could be a supplementary method by which empire citizenship could be created through certificate along the lines suggested in this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That may be so still. Under the legislation of the home Parliar ment, if we desire to have the two different kinds of naturalization, there is absolutely nothing to prevent our having it. Our Bill does not purpose to have it; we thought it more desirable to have one system.

I have always been a strong believer in the desirability and importance of settling the question as to the rights of empire citizenship. It does occur to me that a matter worthy of consideration is whether or not this Canadian Parliament should give up altogether for the time being-although they still possess the constitutional right to legislate in regard to it-the method under which they admit to citizenship in Canada aliens who come into this country. My hon. friend showed very clearly the exact status of this Parliament in that regard. Section 91 and the particular subsection of it which speaks of naturalization and aliens unquestionably confers upon the Canadian Parliament the right to legislate in regard to naturalization within the territorial hounds of this Dominion and the effect of that naturalization, while its extent may be a matter of argument, unquestionably is absolute within the bounds of Canada. The broad question involved in this legislation is that of imperial citizenship, and I am sure that we are all agreed as to the desirability of having it settled, but the question for us to consider is as to the wisdom of obliterating from our statute books altogether the provision under which aliens may be admitted to citizenship in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You mean a double system of naturalization?

The way it was discussed last year, I think, was along these lines: there are persons who come into Canada, who become Canadian citizens, who make their homes here, who never go abroad and in regard to whose rights and citizenship no question will hereafter arise. The period of residence, three years, has always entitled them to the rights of citizenship within this country. It .has long been recognized that the Imperial Parliament would require a period of five years, and I think that in the discussion last year, if I remember correctly, it was pointed out that it would be quite possible to arrange some such system. The point for consideration at the moment is whether it is wise to do away with this provision in Canada of creating citizenship so far .as Canada is concerned. Perhaps my hon. friend the minister-I am sure that he is au fait on this subject-will tell us something about the conditions, for instance, in New Zealand. This country has always admitted to its citizenship persons without any residence

whatever, simply upon proof being submitted as to their intelligence and as to the likelihood of their being good citizens. Australia, I think, requires a (residence of only two years; we have required three, and the mother country five. It would be interesting to know the position adopted in the other self-governing colonies. It must be remembered that the rules governing naturalization in Canada under this Bill are very rigid. There has long been a vexed question of law as to whether domicile or nationality was the best test of a man's place in law. That question arises in connection with the distribution of estates, the rights of parties in regard to marriage and contracts of all kinds. The domicile of the party has always been the governing factor, but by virtue of this measure the distinction between domicile and nationality is practically swept away because the person who wants to take on nationality in Canada hereafter must swear that he intends to have his residence in His Majesty's domain or to continue in the service of His Majesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He has to swear his intention under our present law.

Hardly in that
definite way. I hardly think it was as stringent as this. For instance, a Canadian citizen who has gone to the United States, as unfortunately they have gone in great numbers in the past, under the existing laws can become renaturalized in Canada on a residence of three months. Under this it would require a residence of five years. I have had experience with ' this question, and in the industrial centres in my province numbers of men have come from-other countries and have become good citizens, taken up homes and interested themselves as Canadians. It is not desirable to practically compel a foreign citizen who has been here for five years to retain a lawyer to go through the cumbersome process provided in this Act, because in practice a person wishing to become naturalized would require to employ counsel. I have never seen that any great trouble has come to this countiy by extending to people who have taken up their homes here, once they have complied with the terms of residence, the rights of naturalization without very much trouble. While it is a priceless privilege to possess the right of being a British citizen, our legislatures have gone so far in recognizing the rights of aliens who hold property, and so
on, that so far as business reasons are concerned, no difficulty exists at all. The only privilege gained by the alien who takes out citizenship is the right to the franchise. I am inclined to the opinion that we ought to preserve upon our statute book legislation under which a son or daughter of Canada who has gone to the United States and wishes to come home again will not have to wait five years before resuming full British citizenship. There are many reasons well worth consideration why we should keep open the avenues by which a person can come in, and after three years' residence, secure naturalization. The preservation of those rights would not in any way impair or affect injuriously the creation of the method which my hon. friend proposes under which it will be possible for those who desire to do so to obtain through this channel certificate under which they become citizens of the empire in the fullest sense of the word. This is a matter in which, personally, I have always taken a great interest. I have always felt that while we talk a great deal about empire glory and about the desirability of the maintenance of the empire, a tremendous anomaly has existed in Great Britain and in every part of the dominions which form the empire in that we did not have legal machinery under which those who came to live amongst us and who desired to assume the responsibilities and to claim the advantages of British citizenship could do so by any process known to the law.

I agree with the Minister of Justice when he says that certain safeguards should be placed around our naturalization laws. British citizenship is not to be lightly regarded. At the same time, we in Canada have been bringing in people by the hundreds of thousands during the past number of years under representation that they can become British subjects in a period of three years; and I think that any changes that are made now should be made with a view to protecting people who have already come to Canada. I understand from the Minister of Justice and	the Minister	of	the	Interior
that some steps	will be taken
to protect people who have come in here and taken up homesteads so that they will not be deprived of the right of obtaining patents on the completion of their term of residence, as provided under the existing law. If the five-year period of residence should be enforced as against them, they

could not obtain their patents for two years if they had earned them. But it seems to me that there are some safeguards being thrown around the question of naturalization under this law wdiich are really not necessary. In the prairie provinces to-day the only procedure that is necessary to become a British subject is to take the oath of allegiance, get certificates from some justice of the peace, notary public or commissioner and from some person who knows the applicant, and to post these in the court house in the judicial district in which the applicant resides. Then I think in forty days it automatically comes before a judge of the district court and the applicant is naturalized if the papers are found to be in order. It is true that some abuses have crept into the naturalization proceedings in western Canada. I have known cases, in which I believe men have taken the oath of residence, followed by the oath of allegiance, without having resided three years in the country.
I find that the provisions of this proposed Act add to the existing qualifications one in respect to language. In addition to changing the period of residence from three to five years and providing that the applicant shall be of good character, the proposed law says that he shall have an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language. I know a man living not very far from where I live who has been in this country a great deal longer than I have and who speaks neither the English nor the French language. I know that English and French are the dominant languages in Canada but there are just as good citizens as any Englishman or Frenchman who have been in the country twenty or twenty-five years, men who have come from countries in central Europe and who cannot speak either English or French. Their sons and daughters, who have gone to school, have learned the English language and in that case when the father goes to the office of an attorney he takes his son or daughter along with him to interpret. It seems to me that to insist on a qualification that a man must have an adequate knowledge of the English or French language is going a little too far, and I shall take the opportunity of calling the attention of the Minister of Justice to that point when the Bill is 'being considered in committee.
I can only reiterate what was said by my bon. friend 'from Piotou (Mr. Macdonald) in respect to the cumbersome nature of this Bill. In 'the West it will 'be imposing a hardship on a man who has resided for

five years in the country to insist that he shall go either himself or with witnesses before a judge and show that he has an adequate knowledge of the English or Trench language and that he possesses the other qualifications. I know from personal experience that it will be necessary for a man to employ a solicitor to go with him before the district or Supreme Court judge and see that the evidence is properly placed before the judge. Then it is provided that the certificates shall be sent by the judge to the Secretary of State. The judges or our courts are just as well qualified to issue the certificates and to place upon the 'applicant the stamp of British nationality as the Secretary of State is. Why is it necessary to send these papers all the way to Ottawa? Instead of it taking a month for a man to get his naturalization papers it will take two or three months. There are some other points that I propose to bring to the attention of the House when the Bill is before the committee.

I think the trouble with
this Bill is that we have been looking to establishing for Canadians an imperial citizenship. We have not recognized that in undertaking to do that we must necessarily make provision for allowing Canadian citizenship to people throughout the empire. It is to that feature of the case that I desire to draw attention. At the present there is a demand made for certain rights on the part of certain citizens of the empire who, I believe, are busy landing, ox who are being held in quarantine, at Vancouver, and who claim entrance into the Dominion on the ground that they are British subjects. Our immigration law provides that as long as they are not Canadian citizens they do not acquire certain privileges. We, by this legislation, if I understand it correctly, give them all the status of British subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All the status of the
native-born Hindn; that is the limit of what we give and it will not affect their Canadian citizenship.

I think it is a matter well worthy of consideration as to just how far we are warranted in building up in the minds of these people the idea that we are giving them a degree of British citizenship that they do not enjoy to-day. We have drawn around ourselves the idea of Canadian citizenship as a protection to the welfare of the Dominion. While I know what my hon. friend says, it does not alter my opinion. At the same time he is, by this

Bill, building up in the minds of people in the outlying parts of the empire an idea of common citizenship, and common right throughout the empire capable of being asserted in Canada as well as in other parts of the empire. That may he a good thing. It inay be that a citizenship thus 'built up will have no effect at all but I think we are close enough to a difficult situation to warrant my suggestion to the minister that in any case, instead of this Bill going into effect on the 1st of January, 1915, it should not go into effect until after another Parliament sits because there are conditions that may arise, just as in the case of this homesteading business, which has been mentioned. There may be conditions arising in connection with the exercise of the franchise and this matter should be thoroughly considered before the Bill goes actually into law. My bon. friend says that it may be repealed; so it may, but it is always a difficult thing to do away with rights once they are granted.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 195, to incorporate the Canadian General .Council of the Boy Scouts Association.-Mr. Wright; Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

I am not opposed to the Boy Scout movement in Canada; on the whole, I think it is a very healthy organization for our young boys. I would have preferred, however, to see this Bill promoted by the Minister of Militia, rather than by a private member. Could the hon. gentleman who leads the House inform me at what age .a boy is admitted to the organization? I believe that this organization
will ultimately give us a generation of good sound Canadians. I am not averse at all to military exercises for the boys, for I think it is a good thing that they should know the rudiments of militia and defence. While I would like to see the boys follow the drill at college under the eyes of their professors, I question the advisability of boys twelve, thirteen, fourteen or fifteen years old being taken away from their parents during the summer months and sent to camp. It is a matter of very great importance, and it seems to me that the Minister of Militia or the Government should have fathered this measure in order to give fuller explanation. In all our colleges, as the Minister of Justice knows, we have Cadets; and the Department of Militia sends every year, during the months of April, May and June, an officer to drill those boys. All of us who have been at the various colleges in the province of Quebec have followed those drills; and we do not complain noT object; but to take the boys from home during the holidays and send them to the camp during a certain number of days- may be found objectionable for many reasons. I only regret that the Minister of Militia is not in his seat so that he might have explained more fully the effect of this legislation.
I wish to reiterate here what was stated a few days ago by the Lieutenant Governor of the province of Quebec, Sir Frangois Langelier. One of the papers of that province stated that this organization was1 more or less connected with Free Masonry; and the Lieutenant Governor of the province immediately, when inspecting the Boy Scouts, denied this statement and denounced the paper as expressing merely the opinion of its editor and not the opinion of the people of the province of Quebec. I agree with the Lieutenant Governor in what he says. I think that the Boy Scout movement is a healthy one; but the Government should take hold of the movement, and it should be under the control of the Minister of Militia instead of being under another control; that is to say, the Government should lead in this matter and not follow other organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Boy Scout movement is not a military one.
Well, it is half military.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

Well, I would like my hon. friend to explain the movement. I do not know very much about it, except

what I have seen in the newspapers. I am not opposed to it at all; hut I would like to have a .measure of this kind, which affects the yeomanry of the country, and which, to a certain extent, will encourage our young men to join later on our militia system, explained more fully. I do not see the promoter of the Bill.
Does my hon. friend favour the Salvation Army being placed under the Department of Militia? The same religious idea prevails in both movements.
I do not see what there is in the remark of my hon. friend.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) is entirely mistaken as to the aims and purposes of the Boy Scout movement. I had the pleasure of hearing the founder of this movement deliver an address in Calgary at a meeting very largely attended. We have in Calgary now a strong organization of boy scouts as well as cadets. The Boy Scout movement can in no sense be said to he military; it has no military purposes nor aims. Primarily it desires to make young boys understand that they have a sense of duty towards those with whom they are associ-ated'.and towards those amongst whom they live. It teaches them courtesy-old-world courtesy, if you will-the desire to oblige those with whom they come in contact; to do kindly acts, and to live their lives as though they were trustees for what they hold, not for themselves, but for those
about	them,	and for the	generations	notyet	bom.	It is	really one	ofthe	most	inspiring	things in	theworld	to	see what	good has come	
of this movement among young hoys I have watched them come, sometimes from homes where they have been indifferently trained; and the result has been that they have been inspired by noble purposes, high aims, lofty ideals, to have a high regard for their duties as citizens, and to be a living example in the community sometimes to men much older. I am sure, if my hon. friend will look into the history of the movement, and analyse the conditions under which it has been founded, he will give it his hearty support. It could not possibly be placed under the control of the Minister of Militia, because that would destroy the very purpose for which it was founded. When Sir Robert Baden-Powell founded this movement, he had the idea of inducing young men and boys voluntarily to band themselves together and to strive towards a 
higher standard of manhood and citizenship, not under compulsion, but actuated by the high purposes, the splendid traditions of honour and duty that have come down to mankind from the past. He has been able to inspire these young boys with such sentiments as these, and it was for that voluntary purpose and not that they might become a military force that the movement was founded.
There has been some confusion between the Boy Scout movement and the Cadet movement. The Cadet movement in a certain sense is military. The Boy Scout movement is in no sense military. In so far as camps are concerned, they are purely voluntary. In the city in which I live a large number of these boy scouts go to Banff and form a camp. Their parents see that their scout master is a man of high character, and under his control they are willing that their sons should go to this near resort. The boys are taught to take the initiative in certain things. They go for long strolls, for the purpose of learning to reconnoitre, to get some idea of the geographical and physical aspects of the country, so as to be able to find that which may be lost. It is only a confusion of terms on the part of my hon. friend; he is confusing the Cadet movement with the Boy Scout movement. The main idea of the Boy Scout movement is that they must each day do some kind act, or act of chivalry, as it would have been called in the days gone by; and I think that inspiration will remain with them in years to come, making them loyal and good and true citizens in the community in which they live, and perhaps making them do something to offset the trend of the times towards militarism, because, if the golden rule is that the boys shall do a kind or chivalrous act each day, perhaps there will be less disposition to refer to some other rule which is not necessary.
That is the very explanation I was seeking, and I am grateful to my hon. friend for giving it.

I think I would be
wanting in my duty if I did not say a good word for the Boy Scouts. They have had such an admirable effect in the riding from which I come that there certainly would be a great void if they did not exist. As so admirably expressed by the member for Calgary, there is nothing really military about the movement. It is an offset, not so much to militarism as to material-

ism. It is a revival in a mild way of the days of chivalry, which have altogether disappeared under the ban of modern materialism.
Not altogether.

Well, of course, not amongst the Opposition. One of the most touching instances that I ever knew of occurred here in Ottawa two years ago. A little chap five years old was severely injured. He was hurried to the hospital in an ambulance and a surgeon performed an operation upon him. When he was asked why he did not cry, he drew himself up as best he could under the circumstances and said: 'I am a scout.' I sent the details to Baden-Powell, and I got an answer from his secretary that at that time the chief scout was on the Indian ocean, but that he would see that this newspaper clipping was forwarded to him. He said that we could rest assured that this was an instance in which they would all rejoice. I have found boys who were likely to go to pieces on the streets, who received no inducement to behave themselves, who were not being told to do so by anybody, and in whom the ethical side of Christianity seemed to have been entirely neglected. When, however, they found it incumbent upon them to behave themselves- why, I almost expect some day to see them members of this House, they realize their sense of responsibility so acutely and have developed the chivalrous side of their nature so admirably.
I am very much in favour of this movement, but I do not see why the amount is so large.
I do not think that the amount is very large, considering the fact that the movement is spread over every province in Canada.
What is the capitalization for ?
The same as in almost any other corporation of the kind: For the development and advancement of their undertaking. They may hold lands in the different provinces, have their offices and so on.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) for second reading of Bill No. 173, respecting British nationality naturalization and aliens.

In my judgment, no subject affecting the domestic welfare of the people is of more importance, especially so far as western Canada is concerned, than the Bill now under consideration. No subject has engaged more closely the time and attention of thoughtful men in western Canada than this. Our Canadian clubs, our boards of trade and allied institutions have been giving this matter a very great deal of attention and consideration. It has been the universal view-when I say universal, I mean that it has been the view of men of business, of professional men, of ministers of the gospel, and of others-in fact, of all the citizens of communities that have thought it well to interest themselves in this matter-that the period of residence in Canada necessary to obtain citizenship under the laws of our country has been entirely too limited. In other words, citizenship was entirely too cheap. This is not in any sense a party question. Men who have spoken to me most strongly on the subject have been men who differed from me in political matters; but they have been actuated by a patriotic desire to see placed upon the statute books some provision whereby there would be an assurance that those who had the benefits and privileges of British citizenship or of Canadian citizenship, in the sense in which the words have been used this afternoon, would have some proper and due appreciation of the benefits and privileges which they were obtaining. It seems to me that it is fundamental that that should be so. I am sure that the hon. gentleman who preceded me will agree with me that in the province in which we both reside there has been a very great laxity in so far as the enforcement of proper regulations is concerned with regard to the obtaining of citizenship. I once said in addressing a large gathering under the auspices of one of the Canadian clubs in Alberta, that it was not the fault of one party or of another that vast numbers of foreigners, using the word in the broad sense of the term, were gathered together a few weeks before an election, that suddenly there appeared amongst them a man whom they did not know and who had been



authorized either by the local or by the federal authorities to administer an oath; who asked them their names, who asked them to stand up, had them sign, or make their mark where they could not sign their names to oaths which they did not understand, took the papers and put >a certificate upon the back that he knew these men to be of good character.
These papers were hung up for a few days in the court house, and shortly after a certificate was issued on the payment of twenty-five cents, declaring the applicant a British subject. There was no going before a judge, as in eastern Canada. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked that question. There has been no change in this respect in Alberta and Saskatchewan since the early days. When courts were difficult to get at and only Supreme Court judges were in office it was not possible to enforce the law regarding naturalization as in the older provinces, and men became citizens of this Dominion in the easy way I speak of. And as a matter of fact in some instances they regarded themselves as being British subjects in the broad sense without having any proper appreciation of what they were doing, or what they had done, or the benefits and privileges they were obtaining. I really think there are very few men in this House who have an appreciation of exactly what took place in the western provinces in those early days. I have seen forty men converted into British subjects in an evening. The same has taken place with men to whom I was opposed politically; I have seen it time after time. Men were called up, perhaps an interpreter present, a question or two asked-' So help me God '-kiss the Bible, then let them make their mark or sign their name. By this process these men acquired a slip of paper, and when an election came they said they were British subjects, and produced the evidence. I remember a discussion I had a few years ago with a very thoughtful member of the Liberal party regarding the situation, and he said that possibly there was no matter of greater importance affecting our democracy than the naturalization of our alien population. It is for that reason that I am so glad that this Bill has been introduced-a step in the right direction.
My hon. friend said the term had been lengthened from three to five years. True. In all seriousness, and I am sure that those who live in the large centres of our western life will agree with me-places where you have a very large alien population, cities like Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and
[Mr. R. B. Bennett 1
Vancouver-no words that I could use would clearly indicate just what the difficulties are of assimilating that population to British ideas and British ideals and giving them some aspiration for and appreciation of the future of this country. In view of the conditions, I think you will agree that if the time is extended to five years it is not too long. If the benefits of our citizenship and participation in our future are, as I think they are, privileges so great that they cannot be measured or expressed in terms that I might use, and if its obligations involve the engaging of the empire to which we belong in war, if insult is offered to our citizens, five years is not too long a term. I have been watching the progress of the United States in this matter, and in that great republic the period of probation is five years-so far as I can see it has been five years at any time during our lifetime. At one time they had an immigration of 700,000 a year for years together, and once it ran up over a million. And with these facts before them, and in spite of the desire of the politicians to get office, the common patriotism of the law makers of the United States raised them far above political considerations and they united to pass naturalization laws of the most stringent character. Under that law it became necessary for the alien who wished to attain what they considered the priceless benefit of American citizenship to first make a declaration of his intention and afterwards present a petition to the courts. My hon. friend from Pictou said this might be a costly process. Yet in the United States, with that vast cosmopolitan population looked after by trained politicians and widespread political organizations, the alien must declare his intentions, afterwards petition that court and have witnesses to speak for him, and only after he has shown that he has the necessary qualification does he receive his certificate. He is examined as to his knowledge of the Constitution, Declaration of Independence, the list of presidents. He is supposed to have some knowledge of geography-of the border communities, north and south. If the House is at all interested, I would like to refer to the Naturalization laws of the United States, which provide as follows:
Sec. 4. That an alien may be admitted to become a citizen of the United States in the following: manner and not otherwise:
First. He shall declare on oath before the clerk of any court authorized by this Act to naturalize aliens, or his authorized deputy, in the district in which such alien resides, two years at least prior to his admission, and after

he has reached the age of eighteen years, that it is bona fide his intention to become a citizen of the United States, and to renounce for ever all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty, and particularly, by name, to the prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty of which the alien may be at the time a citizen or subject. And such declaration shall set forth the name, age, occupation, personal description, place of birth, last foreign residence and allegiance, the date of arrival, the name of the vessel, if any, in which he came to the United States, and the present place of residence in the United States of said alien: Provided, however, that no alien who, in conrormity with the law in force at the date of his declaration, has declared his intention to become a citizen of the United States shall be required to renew such declaration ; Provided further, that any person belonging to the class of persons authorized and qualified under existing law to become a citizen of the United States, who has resided constantly in the United States during a prior of five years next preceding May first, nineteen hundred and ten, who, because of misinformation in regard to his citizenship or the requirements of the law governing the naturalization of citizens has laboured and acted under the impression that he was, or could become a citizen of the United States, and has in good faith exercised the rights or duties of a citizen or intended citizen of the United States because of such wrongful information and belief may, upon making a showing of such facts satisfactory to a court having jurisdiction to issue papers of naturalization to an alien, and the court in its judgment believes that such person has been for a period of more than five years entitled upon proper proceedings to be naturalized as a citizen of the United States, receive from the said court a final certificate of naturalization, and the said court may issue such certificate without requiring proof of former declaration by, or on the part of such person of their intention to become a citizen of the United States, but such applicant for naturalization shall comply in all other respects with the law relative to the issuance of final papers of naturalization to aliens.
Second. Not less than two years nor more than seven years after he has made such declaration of intention he shall make and file, in duplicate, a petition in writing, signed by the applicant in his own handwriting and duly verified, in which petition such applicant shall state his full name, his place of residence (by street and number, if possible), his occupation, and, if possible, the date and place of his birth; the place from which he emigrated, and the date and place of his arrival in the United States, and, if he entered through a port, the name of the vessel on which he arrived ; the time when and the place and name of the court where he declared his intention to become a citizen of the United States; if he is married he shall state the name of his wife and, if possible, the country of her nativity and her place of residence at the time of filing his petition; and if he has children, the name, date, and place of birth and place of residence of each child living at the time of the filing of his petition: Provided, that if he has filed his declaration before the passage of this Act he shall not be required to sign the petition in his own handwriting.
The petition shall set forth that he is not a
