disbeliever in or opposed to organized government, or a member of or affiliated with any organization or body of persons teaching disbelief in or opposed to organized government, a polygamist or believer in the practice of polygamy* and that it is his intention to become a citizen of the United States and to renounce absolutely and for ever all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty* and particularly by name to the prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty of which he at the time of filing of his petition may be a citizen or subject, and that it is his intention to reside permanently within the United States, and whether or not he has been denied admission as a citizen of the United States, and, if denied, the ground or grounds of such denial, the court or courts in which such decision was rendered, and that the cause for such denial has since been cured or removed, and every fact material to his naturalization and required to be proved upon the final hearing of his application.
The petition shall also be verified by the affidavits of at least two credible witnesses, who are citizens of the United States, and who shall state in their affidavits that they have personally known the applicant to be a resident of the United States for a period of at least five years continuously, and of the state, territory, or district in which the application is made for a period of at least one year immediately preceding the date of the filing of his petition, and that they each have personal knowledge that the petitioner is a person of good moral character, and that he is in every way qualified, in their opinion, to be admitted as a citizen of the United States.
At the time of filing his petition there shall be filed with the clerk of the court a certificate from the Department of Commerce and Labour, if the petitioner arrives in the United States after the passage of this Act, stating the date, place, and manner of his arrival in the United States, and the declaration of intention of such petitioner, which certificate and declaration shall be attached to and made a part of said petition.
Third. He shall, before he is admitted to citizenship, declare on oath in open court that he will support the constitution of the United States, and that he absolutely and entirely renounces and abjures all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty, and particularly by name to the prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty of which he wras before a citizen or subject; that he will support and defend the constitution and laws of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic, and bear true faith and allegiance to the same.
Fourth. It shall be made to appear to the satisfaction of the court admitting any alien to citizenship that immediately preceding the date of his application he has resided continuously within the United States five years at least, and within the state or territory where such court is at the time held one year at least, and that during that time he has behaved as a man of good moral character, attached to the principles of the constitution of the United States, and well disposed to the good order and happiness of the same. In addition to the oath of the applicant, the testimony of at least two witnesses, citizens of the United States, as to the facts of residence, moral character, and attachment to the principles of the constitution shall be required, and the name, place of residence, anrl

occupation of each witness shall be set forth in the record.
Fifth. In case the alien applying to be admitted to citizenship has borne any hereditary title, or has been of any of the orders of nobility in the kingdom or state from which he came, he shall, in addition to the above requisites, make an express renunciation of his title or order of nobility in the court to which his application is made, and his renunciation shall be recorded in the court.
Sixth. When any alien who has declared his intention to become a citizen of the United States dies before he is actually naturalized the widow and minor children of such alien may, by complying with the other provisions of this Act, be naturalized without making any declaration of intention.
Sec. 5. That the clerk of the court shall, immediately after filing the petition, give notice thereof by posting in a public and conspicuous place in his office, or in the building in which his office is situated, under an appropriate heading, the name, nativity, and residence of the alien, the date and place of his arrival in the United States, and the date, as nearly as may be, for the final hearing of his petition, and the names of the witnesses whom the applicant expects to summon in his behalf; and the clerk shall, if the applicant requests it, issue a subpoena for the witnesses so named by the said applicant to appear upon the day set for the final hearing, but in case such witnesses can not be produced upon the final hearing other witnesses may be summoned.
Sec. 6. That petitions for naturalization may be made and filed during term time or vacation of the court and shall be docketed the same day as filed, but final action thereon shall be had only on stated days, to be fixed by rule of the court, and in no case shall final action be had upon a petition until at least ninety days have elapsed after filing and posting the notice of such petition: Provided, that no person shall be naturalized nor shall any certificate of naturalization be issued by any court within thirty days preceding the holding of any general election within its territorial jurisdiction. It shall be lawful, at the time and as a part of the naturalization of any alien, for the court, in its discretion, upon the petition of such alien, to make a decree changing the name of said alien, and his certificate of naturalization shall be issued to him in accordance therewith.
Sec. 7. That no person who disbelieves in or who is opposed to organized government, or who is a member of or affiliated with any organization entertaining and teaching such disbelief in or opposition to organized government, or who advocates or teaches the duty, necessity, or propriety of the unlawful assaulting or killing of any officer or officers, either of specific individuals or of officers generally, of the Government of the United States, or of any other organized government, because of his or their official character, or who is a polygamist, shall be naturalized or be made a citizen of the United States.
Section 8 deals with a point referred to by my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin). No country bas invited to its shores a more polyglot or more cosmopolitan population than the United States, yet this section provides as follows:
fMr. R. B. Bennett]
That no alien shall hereafter be naturalized or admitted as a citizen of the United States who can not speak the English language: Provided, that this requirement shall not apply to aliens who are physically unable to comply herewith, If they are otherwise qualified to become citizens of the United States:	And
provided further, that the requirements of this section shall not apply to any alien who has prior to the passage of this Act declared his intention to become a citizen of the United States in conformity with the law in force at the date of making such declaration: Provided further, that the requirements of section eight shall not apply to aliens who shall hereafter declare their intention to become citizens and who shall make homestead entries upon the public lands of the United States and comply in all other respects with the laws providing for homestead entries on such lands.
This country having itwo official languages -not as the hon. member for Regina indicated because of the dominant character of the one or the other, but because there are two official languages-it is provided in the Bill before the House that the applicant for naturalization shall be able to speak either English or French. Section 9 of the United States law provides:
That every final hearing upon such petitions shall be had in open court before a judge or judges thereof, and every final order which may be made upon such petition shall be under the hand of the court and entered in full upon a record kept for that purpose, and upon such final hearing of such petition the applicant and witnesses shall be examined under oath before the court and in the presence of the court.
1 admit that in days gone by it would have caused extreme difficulty and hardship, and would have involved very great expense, if every -man desiring to become a citizen under our naturalization law had had to attend a court. But now that our population is increasing, now that district courts are held in nearly every village along the line of railway, it cannot be said that we ask too much of an applicant seeking the great benefits of our citizenship when we provide that he shall appear in open court.
I daresay that many men in this House have read that very thoughtful series of articles in The Century by one of the foremost professors of Wisconsin University, in which he referred to the grave and manifest danger confronting the people of the United States, by reason of the difficulties they have experienced in assimilating their population, notwithstanding the many safeguards in their naturalization laws. I have been told of these difficulties by many eminent Americans, professors in universities and men who have to do with naturalization in the United States. If that be so, let us

learn something, at least by history, and let us take a step in the right direction by imposing restrictions in this Bill, not in any sense a party measure, but as representing a combined effort on the part of the representatives of the people of Canada to see that those who come after us bear the standard of our civilization, and carry it forward with a due and proper appreciation of their responsibilities and their duties and their obligations. We cannot do that unless we do something to acquaint those who desire to take on our citizenship with its benefits and privileges, and also with its responsibilities and obligations. It is for that reason that I have ventured to make these observations regarding this Bill, because it is a matter in which, for some years past, I have taken a deep and abiding interest. I am not so much concerned about imperial citizenship as in having a proper domestic citizenship in the first instance; but I am glad that this Bill does make a move in another direction, because I had the pleasure not many months ago of addressing a Women's American Club, and one of the difficulties they had experienced had been to understand exactly where they stood with relation to citizenship. Many people in this country have been unable to understand exactly why they should come into this country, and, having taken an oath of naturalization, find themselves debarred from all the benefits and privileges which should belong to them as British subjects. You doubtless know that some people have left our shores believing that they were British subjects, but have found that the certificate of naturalization which they carried did not give them the benefit of British citizenship, and that beyond the three mile limit they were again citizens of the land from which they came, that they had to look to the protection of that flag and as they had disowned that flag in a sense, it was humiliating to them to have to make an appeal for protection under it. This Bill removes that difficulty and provides that the man who has British citizenship under it is a British subject wherever he may go, alike in India, South Africa, Australia and Canada; and that he carries with him the certificate that entitles him to the privileges of British citizenship and the protection of the British flag wherever he may go. If he be insulted in a foreign land, he will no longer meet with the difficulties that would confront him if he had only Canadian naturalization. He will now be able to say, as one of old did
when he was confronted by his enemies:
' I am a Roman citizen.' He will be able to say. 'I am a British subject, by reason of the naturalization conferred upon me by this Act.' My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) referred to the fact that after a certificate had been granted by a judge there should be a final certificate conferring upon the person naturalized the priceless benefit of British citizenship, and that that certificate should be issued by the Secretary of State. Why? Because it is an official state act and no longer the act of a court. It is an act of the state, speaking as a state. It is an act of one of these self-governing colonies of the empire and, if you like of the British Empire itself, speaking through its Secretary of State, under the seal of the department, conferring upon the individual the benefits, rights and privileges of British citizenship. That is the reason that it is so provided in the Bill. Hon. members have observed that the sections of the Bill are not peculiar to Canada at all, they are sections identical in term and form with those of a Bill now being passed by the Imperial Parliament. I have observed in the press that the Bill now presented to this House, with 'such changes as are made necessary by reason of our geographical position, has been passed by the House of Lords and is now before the House of Commons. The hon. member for Edmonton this afternoon referred to certain difficulties and dangers that might arise by reason of the passing of this Bill and the change which it might effect in what he properly termed purely Canadian citizenship. I think he confused immigration with naturalization. We have the power, under the constitution, to determine who shall come within our geographical boundaries. That power is given under the British North America Act. We may decide that a British subject from one section of this empire may not come within the boundaries of this country, so broad is the power conferred upon us by our constitution. The power of naturalization and the power to determine the class and character of immigrants who shall come within our boundary, are two powers separate and distinct. We are exercising to-night power to determine on what condition and on what restrictions and on what responsibilities and obligations men may take upon themselves the burden and privileges of British citizenship. We would exercise under another section of our constitution the power to determine what class of people we think should be admitted within our

boundaries. With deference to my hon. friend from Edmonton, I think possibly there is a confusion of terms in the expressions he used this afternoon. I cannot express very readily the pleasure I have in seeing such a measure as this placed upon the statute book, not in any sense as a party measure, but as one which embodies the best views and the soundest and most reasoned conclusions that representative statesmen have been able to arrive at after consideration of the views of every section and of the peculiar conditions that surround every portion of the King's dominions.

I do not want to be considered altogether reactionary, but there are one or two features of this Bill to which I must take objection 'before it receives its final reading. Every one of us is very anxious that all citizens of this country coming from alien countries should have a working knowledge of one of the official languages of this country, English or French. But I want to point out that this particular piece of legislation may have a very serious effect upon a considerable number of settlers on the western plains, if not in other parts of Canada. Subsection (b) of section 2 provides:
The applicant for a certificate of naturalization must he of good character and have an adequate knowledge of either the English or French language. I
I would like to know what the Minister of Justice means by the word ' adequate.' What does he propose to consider an adequate knowledge of the English or French language? Would the knowledge of the Speaker of this House who reads the prayers in French be considered an adequate knowledge of French? Would the ability to say ' yes ' and ' no ' to some very simple questions be considered an adequate knowledge *of the English language, or sufficient to qualify for a certificate of naturalization under this Bill?
We shall require a board of examiners who will have to lay down certain rules as to what constitutes an adequate knowledge, inasmuch as the Act does not define what is meant by an ' adequate ' knowledge of the English and French languages. Even amongst the members of this House I think you will find that there is a very great variety in the vocabularies which they possess in reference to both the English and French languages. Some of us may be conversant with, and may be able to use, so many thousand words, while

others may have a somewhat limited vocabulary. There is no limitation and no definition of the term ' adequate ' knowledge of English and French. If I may be permitted to give a personal illustration, when I first came here I conceived that it might be of great service to me if I spoka the French language so that I would understand a great many of the excellent speeches which are delivered in that language in this House. I took a few lessons, but I came to the conclusion that even at my comparatively early stage of existence learning a new language is a very difficult proposition. We have persons coming from European countries who do not know a word of English. Many of these people, even if they never learn a word of English, become good citizens and are just as loyal to the flag of this country as many who have been born under that flag. It is going to impose a severe penalty on this class of immigrant, who may be a first-class citizen in every other respect, if we are going to make his inability to learn a new language a bar to his securing a certificate of naturalization. I protest' with all the vigour in my power against the insertion of this provision in the Act. I shall be very glad indeed if when we go into -committee the Minister of Justice will kindly explain what he understands to be the meaning of the word ' adequate ' in paragraph (b) of section 2 of the Bill.
There is another feature of the Bill which looks to me, upon a cursory examination, to be exceedingly objectionable. I find it in various places in the Bill, particularly in sections 2 and 6. Section 6 reads as follows :
An alien who has been naturalized before the passing of this Act may apply to the Secretary of State of Canada for a certificate of naturalization under this Act, and the Secretary of State of Canada may grant to him a certificate on such terms and conditions as he may think fit.
The same authority is given to the Secretary of State in section 2 of this Bill. I do not think that any officer of the Government, or any member of the Government, such as the Secretary of State, should have any such power as it is proposed to give him by this Bill. It is altogether out of the question that the Secretary of State should be authorized to issue certificates of naturalization on such terms and conditions as he thinks fit. We should say here and now in drafting this Bill upon what terms and conditions the Secretary of State

shall issue a certificate of naturalization. Certainly this Parliament has the authority and responsibility and it would be taking away the right of the people through their representatives to delegate the authority to the Secretary of State or to give him any such power as that which is proposed here. I protest very strongly against this feature of the Bill. We have prescribed the method of application for a certificate of naturalization. In my own province, for instance, the application must be made-
-to a judge of the Supreme Court of the province or of any district court, sitting in chambers in the judicial district in which the alien resides.
Certain forms are gone through, the judge certifies that the applicant is entitled to his certificate of naturalization, that certificate is forwarded to the Secretary of State and still, after the judge who has made an examination into the facts of the 9 p.m. case has declared that the applicant is a fit subject for naturalization, it is left entirely at the discretion of the Secretary of State whether or not that certificate shall be granted. In a case where a judge of the court decides that the applicant has the necessary 'qualifications to become a British subject it should not be in the discretion of the Secretary of State, but ipso facto, the Secretary of State should be required to issue the certificate to the applicant.

The observations that I have to make are practically along the lines of those which have been made by my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely). I believe that considerable caution should be exercised in granting certificates to aliens who wish to become naturalized British or Canadian citizens, but I am not one of those who believe that- these safeguards should be of such a character as to place an absolute discretion in the hands of the Secretary of State to say whether or not a person shall become a British subject, a person whom he has never seen and knows nothing about. When a judge, after having seen the gentleman who may be making application for naturalization, after having examined him, after having heard what he had to say, decides to grant a certificate, his decision should not be overridden by the Secretary of State and we should not empower that officer to say: I do not think I shall grant this man a certificate and to decree that under such circumstances his word shall be final is not in accordance with the principles of justice and fair play.
As far as the question of languages is concerned, it is quite true that we have two official languages in Canada but I think the Aot is going a little too far in saying that only those who have an adequate knowledge of French and English shall become naturalized British subjects. It would be a good thing for all the people within the confines of Canada, for their own benefit, to have an adequate knowledge of French and English.

What about the
Germans?

Yes, I am coming to the German question. We have in our part of the country a great many Germans and we have no better citizens than the gentlemen who come from Germany. Somehow or other the Germans, as, I suppose all other races, live in the same vicinity.
They do not mix with the people who speak English or French, and consequently they may live in Canada for ten or fifteen years without having an adequate knowledge of either language. It would be unfair to debar such people, if they are otherwise desirable, from becoming British subjects. In some of the eastern counties of Nova Scotia we have men who understand neither French nor English, who speak only the Gaelic, and it would be just as fair and proper to say that these men should be called aliens as it is to deny those of German extraction British citizenship because they cannot speak English or French. Section 6 of the Act is legislation which has never before been attempted in any parliament. It means that if twenty years ago a person came to Canada and after three years he became naturalized under the law as it then stood, when this legislation passes if that man wants to have the status of British citizenship he has to apply to the Secretary of State, and it is absolutely in the discretion of the Secretary of State to say whether he shall be granted a certificate of British citizenship, although he was granted that certificate fifteen years ago by a competent tribunal. That is the worst feature of the whole Bill. Under sections 18 and 21 it would appear to me that the applicant must appear personally in court, but to that I have no great objection, although, under the law as it now stands, he may appear by affidavit through his solicitor. But having satisfied the judge that he should become a British subject, it is still discretionary with the Secretary of State to say whether he shall or not. I lake objection to that, but not such strong objection as I do to section 6, which means that

hundreds and thousands of persons who have supposed they were British subjects for the past fifteen or twenty years, are really not so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The effect of section 6 is not to deprive a man, who was naturalized twenty years ago, or last year, or yesterday, or to-day, of all the rights he got in virtue of that naturalization which is a local naturalization in Canada. But if he wishes to have the additional benefit that comes from a certificate under this Act, he must go to the Secretary of State and get one. The purpose is to give a man, because he has been already naturalized, the advantage that a man naturalized under this Act would get.
That being so, I withdraw my objection to the section, but I would point out that the draftsman does not make plain what is meant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was drafted by about the best draftsman in the world.
Notwithstanding that, I say that the section is not clear if it means what the Minister of Justice says it means.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It has been drafted under the supervision of the drafting staff of the British House of Commons. It is copied precisely from the British Bill.
The draftsman may not have been familiar with Canadian conditions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not a question of conditions; it is a question of formally drafting the wording of the section.

Let us look at what the section says. It starts out by saying that the Naturalization Act i3 repealed by this Act, and then it goes on to say that an alien who has been naturalized before the passing of this Act may apply to the Secretary of State of Canada for a certificate of naturalization under -this Act. It does not say a certificate of naturalization under this Act will entitle him to British citizenship.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: * Under this Act,' will so entitle him.

And so will a certificate that will be granted to any person hereafter under this Act. The section is certainly obscure. I believe that a judge would decide under this section that a person who had heretofore become naturalized must re-

ceive a certificate from the Secretary of State before he be a recognized British subject, because the existing Naturalization Act has been repealed and this will be the only Naturalization Act there will be on the statute-books of Canada when it becomes law. Notwithstanding the ability of the draftsman, in my humble opinion the section is obscure and of doubtful meaning. This is very important legislation and any regulation which will be incorporated in this Bill should be made by the Parliament of Canada and not delegated to the Governor in Council or to the Secretary of State. Some of the most important things connected with naturalization do not come before the view of Parliament at all, but are handed over to the Governor in Council to-provide for by regulation. Parliament has the power to make laws, and in an important Bill like this everything that has to do with naturalization should come under the view of Parliament, and be passed on by Parliament, and not handed over to the Governor in Council.
Although I am not a profound lawyer, I have very serious doubts as to what a judge would hold to be the meaning of that particular section, in view of the fact that the present Naturalization Act will be absolutely repealed by this legislation.

With all due deference to my hon. friend, it strikes me that the explanation of the hon. Minister of Justice of section 8 is quite reasonable; and I believe that a judge, in deciding as to the meaning of that section, would decide it exactly as the minister has explained it. Will an applicant who has been naturalized under the old law have to go through all the forms that an alien will have to go through, or will he merely have to apply to the Secretary of State?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention of the section is to enable a person who has been already naturalized under our existing law to get the further advantage under this legislation without having to go through the whole procedure again.
What is the status of the man who is naturalized now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The man who is naturalized now will continue to be what he is- a British subject within Canada.
Where is the section that says so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We do not require to say so. Under the existing legislation he has become a British subject within Canada; he is that, and there is nothing in this legislation to take that away from him. The effect of the repealed Act is entirely exhausted with regard to every man's naturalization under it, and this Bill does not say that he will lose anything he has. Some men will get more than they have at present.

The Act was good
at the time he became naturalized, and this legislation does not take the naturalization away from him.
Something has been said about fraud being perpetrated in cases of naturalization. 1 am very doubtful if this Bill will prevent fraud absolutely any more than the existing legislation does. Stories have gone abroad that fraud is frequently perpetrated in regard to naturalization. My experience of naturalization has been in the country; and although there are now very few cases of naturalization in my constituency, because nearly every person there has been naturalized, I have seen hundreds of people who have been naturalized, and I have never heard of a case where any fraudulent act has been perpetrated with regard to time or otherwise. There may be some cases of fraud in the cities, but I think that most of the cases that we hear of with regard to fraud are made up. There may be some sin in the way of fraud in Tegard to naturalization, but there has been a great deal more sin, 'to my mind, in the lying and exaggeration that has' been done in regard to the cases of fraud. While in the cities there may have been much more of it than in the country places, I think there has been practically none at all. It would be a very sad thing for the impression to go abroad that there is much truth in these stories we hear. It is better for the people to conclude that there has been lying done in the country than that there has been fraud and perjury perpetrated, as has sometimes been claimed.
Perhaps the minister will tell us if this Bill is an exact copy of the Imperial Bill, as far as it is possible to copy it here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
The provision with regard to language is in the Imperial Bill also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, in the United
Kingdom the English language alone, with the proviso that in any British possession, where there is any language that stands
on an equal footing, then either the one or the other, and we act on that.

In regard to language, it may be necessary to have that provision in order to entitle us to make our naturalization empire-wide; but it does not strike me as being very fair. In my boyhood days in Ontario, I came in contact with a great many Highland Scotchmen, who have made the best settlers, but who have never had a good knowledge of English in their lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They would not need
to be naturalized; they were bom that way.

That is begging the
question. The principle is the same, that a man must have an adequate knowledge of English or French.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At the end of five years.

Well, they have not.
Some of these men have lived there for fifty years and have not an adequate knowledge of the English language, but they make the best settlers in Ontario and they have made Ontario what it is. The same may be said as regards the Germans; in some of the constituencies where there are a great many German settlers, there are probably some old Germans who have made the best settlers, but who have not an adequate knowledge of English.

How does the hon.
gentleman interpret 'adequate knowledge'?

It is not my duty to
interpret the language of statutes provided by the minister.

I was just asking for
information.
If my hon. friend will permit me, I was just going to ask the question myself of the minister. I think it is my place to ask him.
Two in the dark seeking liglht.

I just want to throw
out that suggestion to the minister. The provision may he entirely necessary, but I shall be very much surprised if the imperial Bill uses the word ' adequate '.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Well, I think the British authorities should be induced to change that. We have heard so much of adequate protection in this country and every man

who bblieves in protection believes in adequate protection. It does not matter how high or how low it is, it is adequate protection, and we shall have hundreds of judges interpreting this taw, and there will be hundreds of different interpretations as to What the word 'adequate' means. I think it is a very unfair term, because it can be made to mean practically anything.
My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is not now in his seat. I think he stated, in speaking of the terms of the American Act, that applicants must be able to speak the English language, so as to be able to be understood. If the qualification was that the applicants must be able to speak the English language so as to be able to be understood, or to be able to write it so as to be able to be understood, a test of that kind could be very readily applied. I hope that my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) will not ask me to explain the word ' adequate ', because I cannot do so and I do not think that he can. One person will give one explanation and another, another.
With regard to the matter of good character, I do not know whether there is any way of getting over that or not. In my constituency there has to be an affidavit that the applicant is of good character before he is given a certificate, and I have never seen any one fail to get that affidavit; and I do not think any one will fail, unless he is a notorious reprobate of the worst character who has been convicted several times. This provison has been ineffectual in the past; and while it will not be as ineffectual as the word ' adequate ', it will be ineffectual in the future.
I think it would be well for the minister to consider whether some better means might not be found to test the applicant's qualifications in that particular. The reading which the hon. member for Calgary gave from the American statutes indicated a course that seemed to me a little better. It is true that the applicant there must show that he is of good character, but he must also show that he believes in constituted government. It is more important to show that a man has not been convicted of any offence and that he is a believer in constituted government, and therefore not dangerous, than to depend on evidence of good character, because every man can supply that.
But the most serious feature of the Bill to my mind is that referring to the Secretary of State. It seems strange that after a judge, who has been solemnly appointed

to his position, has had the applicant before him and has been in the very best position to judge whether the man is entitled to naturalization, when the judge's decision comes before the Secretary of State the Secretary of State has absolute discretion with regard to it. He may refuse it for a mere whim, if he be whimsical; he does as he pleases, and is not accountable to anybody. With all due respect, I think that very unwise. Many a time in the case of an appeal to a judge from the decision of a magistrate, I have heard the judge say that as to the credibility of witnesses he did not pretend to form an opinion different from that of the magistrate, the magistrate having heard the evidence and seen the parties must be the better judge of credibility. But in this case we reverse that principle entirely. Here is a case decided by a judge who is accustomed to testing such matters and is in the best position to test them. The Secretary of State may be a lawyer or he may not, he may have no knowledge of law, yet he is given power to throw out the judge's finding absolutely. I think the minister must see that that is a very unwise proceeding, and that there is no good reason for it. It may be well that the papers should go before the Secretary of State and I do not think there would be any harm to have a little delay- these things are often rushed through too quickly. It might be well to have the official signature to the document if the minister thinks it wise. But to say that it shall he in the discretion of the Secretary of State to decide whether the certificate shall be granted or not would be pure nonsense in my opinion. This I think one of the most objectionable features in the Bill, and one of the most objectionable features one could imagine in any Bill.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
The House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Blondin in the chair.
On section 1-definition of a natural-bom British subject:

A resident of the protectorate of Uganda, under this Act will, of course, have all the rights of British citizenship and be able to assert them in Canada. Whatever our law here is, he will be entitled to all the privileges under that law. Is that the same as the law is at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only difference in regard to that, I think, is that the la/w here makes it clearer than it was before that a person who is .bom under the jurisdiction is held to be born within the King's allegiance. A person is born a British subject if he is born in a place which is within the British allegiance.

Subsection 3 provides:
Nothing in this section shall, except as otherwise expressly provided affect the status of any person born before the commencement of this Act.
Suppose a person is born in the United States and becomes naturalized in Canada, would he not, 'by the efflux of time, become a full-fledged British subject within the empire?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under section 6, a person in that position, by applying to the Secretary of State, may get a certificate under the Act which makes him a subject throughout the empire.
Is there a departure from the present law under this first section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under subsection (a)
there is no departure. Under subsection (b) there is this difference between the law as enacted by it and the law as it stands tc-day: the privilege of being a British subject, granted to persons bom outside of tl'J dominions, is limited to persons whose fathers were British subjects, whereas under the law as it stands that privilege was granted to persons born outside of the dominions whose fathers or granfathers had been natural-born British subjects. Under the law as now amended, the privilege dies not extend to the grandchild; on the other hand it is widened to the extent that under the law as it now stands it was required that the father, or grandfather, as the ease might be, should have been a natural-born British subject, the grandchild of a naturalized British subject or the child of a naturalized British subject would not have been a British subject. Under this provision as it is now to be enacted, the child of any British subject who is born outside of the dominions will be a British subject whether his father was a naturalized or a natural-born British subject, but the grandchild will not be a British subject.

Take the case of a child born in the United States of a British subject. Under the law of the United States he is an American citizen. If
that person, who is a citizen of the United States, comes to Canada, may he claim to be a British subject also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
He can choose between the one and the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, he can choose. So long as the two tests co-exist the test which makes nationality depend on the place of birth and the test which makes it depend on relationship, you will have the possibility of a man having a double nationality.

Suppose that person returns to the United States, having that double nationality, and certain duties are imposed upon by the law of the land; let us say, for instance, enlistment in the army. Would he be able to claim his privilege of Canadian citizenship to avoid enlistment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think he would, because he would then be in the country whose law declared him to be a citizen of its own and no legislation that we could possibly enact would prevent that country from enforcing its own law'. Assuming that under their law the child of an American citizen born in Canada would be an American-about that I am not quite clear-the same thing might happen if he were born here of an American father, but we would not expect to submit to the American's contention that he was their subject and not ours, when our law says that because he was born here he is a British subject. So, as I said before, until all the nations come to adopt one single test of what constitutes being a citizen or a subject, we will never avoid the possibility of a double nationality. There are provisions further on in the Bill enabling subjects to throw off their nationality, .affording a means of getting rid of the double nationality so far as getting rid of the quality of a British subject is concerned. As between the United States and Great Britain, there is a convention of 1872, if I remember correctly, under which, by agreement between the parties, an American citizen who becomes naturalized as a British subject is no longer claimed by the United States as being a citizen, and vice versa. As to the British subject who becomes naturalized in the United States under the treaty, Great Britain agrees to recognize that naturalization and to recognize that change of nationality. But short of treaties and arrangement of that sort, it is very difficult to avoid the condition where a man may be of two nationalities.

Mr. 'SAM. SHARPE:	Will this legislation have the effect of naturalizing the children of foreign consuls residing here during their term of office ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I understand it, the child of an ambassador that is born within the British dominions is not a British subject, because, although he is born within the Dominion, he is not born within His Majesty's allegiance. You will notice that it is required that a man shall be born not only within the dominions, but also within His Majesty's allegiance. The child of a foreign sovereign born within the Dominion would not be a British subject, because his, father is recognized as a sovereign within the empire and as not coming under the control of its laws, and the same privilege is extended to the Ambassador as the personal representative of the Sovereign. As regards a consul, I do not think he has any such status as will prevent this law being applicable to his child.

In my judgment, an
amending statute would be more in line with present requirements if it provided for exclusion from British citizenship in Canada instead of confirming an inclusion in British citizenship in Canada of races and peoples who are not desirable in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are dealing with the definition of a British subject by birth and it is not very easy to delimit that into sections of the empire. A man is a British subject by birth at the moment of his birth; that quality is stamped on him, and I doubt very much whether the Parliament of Canada-and I am always inclined to take the widest possible view of our powers-has the power to determine that a person who at common law is a British subject shall not be a British subject in Canada. We are not talking about citizens, Canadian or otherwise; we are talking only about British subjects, and if we could get a clear idea of just what it means to be a British subject we could avoid a good many of the things that are apprehended. The fact that a man is a British subject makes him owe allegiance to the sovereign and entitles him to the protection that the sovereign gives to the subject, and that is all. It does not entitle him to live in Canada, it does not entitle him to come into Canada, it does not entitle him to vote, it does not entitle him to anything that the law of this country does not choose to give him. That is the full extent of it, and I do not know that

it would have any great influence, if we had the power, to undertake to say that classes of persons who, under the common law from time immemorial, have been British subjects shall not hereafter in Canada be British subjects.

I do not know that I agree. It would be very important to have the power, but I do not think we have it If we had the power-and this is a question which is constantly recurring in British Columbia, where the province has excluded Asiatics from certain privileges of British citizenship-1 daresay it would avoid a good deal of the conflict that is sure to arise in that province. I agree that we have not the power, because under the Confederation Act we have the power to legislate on naturalization, that is, to give by legislatioin the right to certain parties who have no right by title of their birth. We cannot go beyond that.

We are confirming the
citizenship in Canada of people born under the King's allegiance; but we are also making provision that those who have not been born under the King's allegiance, but who have acquired citizenship in a part of the dominions whose characteristics and populations are not considered desirable in this country, shall also have citizenship here. For instance, the dependency of Hong Kong is a part of China, and a Chinaman who acquires British citizenship in Hong Kong has British citizenship in Canada, as I understand. That is the purpose of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, the Act does notj
deal with citizenship in the slightest degree. The naturalization portion provides for making a man a British subject. The hon. member himself is the author of an Act which contains the only definition I know anywhere of what a Canadian citizen is. The Act defines a Canadian citizen to be a British subject, plus a three years resident of Canada. That is the only definition of a Canadian citizen. If a man becomes naturalized under this Act he will not be a Canadian citizen any more than he was before. He will be a British subject; he will have that quality without^ which he cannot become a Canadian citizen; but in so becoming a British subject he will be no further advanced towards Canadian citizenship than the Hindu or the British subject who arives here from India. But we are not making Canadian citizens

il45
under this Act; we are providing to make British subjects.
Did not the old Naturalization Act make British subjects?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, in Canada.

Is it within the knowledge of the minister whether any Chinese have been granted the rights of citizenship under the old Naturalization Act? I asked a question covering eastern Canada for the last ten years, but I can find no trace of any in that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not aware
whether any Chinese were naturalized or not. I know of nothing under the old Act that would prevent a Chinaman being naturalized, but I do not know of an instance where one was.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Two were naturalized in Truro in 1907.

It seems rather ludicrous that we should enact legislation permitting Chinamen to become British subjects1 when we impose on them a penalty in the form of a head-tax before they enter our territory and when, as a matter of fact, we will not admit any Chinese women to Canada.
Oh, no; there are Chinese women coming in the same as Chinamen.

It seems rather ludicrous that we are trying to exclude Chinamen from Canada, as we impose a penalty in the shape of a head tax; yet, under our naturalization laws, we permit them to become British citizens.
He would not be a Chinaman, then.

I suppose there could
not be anything in this Act to exclude them or to prevent them becoming British subjects, as that might take on an international character.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not see what we
would gain by saying that they could not become British subjects the same as other people.

I think it is wrong to
have them against British subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then, perhaps it might occur to the hon. member that the provision that the Secretary of State should have discretion is not so utterly without reason as was suggested a moment ago. The theory in this Act is not to create in any man an absolute right to be naturalized, but simply
to create certain conditions without which a man shall not be naturalized. I am not referring to the Chinaman in particular, but there are conditions where it might not be good policy to naturalize certain people or certain classes of people; and I think the discretion of the Secretary of State might be a very useful thing under the circumstances.
It is too wide.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Sometimes you have to give a wide discretion if you want to create a position where the power may be useful in certain cases.
You may give such a wide discretion that it may be exercised when not intended to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, if our position is that in Canada we can never produce any man to fill any position to whom discretion can be confided, then this is too wide a power to give to the Secretary of State; but, if it is a useful thing to this country that there should be a discretionary power, I would hate to admit that we could not do it, because we never can get a Secretary of State who can be trusted to exercise his discretion about a matter of this sort.

I quite appreciate the discretionary power of a minister of the Crown; but I would like the minister to tell the committee upon what he is going to exercise that discretion. I can find nothing upon which the Secretary of State is to exercise his thinking powers or his discretion except the certificate that he gets from the judge. The judge is supposed, after hearing the evidence, to furnish a certificate, which the applicant forwards to the Secretary of State, and that is all the evidence, as far as I can understand the Act. Apart from that certificate, is there anything else upon which the Secretary of State can exercise discretion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The judge's decision that goes to the Secretary of State is to the effect that the applicant has complied with the express requirements of this Act; but this Act does not intend to say that every man who has complied with the requirements of this Act shall have the right to be naturalized; It provides the condition, without which a man shall not be naturalized. When he goes to the Secretary of State, there are many things that may present themselves. But if the policy of this country were that it was not desirable to encourage a particular kind of immi-

gration, that a particular class of people, for reasons that perhaps you do not want to go into or discuss, were not desirable, there might be a field there for the exercise of the discretion of the Secretary of State. The Secretary of State might also have information, say that an individual who was seeking naturalization, was using our naturalization for the purpose of evading some responsibility to his own country, and we might put ourselves in a false position with regard to the inhabitants of that country, to which he owed an obligation. These things are conceivable. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) read a list of things that the United States lay down as matters concerning which the judge must inform himself. Let us suppose the applicant has laid evidence before the judge to satisfy him that he was of good character and the Secretary of State has certain information that leads him to know that the man is an anarchist-are we going to tie the hands of the Secretary of State and compel him to say that inasmuch as he has passed a judge in some remote corner of Canada where the evidence was not available, and he has succeeded in passing himself off as of good character, the Secretary of State has no option but to hand hmi a certificate of naturalization? There is a wide field for the exercise of discretionary power. If we prescribe certain conditions for naturalization, and then say simply that upon these being fulfilled the Secretary of State shall or may issue a certificate of naturalization, every man who complies with these conditions shall have a right to a certificate from the Secretary of State, no matter what the circumstances may be. The whole purpose of the provision, which is looked upon with so much apprehension, a provision which has existed in England since there has been a naturalization Act-
For a very good reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know the reason.

The reason is that the British people do not favour immigration into their territory. It was only at as recent a date as 1844, as my hon. friend said, that they had an immigration Act in England. Up to that time naturalization was a matter of the grace of the sovereign. But in this country it is altogether different; we want to open up our country to the world, and if we open up

our country to the world that implies the promise that everything we have we will share with those who come to help us to develop the country. That is the reason of the difference between this country and England. I am quite prepared to admit all the restrictions that my hon. friend has stated. There may be reasons why these restrictions should be imposed in the manner in which my hon. friend suggested impliedly when he recalled the words of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) in quoting the law of the United States. The reasons are stated why a certificate should be refused. If a man is an anarchist, or there is some other reason why he is not to be admitted, let those reasons be stated. If a man applies to a judge for a certificate, and a neighbour comes and says that he is not of good character, that he is a fugitive from justice, or has been liable to police punishment, the judge is bound to take cognizance of those matters and refuse the certificate. But what we object to is the vesting of such a discretion in a man who is not a judicial officer, but who has political responsibility only. I quite conceive there are many occasions when a discretionary power has to be exercised by the Secretary of State, but the possession of such power is always liable to very serious abuses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not question that
this power might be liable to abuse. Almost any power may be liable to abuse. It may be said that discretionary powers are particularly liable to abuse but you cannot enumerate all the things that may be good reasons why a man should not become a British subject. If we were legislating in order to create a right in somebody's favour it would be proper that a judge should determine it and that the matter should be ended. But we are not. We do not contemplate that a man, because he does certain things, is to have the right to be a British subject. After all, it is a matter of grant by the state. We must either allow somebody to have discretion or we must undertake to specify here and now, and put in the statute, every reason conceivable why it is desirable that a man should not be a British subject. Then our legislation wi'l assume such a shape that we will have created conditions undert which a man shall have the right to say; I must have a certificate of naturalization;, 1 have a right to it-no mattter what strong reasons may be in existence at the time.-which were not known before, why he should not be a British subject. It is true

that we will do our best under the section to see that he shall be of good character,, and to make him prove it, but it is obvious that in a country of this size a man who may not be of good character, is not going to the centre, to the place where people are likely to have information concerning his past life, to apply for a certificate of naturalization. The character of this man has been 'built up and acquired out-
10 p.m. side of this country very possibly. He is not going to go where people know all about him and his character. That is the kind of men we do not want. He may be a refugee and he may go to some Temote corner of the country and because there are no witnesses in that remote corner of the country he may be able to convince the judge that he is a man of good character. The Secretary of State may have information that that man is an anarchist or that for any other good reason he is an undesirable. Shall we compel the Secretary of State to say: This man went to the remotest corner of the Yukon and applied for naturalization; there was no evidence brought before the judge to show that he was of bad character, therefore, I, the Secretary of State, have no alternative but to grant him a certificate. If we want to create that sort of a situation there is nothing more to be said. But in the drafting of this Act we did not conceive that that would be desired. In the United Kingdom the Secretary of State has exercised this discretionary power from the outset- my right hon. friend says for the very simple reason that in England they do not want to encourags immigration while in this country we do.
There is another reason; in the old country they have social laws, old age pensions, and the like and they do not want to encourage old men to become citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is one reason why they do not want to encourage immigration. The reason why the right hon. gentleman thinks the Secretary of State ought to be trusted with this power in England is that they do not want to encourage immigration while in this country we do. If in this country we want to encourage immigration that is a very good reason for supposing that the Secretary of State will be reluctant to turn people down. The Secretary of State is going to be that very untrustworthy person, a politician, and he will want to encourage immigration, and therefore, will not be disposed to unnecessarily turn people
down. If it was claimed that there were too many people coming into Canada and that we did not want to encourage them to come something might be said against this provision. This discretionary power is a repressive power. For instance if a person comes before the Secretary of State and the facts are established, the ordinary course will be that the certificate will be issued.
The Secretary of State who would exercise [DOT]his discretion capriciously and without being able to put forward reasons for it, would find himself confronted with a publio opinion that would very soon put a stop to that, and the Government to which he belonged would find that it could not afford to stand behind a Secretary of State who was using that discretion in a capricious or unfair manner. I do not think we should lack sufficient confidence in our public men to allow this discretion which might, under given circumstances, be so valuable to this country. We do trust ministers with matters as important, and in view of the great safeguard this discretion may be I think we might very w'ell take the risk. I admit that the words; it shall be in his absolute discretion, do sound formidable, but it is felt that it ought to be made perfectly clear so as to avoid the application of the doctrine that wrhen you describe conditions that a man must fulfil, and then say that a public officer may, upon fulfilment, grant him a certain thing, that imposes an obligation on the public officer. These words are as strong as they are, because it is thought wise to make it perfectly clear that the Secretary of State is not bound absolutely, because these things are produced, to hand out a certificate of naturalizaion to a person to whom he may have excellent reason for refusing it. If he does refuse it will be in an exceptional case and he will be answ'erable to Parliament and to the people.
The trouble is that he will not be answerable to Parliament because the clause says he may do this without assigning any reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There may be circumstances in which it would not be possible to give reasons, but in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred there would be no such contingency. I realize that probably one of the most difficult things to find in this country is willingness to trust anybody. That may be a good quality, but because of it we lose a great deal of the advantage the country might derive if it had servants whom it could trust and was willing to trust. After all, there is more wisdom in

the old country which looks upon this provision, as they have looked upon it from the beginning, as essential.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has always been that
way in England.	-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly since the Act of 1870 if not since the Act of 1844. The original law enacted in England has been preserved ever since, and it says:
The Secretary may, with or without assigning reason, give or withhold a certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from such decision.

England has not
much immigration for the purpose of settlement, but it has 'been the home of political refugees for centuries, and for political reasons the power was properly placed there in the hands of the secretary. But the conditions in Canada are different. We are in a new world, we are looking to get people from every nation, and there never has been in Canada a demand that there should be the absolute and intricate legal procedure which is set out in this law, before a man can get naturalization. We have been talking about imperial naturalization in this country and in England for years, the idea being to get some machinery by which we could get over the anomaly that in the various dominions, on account of constitutional difficulties, there was no way to make any person a British subject in the broadest sense of the term. I think the minister should have preserved our naturalization law, so that a man who came to this country, made his home, brought up his family, looked to live here the rest of his 'life, should be able to participate in Canadian citizenship without confronting him with technical difficulties. Canada is not the home of political refugees, and the conditions are different here from those in England. The idea of giving the power to the Secretary of State in England is, to prevent a political plotter from going over there and dbtaining citizenship with a view to protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not aware from the record of political refugees in England that they have usually looked for naturalization, and I do not think that is the only reason for reposing this confidence in the English secretary.
The English secretary would naturalize a hundred in a year where we would have to naturalize thousands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can quite understand there are not so many cases of naturalization in the United Kingdom. That is undoubtedly true; and probably the real reason why we have to provide for the proof being taken outside is in the first place by reason of the immense size of our country, and in the second place by reason of the very large number of people who come to be naturalized. But neither of those things has any bearing upon the question of the discretion of the Secretary of State. We might go back to the old system under which it was so absolutely simple that men who had no comprehension of what they were doing and with regard to whom there was not any responsible person to certify that they knew what they were doing were naturalized because a paper hung on a wall in an office for three weeks.
But you can let the paper hang now. You are following the same procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The paper would hang, but the man would also have to go before a judge and adduce evidence. Whether he goes personally or otherwise, he will have to prove to the judge that these things are true. At present the judge says: 'Nobody opposes; you are naturalized.'

The hon. Minister of
Justice is wrong. The applicant must produce affidavits taken before a stipendiary magistrate that he is a respectable citizen of reputable character.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And those affidavits the judge need not read.
But when he does read them, as you are going to make him do now.
Why do you not trust his judgment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do trust his judgment. The hon. member has only come in since I gave the explanation of the position of the judge. I trust the judge on the one thing he decides; and the Secretary of State will take as absolutely decided what the judge has decided that the man has met all the requirements of the Act; but if the Secretary of State knows of other things which are good reasons why this man should not have a certificate, are we going to tie his hands? That is the question. All this means is, that the Secretary of State is not under absolute obligation to hand out the certificate of naturalization, because an

applicant has succeeded in making his way through the procedure. It is a power that I have no doubt will be seldom or never exercised; but it is a power that, when the occasion comes that it is desirable that it should be exercised, will be an important one.

Does the minister say
that under the present Act the applicant must now go personally to the court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is most assuredly not the case. Just let us look at the things with which we trust the minister, now. The Secretary of State or the Governor in Council now can appoint a man as a commissioner to take affidavits under the Naturalization Act. I do not want to say that every one of these commissioners is not thoroughly respectable, but they are exceedingly numerous. What is the guarantee you have now? The commissioner takes the oath of the applicant; and if he is satisfied, he gives a certificate to that person of the taking of the oath. Then that person takes the certificate or some other gentleman takes 400 of them; goes down to the office of the court and hands them in, and they are hung up on- the wall where they stay for three weeks. At the opening of the court the names are read out; and ten days afterwards, or whenever the close of the court comes, the clerk -says to the judge, ' 400 applications for naturalization; is there any opposition?' And then-

The person's counsel
must -make application?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just let me read the
statute. It may be that in many instances counsel do go and -make application; but here is what the statute says -shall be done, -and what, I am credibly told, is done. You may have as many counsel as you like; but under this statute if the counsel gets up and says and the clerk affirms it: There is no opposition, then the judge's certificate goes. Therefore a judge is not called upon to verify one -thing except that that paper has hung on the wall -and that nobody has come to make an objection.
What about the affidavits?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He is not obliged to
verify them. I think he would not be failing in his duty in the slightest degree if he did not verify them, because the law prescribes that he is to verify one thing, namely, that there is no opposition.
What is the good of the affidavit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the present Act, I do not know. I want to improve the Act.
I may tell the Minister of Justice that the judges in our part of the country will ask if the counsel or solicitor has the affidavits, and will call upon him to read them in court.
The affidavits are made part of the record of the court; and, if a man commits perjury, he will be prosecuted.

Of course, a man may be prosecuted for perjury, but we are speaking of what is done at the present time. Here is what the court is bound to verify:
Where no opposition has been filed to the naturalization of an applicant, and no objection thereto is offered during the sittings, the court on the last day of the sittings shall direct that the certificate of the applicant be filed of record in the court.
No doubt there is a penalty afterwards on a man who swears falsely; but we ate speaking about trying to provide protection that there shall be proof that a man has complied with the requirements. You can punish that man afterwards, tout he will have exercised his privileges as a British subject; and who is going to take upon himself to investigate the truth or falsehood of the affidavits with a view to punishment? Can any hon. member show me a case where somebody has gone to that trouble?

I can point the Minister of Justice to a case where I was refused a naturalization certificate because I did not have a certain affidavit, which I was supposed to produce in court, in the nature of a certificate from a justice of the peace or a stipendiary -magistrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Did anybody object to
the naturalization in question?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then I say that the judge did a very praiseworthy thing, but the judge is under no obligation to do it. If you will look at section 15 of the present Act you will see who it is that has to be satisfied:
The alien shall adduce, In support of such application, such evidence of his residence or service, and intention to reside or serve, as the person before whom he takes the oaths aforesaid requires; and such person, on being satisfied ,with such evidence, and that the



alien is of good character, shall grant to such alien a certificate in form B.
So that a person, who has no qualification but that he has been appointed a commissioner to take oaths, is the one who has to be satisfied. What does the judge do? The judge says, ' Is there any opposition?' No. Then the law says: You shall confirm that certificate, solely because there is no opposition. I do not know whether hon. gentlemen think that that is a proper course and that that is better than requiring that a man shall make proof before a judge.
I do not quite understand that the procedure is so slipshod in our part of the country as the hon minister thinks it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not say what the judges do. I am pointing out what under the statute is the limit of their obligations. I am glad to learn that they do very much better than the statute calls upon them to do.
They do just what the statute requires them to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The statute says that if there is no opposition the judge shall confirm the certificate.
If there are no affidavits-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there is no certificate, the judge cannot confirm it. But the commissioner having administered the oath that is required, and sent it in, the judge must confirm it if nobody objects.
There is no change in the procedure under this Bill.

I could give several instances illustrating the point. Two months ago the commissioners prepared the affidavits of upwards of one hundred Italians. They got certificates from other Italians as to character. These affidavits with the applications were presented to the judge, and the judge granted naturalization in batches at a time-a batch of one hundred at one time, and at others fifty or twenty-five. I know of applications made to another judge. Realizing that the applicants were of a character who should not be naturalized, yet not being in a position to refuse, he simply withheld his decision. In other words, he exercised his discretion and refused to grant naturalization by refusing to give a decision in the matter.
Then, the hon. gentleman does not agree with the minister that the judge has no discretion under the present law ?
I say he exercised his discretion by simply refusing to give his decision.
But the minister says he must not refuse.

If he makes a decision, he must make it in favour of the applicant. The judge told me that by not acting was the only way in which he could avoid naturalizing those who were unworthy. That judge urged me to bring forward matters relating to naturalization which, I am glad to see, are covered by this Bill. As to the discretion given to the Secretary of State, I would oppose the Bill if that clause were not in it. I could give this House many illustrations of why .a provision of that kind should be retained in the Bill. As the Minister of Justice has pointed out there are many questions of policy on the part of this country which it might be unwise to discuss in a public way, and none know better than those hon. gentlemen opposite who have been in office and have dealt with these troublesome matters, the grave difficulties that present themselves when you are dealing with questions of naturalization and immigration.

Wherein does the procedure under this Bill differ from that under the present law? The minister says that the applicant need not appear personally-just as under the present law. Under the law the applicant has to produce an affidavit that he has been ini Canada continuously for three years-it is now extended to five years-and intends to continue living in Canada. He presents also a certificate of good character. Under the old procedure these affidavits were placed on record at the court either at the beginning or at the close of the session. All this is just what is required under this Bill.
