There is an increase here of $20,000. This is contingent upon the extension of the Dominion Lands Service which causes a corresponding increase in the contingent expenditures. This covers advertising, printing and stationary, travelling expenses of outside service officials including inspectors of Dominion Lands agencies; expenses of forest rangers, timber inspectors and homestead inspectors, including travelling outfits, also freight, express, telegrams and unforeseen expenses.
Protection of timber in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories and the railway belt in British Columbia, tree culture in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and inspection and management of forest reserves, $660,000.
Is the increase in connection with the general protection and management of timber, or in connection with the forest reserves?

There is an increase in respect of tree planting from $57,000 to $61,000, in round figures; an increase in respect of the administration of the forest reserves from $239,000 to $259,000; an increase on fire ranging from $181,000 to $211,000; an increased expenditure at the head office consequent upon the enlargement of the service, $38,000 to $40,000, and an increase in respect of the forest products laboratories.

What success has the department met with in regard to tree planting?
262i

Tree planting is conducted at the Indian Head nursery, and we have opened a branch lately at Saskatoon, which is largely the cause of the increase. Trees are being very numerously distributed through the Northwest, and I believe that in recent years the work has been very successful. I do not just recall the number of trees that were planted last year, but I think that the number runs into the hundreds of thousands. We are having an increased demand for trees, year after year, from farmers, principally in the- provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
What kind of trees do you plant?
I have not a list of them, but I think the elm and the maple are the two principal varieties.

I think that the department of the minister has been rather too comprehensive in its setting apart of forest reserves. I notice on a map of Alberta recently issued that a forest reserve has been laid out northwest of Edmonton, between the Athabaska river and Lesser Slave lake. I am quite aware that there is a territory there, a considerable area of which is, in all probability, not suited for agricultural purposes, but I notice that this reserve takes in a country which, if all reports be true, embraces quite an agricultural area. This territory is closely skirted by a railway line now under construction. I think that that reserve is of an entirely unwarranted area and that it takes in a large amount of country that certainly should not be reserved from settlement. At this particular time, when the prairie country available is largely occupied and when the homestead entries are going down, I think it is an unfortunate policy to make reservations of land that is properly suitable for agriculture and should be available for that purpose.

The Bill that was introduced this session amending the Forest Reserves Act did not make provision for any additional forest reserve in the province' of Alberta, so that this reserve must have been created last year.
It may have been created last year, but it was not mapped. It appears on the map of this year.

These lands are first set aside temporarily and prior to their inclusion as forest reserves they are examined. The report of the forestry reserve experts

that the area embraces land suitable for the purposes of reforestation and unfit for agricultural purposes must be received before the lands are incorporated by Act of Parliament as a forest reserve. I quite agree that if lands are suitable for agricultural purposes they should be kept outside the reserve, but if the judgment of those officers who examine and set aside those reserves is correct, they do not include agricultural lands.

The map shows that a projection of this reserve comes within about half a mile of the shore of Lesser Slave lake. My information is that there is a broad belt of territory between the shore of the lake and the foot of the hills. I notice that there is a large reserve declared north of Lesser Slave river and this reserve immediately south of the river, so that there is only a small neck of land available for agriculture along the Lesser Slave river. There is a railway going through that district, the rails are already laid and that railway is simply cut off from settlement through the creation of this reserve. We have numerous complaints of people being distant from railroads; it is a great drawback to the progress of out country where people axe distant from railroads and the great hope is that railroads will 'be constructed. But here is a railroad actually in operation and the land all along its western side for a distance of some 50 to 75 miles is simply cut out from settlement. I think that that is a m03t unfortunate reservation and I submit that the matter should be looked into. If there were no railroad there, it might be that the land would be unsuitable for some reason for agricultural purposes, but with a railroad right alongside, unless the land is very unsuitable it certainly should be available for settlement in the interests of the country, as well as in the interests of the railroad.
Mr. ROOH'E:	I understand that the
examination of this land was made in 1911, that it was temporarily set aside and that the Act was passed by Parliament last session. The examination went to show that it is a very high and hilly part of the country and that the reserve was, no doubt, set aside prior to the coming of the Tailway into that territory. I do know some places in the province of Manitoba where railway lines run right through reserves, which are shut off from settlement. I am quite at one with the opinion of the hon. gentleman that if the lands are at all suitable for 
settlement they should not be included in the reserve. But these lands were reported by the forestry department as being unsuitable for agriculture; the examination was made, of course, prior to the construction of the railway.

I would strongly urge that an examination be made of the eastern and north-eastern limits of this reserve called the Lesser Slave Lake Forest Reserve, that part of it contiguous to the railway, with a view of withdrawing it if it is found to be reasonably suitable for settlement.
There have been no protests thus far.

Of course, the railroad has only just been constructed; there is plenty of vacant land in that vicinity yet and nobody would need to go in there at the moment, but I wish to put on record my protest and to say that I think an examination should be made with a view to withdrawal.

I think that agricultural land is included in some of the forest reserves, more particularly in the Rocky Mountain forest reserve. At the present time it is not required for agricultural purposes, but with the coming of railways and the development of some of the coal areas, this land will in ten years perhaps, be required for agricultural purposes. I presume it will be withdrawn if required for that purpose. I want to ask about the grazing of sheep. About 1883 an Order in Council was passed prohibiting the grazing of sheep in the area between the international boundary and Highwood river. Is that still in force?

An Order in Council was passed some years ago, and I think it still stands. Some alterations of that Order in Council have been under contemplation, but have not yet gone into effect. I understand that the lands within the reserve have been withdrawn.
So they are now available for grazing sheep? Is it proposed that the sheep shall be under fence or are they to run at large?

The forest reserves are not fenced.
Mr. WARiNOCK: There is liable to be difficulty between the cattle men and the sheep men. If the sheep are grazed on these reserves they should be under fence.

I understand that an
association has recently been formed which wishes to discuss this question of grazing within the forest reserves, and the head of the Forestry Branch is going out to confer with them shortly.

Clause 53 of the grazing regulations makes provision against trespass and imposes increased tolls in case of trespass. It is rather a hardship to find the owners of stock guilty of trespass if they allow stock within the boundaries of forest reserve, especially when the stock have been entering these reserves for years past and the reserves are not fenced.
The regulations are held in suspension pending the conference I have mentioned.
I shall call on the minister and discuss the matter with him, so as not to delay the committee.

It would be very unfair that the department should enforce trespass against stock going on unfenced property. That right is not given to the ordinary citizen, and should not be claimed by the Government. If the Government desire to lease rights on forest reserves, that is perfectly proper; but if they are going to enforce trespass they should fence the property.

How far are the Government prepared to admit responsibility for the results of government in the parks? There is the town of Banff and the Government have seen fit to take the responsibility of providing what may be called modem facilities in that town-the paving of streets, sidewalks, waterworks and fire protection. I am informed that last winter a large hotel and, I think,
11 p.m. some other buildings, were burned down chiefly because of the lack of water pressure owing to the hydrants being frozen up. Are the Government willing to put themselves in the same

position as an ordinary municipality and assume responsibility for this, or will they stand on their rights as a government in defence of their position?

An ordinary municipality, where the hydrants were frozen up, would not be under any legal liability for the loss of a building burned down and I do not see why the Government would be in a worse position. Does the hon. gentleman contend that the municipality would be legally liable for loss by fire 'because the fire could not be put out?

Yes, if the fire fighting apparatus were not in proper working order. I have seen cases where action has been taken against a municipality under exactly similar conditions. The Government having taken upon itself the responsibility of a municipality I want to know if they are willing to assume the liabilities as well?

My information is that
there was no liability until negligence or carelessness on the part of the Government had been established, and these facts were not established 'by an investigation.

Of course, that is an investigation by the Government of itself. Is the Government going to stand on its rights as a government or will it accept the ordinary position of a municipality? I am only asking for information because the people ought to know where they stand. The Government has seen fit to take the responsibility of a municipality and I want to know.

I understand the departmental position in regard to this question was that if the facts were established fixing the responsibility upon us or, if it was shown that there was negligence or carelessness on our part, it was the intention of the *department to take up the point referred to by the hon. member for Edmonton with the Department of Justice in order to estab-iish What liabilities the Government were resting under. The question 'has actually not been determined.

The Government having
held an investigation on itself and found itself not guilty has decided not to do any-tnung more. I think that is hardly a fair position. The occasion having arisen I would suggest that the department, without waiting for further action in this particular ease, have the question decided by the Department of Justice so that people living in such a place as Banff will know whether

they may look for redress or not, I think it is a proper thing to have decided without any further delay.
Protection of reindeer herd, $3,000.

What reindeer herd is
this?

I am sorry to say we have not obtained very good results from our reindeer experiment. We purchased a herd of fifty reindeer from Dr. Grenfell in 1911, which were shipped from Labrador to the Fort Smith country on the Great Slave river. There were seventeen lost in transit and thirty-three were landed, but only eleven remain now. The trouble is largely with the flies in that country, which cause them to stampede, and they have not yet been rounded up.
What number of buffalo have we?

We have 1,500 and they
are increasing quite substantially. There are 152 more than last year, the increase being 700 since the herd was purchased.

Immigration-contingencies in Canada, British and foreign agencies and general immigration expenses, $1,450,000.

The information that is
current through the country is to the effect that we have more people here just now than we have work for, and while the suggestion is not particularly appropriate to this item, I want to say that in my humble judgment the Government would be well advised to take more drastic action than they have yet taken to deal with the question of the increase in the labour supply. There is no doubt that somewhat unfortunate and serious conditions exist. I would take the liberty of saying that the Government is very much to blame for that condition, in not having exercised greater discretion than they did last year. However, that harm has been done, the people are here and the difficulty is facing us. I certainly think the Government should take more drastic action than they have yet taken to prevent until conditions change, any further increase of people looking for work in Canada.

The present policy does not differ from that which has been in existence for a number of years. We advertise only for agricultural labourers and domestic servants, and in all our literature we emphasize the fact that no other class of labourers should come to Canada without assured employment. Recently I read a copy of a circular to the House which was sent to all the agents and to the steamship companies and was disseminated broadly throughout the motherland, stating that we did not require skilled or unskilled labourers to come to Canada at present. In addition to that and quite recently, I have given instructions for the following advertisement to be inserted in a number of the old country papers:
Owing to the world-wide financial stringency and the consequent curtailment of large works of development, the Government of Canada finds that there are now in the Dominion sufficient artisans and skilled and unskilled labourers to carry on all contemplated works during 1914, and consequently advises persons belonging to the above-mentioned occupations and desiring to emigrate to Canada,, to postpone such action until normal conditions again prevail. Demand was never stronger for farm labourers and female domestic servants, and these may come forward with the full assurance of finding work immediately upon arrival. There are also many excellent openings for farmers with capital.
I have taken means to disseminate this information throughout the countries from which we draw immigrants. Therefore I

think the Government have not been at all remiss in their duty in calling attention to the state of things, so far as the classes of immigrants are concerned that we are not desirous of encouraging to come to Canada.

Yet it is a fact, according to what I read this morning, after the meeting that took place yesterday of the labour unions of Montreal, that there are thousands of unemployed in that city, who evidently belong to that class of immigrants who come from central and southern Europe. The other day, when the mayor of Montreal convened the unemployed in order to listen to their grievances-I am glad to see him come in just now-he was obliged to employ five or six interpreters to explain to those unfortunate people that he would do his best to find work for the heads of families. His worship the mayor can speak English and French fluently, but it was found that, amongst those thousands of people, six different languages were spoken. Every day on the Champ de Mars at Montreal, you will see by the newspapers, there are thousands of men convening and clamouring for work or bread. It seems to me that, although the action taken by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior is very wise, it should be more drastic. We have certainly passed through a very serious crisis, unknown before in the annals of this country. I am told that the Angus shops, which are generally very busy, have closed their doors during the past winter, and even during this spring, and that not less than
2,000,	perhaps 3,000 men, have been refused work. The same is true with regard to the Canada Car Company, and other large industries in Montreal. The steamship companies ought also to be instructed to refuse to accept immigrants unless they came as agriculturists or as domestic servants, because all the large centres-I am speaking of the city of Montreal, but the same tale can be told as regards Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg and Vancouver-are glutted with the unemployed. I am more or less connected with the charities in Montreal amongst the Catholics, and last winter they strained every nerve to meet the situation. We have the St. Vincent de Paul Society, the Refuge de Nuit, and various other organizations, and we are simply feeding at present the immigrants who have come during the last few months from central Europe. It seems to me that at present the Government could do no better than to take very drastic measures to prevent the unfortunate immigrants from adding first to 
our miseries, and then to theirs. The mayor of Montreal is here, and I wish he would give his own explanation in regard to the matter.

I am not able to explain myself very well in the English language, but I have never seen such a situation in Montreal since 1896. I heard ttus morning of a foreman employed m the Angus shops, who used to have 700 men working in his department, but who has now only thirty-five. Every day we meet on the Champ de Mars about 4,000 people asking for work, and there are people sending me letters stating that, if I do not get them work, they will kill me. I am not afraid of such threats. Since I took office, the first week I gave employment to 6,000 people, the second week to 8,000, and last week I had 12,895 men working for the city. I think this week I shall have 15,000; but I am not able to do everything alone; I must have help from somewhere. I am very sorry to see the way things are going; and I think the Government ought to do something. I have received a delegation, with Mr. St. Martin at its head, asking us to give the people vacant lots to cultivate. 1 think it is the duty of the Government to go down to Montreal and assist these people to go out West. The shoemakers have been out of work since last November. There is no construction going on; everything is stopped. I do not know what is the matter, but I think we have too much protection and not enough people in the West. In 1911, when I was speaking to my electors, I said that under this Government this state of affairs would come about in two years, and that is what has happened. It is not only in Montreal, as my hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) has said. I have met men in the car going to Montreal who have told me that the same thing is true in Vancouver, Winnipeg and Sault Ste. Marie. People are coming to Montreal because they think Montreal is able to employ everybody in the whole country.
What wages are being paid to the city labourers in Montreal?
$2.25 per day.

Have you advertised
that pretty well?
We have never advertised that at all.

You will get lots of
people if you do.

I do not think $2.25 per day is too much, considering the present high cost of the necessaries of life. I think that question must be settled, and those who are responsible for it are the Government-nobody else. Why do not they start the work on the harbour? A few days ago $9,000,000 was voted. But though the weather has been fine and that work might have started six weeks ago, everything in the harbour is stopped. Why? We do not know. I have asked the Prime Minister to give orders that that work should go ahead in order to help these people. This Government may be very able but it is not very lucky. As soon as these hon. gentlemen came into power everything started to go down. If the Department of the Interior will make known among these people that there are good farms for them in the West, and will assist them to go on the land it will be a good thing for the country as a whole and certainly for these people.

I think that the experience of the hon. member simplifies the saying, ' It pays to advertise.' If I read the Montreal newspapers correctly, the hon. member on being elected mayor of the city advertised very extensively that he would find employment for all who desired it.
That is what we are trying to do.

The result was that people who were out of employment not only in Montreal but in other places in the province of Quebec rushed in seeking employment at the wages the hon. gentleman offered which were higher than the current rate. In any other city, were the mayor so indiscreet as to issue a similar advertisement, 1 am sure many unemployed would be found. He displays more anxiety to place responsibility on the Government than to improve conditions. If there is anybody who is more responsible than others for the large number of unemployed in Montreal ,t is the hon. gentleman himself with his indiscreet advertisement offering the unemployed more than the market rate of wages. Everybody knows that the same conditions do not obtain in such cities as Winnipeg and Vancouver. Building permits show that there is more building in Winnipeg than there has ever been before in the history of the city. But when we have the chief magistrate of Montreal putting in such an advertisement as he did, we know that he is not interested in doing away with unemployment so much as in making political capital.

I took the course I did because when I was elected mayor I found so many people out of employment and some of them robbing people in different parts of the city. I took the responsibility of ordering work to proceed to the value of $1,500,000 without the regular vote of the board of control and the city council.

Did not some Montreal newspapers accuse the hon. gentleman of putting in an advertisement that had the effect of causing people to give up their employment and seek employment in the service of the city?

No. In Montreal there has been a great deal of unemployment; every trades union has men out of work, and this condition has continued since last November. I never advertised to the effect my hon. friend has stated. I do not care what the newspapers say, for many times they do not tell the truth. When I was elected, I tried to help every one; I took the responsibility of ordering work to go ahead, as I have stated. It is not only in Montreal that there is unemployment, but in every city in Canada.
Nonsense.
The hon. member may call it ' nonsense,' but everybody knows that what I have stated is the truth.

I think it a pity that the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) should undertake to minimize a condition which exists and which certainly requires attention at the hands of the Government and of everybody interested.
Mayors.

Yes, mayors and ail who occupy responsible positions. It is a very serious situation and it is necessary it should be dealt with. I did not wish to take up so much the actual condition as to urge upon the minister the necessity to take measures under the immigration laws to prevent the situation from being accentuated. While the hon. gentleman has told us that he carried out the plans that prevailed some years ago, the conditions have changed since then. There is an acute condition which requires drastic measures to meet it. The minister shall certainly have my support, and I think he will have the support of hon. gentlemen on this side in taking drastic measures to prevent the condition from being ac-

oentuated by immigration at this time. It is a peculiar feature of the case that immigrants from iCentral and Southern Europe who were formerly almost entirely agricultural and went upon the land, today apparently are not going on the land but are immigrating for the purpose of getting work in the towns. That is a new condition and one that should be met. I read in the newspapers the other day of the arrival of some vessels with immigrants from Southern Europe. These people may be under circumstances to go on the land, but I fear very much that a large proportion of these people are going to toe simply an added burden upon the labour and charity of this country. We may have a recovery, conditions imay toe better next fall -I hope so, tout if we do not have that recovery, every immigrant who comes in looking for work is going to simply accentuate the condition of last winter which "was not too good. I say I take this opportunity of urging upon the minister not to insist on simply following the precedent of two or three years ago when conditions were different, but to be ready to meet the special conditions of to-day with special measures. There has been a change all along the line. 'The people have not been going on the land in recent years as they have been formerly. Whether it is because we are getting a different class of people or what may be the reason, the fact is they have been going into the towns rather than on the land and consequently there is congestion in the towns. I know there is in Edmonton and that fact calls for the attention not only of the civic authorities and provincial governments but of the Dominion also, and especially in regard to immigration. We are not finding fault with what has been done: let that pass if you like. But the question of what ought to be done in the future is what I wish to impress upon the minister.

The immigration returns
do not bear out what the hon. gentleman has said about the tendency of immigrants coming in in large numbers yet not going on the land in the same proportion as formerly. The number of homestead entries has been falling during the last two or three years, but the proportion of immigrants from continental countries going upon the land and getting homestead entries has kept up. For instance, out of
44,000	entries from all countries three years -ago, 8,700 were continental immigrants. In

the following year, out of 39,000 homestead entries, 9,000 were made by continental immigrants. The number of homestead entries dropped down to 33,699 during the last year, of which 7,757 were made by immigrants from continental countries, so that just as large a proportion of those coming from continental countries have gone upon the land as* heretofore. Another thing to bear out that contention is the fact that we pay bonuses only to those going upon the land and to domestic servants. Although we have had a large immigration from the continental countries, the number of arrivals last year being 112,881, we paid bonuses on 1,928 only. As a matter of fact, immigration has fallen off very considerably this year; there is no doubt that a good many of those who were in the cities were formerly engaged ini railway construction and came to the cities because during the money stringency the railway companies engaged in construction work have been laying off hands or have completed their lines. But many of these people could get employment in the country if they would only go and take it. I understand that many persons in Winnipeg who could get situations on the land if they would accept the same, but many of them will not do so. As the hon. member for North Ontario has said, a great many persons have flocked into the city of Montreal from outside points, having been attracted by the promise made by the mayor that he would find employment for those who were out of work. We do not encourage those who go to the cities and towns. I have impressed upon the steamship companies the desirability of their not bringing any immigrants outside of the classes upon which we are paying bonuses except those who are coming to assured employment. In an 'address which I delivered to 300 or 400 persons in Montreal I impressed upon the representatives of the steamship companies that we were not encouraging any persons to come except the classes upon which we are paying bonuses. Notwithstanding the fact that there is a big falling off of immigration this year, we are urged by hon. gentlemen opposite to take drastic steps to prevent certain kinds of immigration; next session I venture to say that they will make capital against the Government by reason of the falling off of immigration.

It is certainly to be regretted that there are many people in the

city of Montreal and in other cities seeking work and unable to get it. At the same time, there is a certain measure of retributive justice in it; it is the logical result of a policy which has been followed by both parties in this country for years. A policy which fixes an eight-hour day on government works is a policy which is calculated to drive men off the farms and into the cities. The eight-hour day is an im-possiblity on the farm; every gentleman in this House knows that what I say is true. Is it not natural that boys should leave the farm and come to the city under these conditions ? You fix an eight-hour day on government work; labour unions fix their eight-hour day; wages are fixed, as the hon. [DOT]member for St. Marys, Montreal, said, at $2.25 for an eight-hour day, and I presume it is so in that city. You cannot get a man to stay on the farm where he has to work twelve or fourteen hours a day, twelve hours a day at the least; he sees that the man in the city has an eight-hour day and he at once heads for the city. Petitions, largely signed, are presented to Parliament urging upon members to put through legislation favouring the shortening of the hours of labour beyond what is a possibility on the farms, and that has a tendency to drive men away from the farm and into the city. I do not think it is wise legislation. Perhaps from a political standpoint it would be unwise for a man representing a city constituency to oppose a largely-signed petition asking for legislation fixing an eight-hour day. As I do not represent a city constituency, I am, of course, able to speak more freely along this line than, perhaps, some others are. Permit me to repeat that the tendency of our legislation along the line of shortening the hours of labour in the city beyond what is possible on the farm has had the logical effect of inducing the men to go from the country into the city and that, to a certain extent, is responsible for the conditions that exist to-day in respect of employment.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that $2.25 is too much for a labouring man in the city of Montreal?

No, I do not say that $2.25 is too high a wage, but I do say that $2.25 for an eight-hour day is a rate of wage which it is impossible to pay in the country. I do not think that I am extravagant when I say that a twelve-hour day is about as short as you can possibly have on a
farm. If you establish the same rate in the country for the twelve-hour day as you pay in the city for the eight-hour day, it means a wage which the farmers cannot pay, and the natural tendency is for the people to drift into the city I am quarrelling not so much with the $2.25 for eight hours as with the eight hours itself. I think the eight-hour day is too short a day in the city, and that we have made mistakes in the past in listening to the demands of unions and others for an eight-hour day. There are certain occupations where an eight-hour day is quite long enough, perhaps too long. In such an occupation as mining, the hours of labour should be exceedingly short, but I say most emphatically-and I believe that I express the feeling of many people in the country districts-that an eight-hour day for a carpenter or a mason is entirely too short.
Those who get $2.25 a day work ten hours a day.
I am speaking of the eight-hour day on Government work.

In regard to the question of immigration from central and southern Europe, my hon. friend says that he advises only those who are looking for labour on the land to come to this country. I think that the condition is such that he should not advise even those who are looking for labour on the land to come from central or southern Europe, because it is not convenient for those people to secure employment as labourers on the land.
They are not likely to get employment. Those people have come here ostensibly to look for employment on the land but really to get railway work. They are not suitable for farm labourers. Many of those who came in former years had cash sufficient to go on the land. People of that kind would be all right to-day, but those who are looking for employment on the land are not likely to get it because, owing to their lack of knowledge of English and so on, they are not suitable for that employment. The condition to-day is similar to that in 1907 when the Government of that day adopted radical restrictions against the coming to Canada of too many of these people. The conditions to-day call for severe and drastic action to prevent too large an influx this year, certainly from southern and central Europe. There is not the same demand for that class of labour to-day as there was a few years ago. My hon. friend says that the records show that these people

are settling on the land. I need only say that the unemployed in the cities of the West are very largely that class of people. That is evidence to me that they are not going on the land.
Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, $175,000.

There is a good deal of talk as to two members of this board retiring, and there is also a suggestion that the size of the board is to be reduced. There are other rumours as to the gentlemen who are to become members of the Railway Board. In fact it is a current rumour that a member of the present Government is to go on the Railway Board. Are two members to be succeeded by other members or is the board to be reduced in size?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. D. REID (acting Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext: The vacancies, of course, will be filled. I have not heard anything as to increasing or decreasing the size of the board. The Minister of Railways has been away for some little time and I do not know what his intentions are. This is the first I have heard of any member of the Government being appointed to the board.

The rumour is that the hon. the Minister of Inland Revenue is going to be appointed there soon to replace Mr. Bernier. But there are others who say that Mr. Bergeron is entitled to that position. The hon. member should not forget him, he did yeoman service for the party when he sat in the House. In the case of Dr. Mills, some effort should be made by the Government to utilize the services of a man of his experience. I am told that the salary of Dr. Mills and of Mr. Bernier ceased in January. It is felt .by the litigants and the railway companies that the experience of a man like Dr. Mills is very valuable indeed and that something should be done for him at his age, after the service he has rendered his country. It is really too bad to think that he should be left penniless now and without any employment. I am told that the commission would be only too pleased to retain his services in connection with their work.

I do not think there is any truth in the report as to the Minister of Inland Revenue being appointed to the board. As to Mr. Mills, I understand that since his time expired as a commissioner he has received a salary of $3,600 per year as librarian to the commission. I understand that Chief Commissioner Drayton arranged this and that it was quite satis-

factory to Mr. Mills. I have had no conversation with Mr. Mills. I had to sign the Order in Council to make the appointment, and it was on a letter from Mr. Drayton to me as acting Minister of Railways and Canals asking me to recommend it to Council. I suppose Mr. Mills got his salary all the time.
There are two vacancies now on the board?

Yes, and when the Minister
of Railways and Canals comes back I have no doubt he will take the matter ulp.
Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada -to pay expenses in connection with cases before, $25,000.

Mr. MoKENZIE:	I find amongst the

tion for the hon. member within a couple of days.
Governor General's cars-attendance, repairs and alterations, $2,500.

How many cars have
you now?

extra car was bought when His Royal

they must have three now.

'Mr. GRAHAM: There is a great difference of opinion about that. He has displayed a remarkable versatility of talent. One position succeeds another. Rideau canal-repairs and replacements of dams, $30,000.

There was some discussion three or four years ago about the Hydro-Electric Commission, as to whether some powers on the Rideau could be used for electrical purposes in eastern Ontario. Has anything been done about that?
There has been nothing done on the Rideau canal. They have taken up no powers or anything of the kind.

Early in the present
session, I suggested to the Minister of Railways and Canals the advisability of considering the lighting of the Rideau canal from Brewer's Mills to the city of Kingston. Mr. J. M. Campbell of Kingston has leased the power at Kingston Mills, and has erected a power house there with the intention of supplying Gananoque and the township of Pittsburg, between Kingston Mills- and Gananoque, and I thought that possibly the same gentleman might supply power to light the canal between Kingston Mills and the city, and also between Kingston Mills and Brewer's Mills. I received from Mr. Campbell an estimate as to the cost of that work. The initial cost was, according to this estimate, very much more than I had the slightest idea it would be; in fact it was so great that it would seem to me to put the idea out of question. Whether the canal could- be lighted from Kingston, Mills to the city from the power at Kingston Mills, at a reasonable cost for installing the poles and wires, is a question which I think the Government might very well consider. The installing of electric lighting from Kingston Mills to Brewer's Mills would, from the information I have, be very much more costly in' the matter of erecting the poles than it would be from Kingston Mills to the city. I have the estimate of Mr. Campbdl for that, and if the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham,) would like to look it over I am sure he would understand the matter much more easily than I would.
I shall be glad to see the estimate.

I should be glad to
have the hon. gentleman's opinion on it.
Canals-concrete facing, dam at Valleyfleld, $26,000.

The hon. gentleman from
Beauharnois (Mr. Papineau), I understand, wished to ask me a question about this.
I have a statement as to the expense already incurred by the contractor, and I want to submit that the deposit which was confiscated should be refunded.

The hon. gentleman mentioned to me the amount the contractor had expended, and I stated to him that I would recommend that the deposit should

be refunded. That is the way the matter stands, and I will try to arrange it.
Trent canal-construction, $1,250,000.

I would like to know from the minister, what the condition of the work is, and how long it will take to complete. -There is another matter on which information should be given by the Minister of Justice before the Estimates are through. The Seymour Power Company have secured control of a good many powers on the old Trent canal system, and the newly developed power, under an arrangement the details of which I need not give now. I believe litigation between the Dominion and the province of Ontario is now before the courts. As I understand it, one of the large insurance companies is financing to a certain extent the Seymour Power Company, and there is a question of the rights of the power company being taken over by the Hydro-Electric system of Ontario. The Seymour Power Company have a network of wires, and are distributing power in the East quite largely. It is of course immaterial to the people who supplies the power, so long as they get it at a fair rate, and under the old arrangement with the Seymour Power Company, in order to safeguard the people, their rates were placed under the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Ontario Government have contended that the right in these powers is vested in the province, generally speaking, ,and the Dominion took exception to that contention. As a matter of fact, only a few years ago the Ontario Government had a staff of inspectors or caretakers at the different dams, and it paid them to look after these dams and for conserving the water at different points. They were justified in this because they received fees and dues from the lumbermen, and it was the business of the provincial Government to pay the caretakers. Voluntarily, some six years ago, the Ontario Government gave up to the Dominion all its rights in these dams, and were delighted to get rid of them because they had no revenue from which to pay for the care of them.
The supervision of them.

The Order in Council is quite sweeping and it shows they wanted to get rid of them. A little later the only power the Ontario Government then claimed they leased to one Culverwell at the rapids in the vicinity of Campbellford. Later Cul-verwell's rights were cancelled and the

Ontario Government desired to have the power vested in them. It is a question between the Dominion Government and the provincial Government. The Dominion Government contended that the Trent was in a different position from almost any of the other waterways in the Dominion and that the title, owing to the peculiar. conditions existing as to riparian rights and other circumstances, was vested in the Dominion. I would like the minister to be able to give us a statement from the Minister of Justice as to what the case was that was submitted to the courts, whether any decision has been given, and what stage the proceedings are in at present. I would like him to inform the House what powers have been developed over and above these now owned by the Seymour Power Company, how much more are expected to be developed and what this Government proposes w do with these powers. In other words, do they propose to hand them over to the province ot Ontario? I am not arguing they should or should not, but we ought to know what is to be done with these powers that are being developed as incidental to the construction of the Trent canal.

I know that the Minister of Justice has brought the matter before the courts but it has not yet come to trial. I will certainly get the minister to give me a full statement, so that I can have it for the hon. member before we take up any of the other items. There has been a good deal of trouble along the Trent canal in connection with the work. At Campbellford there has been some trouble on account of the removal of the dam of the Trent Valley Woollen Company. I think that matter came up in the hon. member's time. I have had quite a little trouble in regard to the dams all along the canal. Claims are coming in to have the dams renewed, and so on. I will have a full statement of that made, so that I shall be able to discuss the matter with the hon. member and give him all the information possible.

Can the hon. member
tell us the actual condition of the work on the canal? When will the Severn division be completed?

A contract was let a short time ago for the Severn division of the Trent canal. We had six tenders, of which the lowest was $130,278, and the contract was awarded to the York Construction Company, the lowest tenderer. I am informed by the chief engineer that there
are two more sections to let to complete the outlet into Georgian bay.
How long will it take to complete?
About four years yet before it will be completed and ready for operation.
What will be the total cost of the Trent Valley canal?

The Ontario and Rice lake division will cost about $7,000,000, and the Severn division about $3,000,000. There is another section in the interior that will have to be deepened, namely from Peterborough to Lake Simcoe. It is only six feet deep at present. No estimate has been made of that so far.
If that part is not deepened, how much will the canal cost?

$10,000,000, plus the original
cost.
What is the plus?

From the time the work was started until the end of 1913, we have spent on the Trent canal $12,464,651.64. That includes the Ontario and Rice lake division as being practically completed. We shall have to add to" that the Severn division, $3,000,000. Therefore the total cost will be probably $16,000,000. If we deepen that part from Peterborough to Simcoe, of which no estimate has yet been made, the cost of that will have to be added.
If you deepen that, you will have to have more conservation work on the lakes.
Not necessarily.

There is some riprap
work being done on the canal from Balsam lake to lake Simcoe. Will the minister tell us whether that work is going on this summer, because it is very important that the sides of the canal should be preserved by this riprap? A number of men were employed last summer. Will any be employed this summer?
That is only repair work; and if any is necessary, it will be done by the repair gang.
Does that come under the general improvements?
Yes.
The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) wishes to discuss something in connection with Campbellford, but I presume that can be done under the other item?
Yes.

The other night we
passed an item in regard to the Chambly canal. I remember on one occasion voting some money for the construction of a bridge at Iberville. Is any work being done on it?

There has been an item of
$52,000 in the Estimates for the last three or four years, on condition that the Quebec Government and the municipalities pay a certain amount towards this bridge. Nothing has been done up to the present time by the Quebec Government or by the municipalities, and therefore the item has been dropped this year. If the other parties are willing at any time to go ahead with their proportion, we shall then renew the vote.	*

I was under the impression that an arrangement had practically been arrived at by which the other parties were willing to contribute, and that a deputation had urged the Government to consider putting that item in the Supplementary Estimates. Of course, my hon. friend cannot say whether that will be done or not, but does he know of any such arrangement being reached?

One day last week a deputation asked me about this vote; and I explained to them that it was dropped, because nothing had been done for the last three or four years, although the vote had been in the Estimates. I also stated to them, that if the parties interested would do their share, I had no doubt that the Government would renew the vote.

We might take up the items under capital expenditure on the Intercolonial railway. The item 'Halifax-new terminal facilities' might be allowed to stand, as both members for Halifax are absent, and there will probably be some discussion on that item. Then the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), wishes to discuss the item with regard to the shops at Moncton. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), wants to discuss the item relating to Mulgrave, and another hon. member desires to discuss the Sydney Mines diversion. The chairman might take up these items from the

beginning, and there may be others that I shall ask to stand. While I am on my feet I might call attention to the fact that capital expenditure on the Intercolonial railway is called for by this Government just as it was by the late Government. I took a sane view of this capital question and after the next election, when the hon. member (Mr. Reid), is not acting minister or anything like that I hope he also will have sane views on the subject.
I am getting a lot of light.

The Intercolonial railway, so far as my experience goes, does not encroach on the principle of proper capital expenditure any more than a railway company does. It may have done so years ago-I am not discussing that, for I do not know. When, for a short time, I was head of the Railways Department we secured the basis upon which the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States settled capital expenditure and tried to adopt the same principles, except that at that time we used money out of revenue for works that the Interstate Commerce Commission would not let the company pay for in the same way. In a work on railway finance which I have read, the author lays it down that even a nail driven that is new and adds to the value is capital expenditure. The principle is sound. Under the new methods adopted on the Intercolonial railway, in laying aside a certain amount for renewal of equipment account and rail renewal account, money was taken out of revenue to the full extent that would be allowed if you applied the rules of the Interstate Commerce Commission. I suppose the acting minister can assure me that all this proposed capital expenditure is of that kind. I should hate to see the Government backsliding on this matter because the principle is a safe tine.

I believe the policy adopted by the hon. member is continued by the Intercolonial railway; there has been no change. I agree with him that the Intercolonial railway are charging to capital account such items as he speaks of. For instance, we have $900,000 appropriated for the strengthening of bridges. That work is necessary because the heavy engines and cars have made the old bridges dangerous.
You have to take out the wooden ones which you wanted to keep on the National Transcontinental.
These are iron.
But there are wooden ones you have to take out.
Yes.

We want to make you
confess these things before we put through the Estimates.

over the Canada Eastern railway they were operating two lines of railway along the south and north sides of the southwest Miramichi river within a short distance of each other. and facilities at, $40,000.

Has the hon. gentleman had correspondence with a company that has some device for the elimination of accidents to a considerable extent? Has he made any tests on the Intercolonial railway during the past year and if not, has he any idea of making an appropriation to provide for such tests?

I have had correspondence
with some company; I forget the name of it. We are having tests made on the Intercolonial railway, but no reports have been made as yet. I shall have full information on the subject before the Estimates come up again.

I see that some important railway companies in the United States have adopted the Marconi system on trains with considerable success. Has my hon. friend any experiments in this line on the Intercolonial railway, or does he intend to make any?

I noticed in a paper the other day a despatch stating that the system had been tried on the New York Central lines, I think, and had worked very well. We have done nothing on the Intercolonial railway; in fact, I do not know whether any of the other railways in Canada have tried it. At all events, it has not been brought to my attention either by any one interested in the matter or by the management of the Intercolonial railway.

From St. John to Hampton, 20 miles; Moncton to Painsec Junction, 7 miles; Windsor Junction to Halifax, 14 miles; Truro to Oxford Junction, 46-5 miles.

The heaviest part of the
work will probably be finished next year. I

M. REID: We will have it established where, the traffic is heaviest.
Intercolonial railway-installation of telephone system in connection with operation, $64,000. '

How is the telephone
system working out?

The amount voted for 1913-14 is sufficient to cover the installation of a telephone system between St. John and Truro. A contract has been awarded to The Hall Switch and Signal Company for the installation of the system between Moncton and St. John and tenders are being asked for its extension from Moncton to Truro. We have not got it under operation as yet. -
Intercolonial railway-elimination of level crossings and grades, $100,000.
What are you doing in Moncton under this vote?

The railway runs through the heart of the city of Moncton and in consequence there are a number of dangerous level crossings. The amount asked for it is to start work with a view of doing away with these crossings, as well as bettering the grades through the yard. Several proposals are under consideration but, it has not been finally decided which will be the better, from a railway point of view. The plans have not been made out as yet, but the item has been put in order that we may be enabled to start work as soon as we get plans satisfactory to the city and to the railway.
You are not going to put any more tracks on the level through the city?

No.
Intercolonial railway-rolling stock, $1,000,000.
Does the minister have the same trouble about other railroads stealing cars and not bringing them back?
Yes, the same old trouble.

What rolling stock is
required?
576 steel frame box cars at $1,190 each; 20 vans, steel frames, at $1,950 each; 24 passenger refrigerator cars at $1,850 each; 4 special cars for carrying

heavy members for the Quebec bridge, $2,000 each; one motor inspection car, $200; six consolidated type locomotives at $25,500, and five switch engines at $16,600. The orders were given this spring. The orders for the locomotives go to the Kingston Locomotive Works.
Is there any official car in this?
No, not in this.

I cannot think why the Minister of Customs does not have a special car. The Minister of Public Works got a nice new one, a Yankee car it is true, and the Minister of Militia got himself a nice one. He did not have any vote for it. The Minister of Railways is setting a bad example in getting cars first and getting the supply afterwards. I understand that specifications have been asked for another new one for the Prime Minister. The Minister of Customs has nothing. After he gets, out of his temporary estate he will ibe merely a side issue compared with the other members of the Government. Is there no way in which he can get up his courage to make some recommendation along that line? He is now in the department with full power. Perhaps he might have car 28 made over and given to him.
I had the pleasure of using car 28, I think, once-

That would be enough.
Mr. REID-and that satisfied me with using private cars. Therefore I have not had any desire to have one for the Customs Department since. I think I had better continue to do as I am doing.

This is to improve the accommodation at a great number of places along the line, most of the votes running between $1,000 and $3,500.
